# CS 3410 Software Engineering — Assignment 2  
## Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

**Student ID:** `<studentid>`  
**Semester:** Fall 2026  

---

## 1. Context and Scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s existing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three campus libraries. Students will search for rooms, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with three external systems: the university identity provider using SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The system must also provide utilisation reports for library staff.

This design covers the first release of the application architecture, deployment approach and quality plan. It does not specify detailed user-interface designs, infrastructure vendor selection or the implementation of every business feature. The key architectural concerns are correct enforcement of reservation rules, reliable integration with external systems, fast availability searches, timely kiosk updates, secure staff auditing and simple operation by a two-person team.

The selected primary architectural style is **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a single deployable modular application. The domain and application logic will be independent of frameworks, databases and external services. Infrastructure concerns such as SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email/push delivery and kiosk connections will be implemented as adapters behind explicit ports.

---

## 2. Architectural Decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **hexagonal architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture.

The system will have:

- A framework-independent **domain core** containing reservation entities and business rules.
- **Application services** that coordinate use cases such as searching, creating reservations and creating block bookings.
- **Inbound ports** representing supported use cases.
- **Outbound ports** representing required external capabilities.
- **Adapters** for HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, notifications, reporting and kiosk updates.
- A single deployable application and primary relational database for the first release.

The domain core will not import web frameworks, database libraries, SAML libraries or notification providers. This separation is particularly important for QR-5: reservation rules can be tested using in-memory objects and fake ports without a database or network.

The architecture may use an internal transactional event or outbox mechanism to notify kiosks and reminders after a successful reservation change. This is an implementation technique within the hexagonal design, not a change to the primary architectural style.

### 2.2 Rationale and quality trade-offs

#### QR-1: Availability

A single deployable application is simpler to operate and can be deployed with at least two application instances behind a load balancer. Health checks, database backups and rolling deployment reduce downtime. Kiosk adapters will use a local cache of the most recently received schedule. If a kiosk loses connectivity, it will continue displaying the cached schedule with its last-updated time rather than showing an empty or misleading screen.

Hexagonal boundaries also allow external systems to fail independently. For example, a temporary iCal failure need not prevent users from viewing or creating reservations based on the last successful synchronisation.

The trade-off is that a single application remains a shared failure domain. A severe application or database failure could affect searching, reservations and reporting at the same time. This is accepted for the first release because the operational simplicity benefits a two-person team.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability search will use a dedicated read path through a repository port. Room inventory and normalised calendar data will be indexed by campus, capacity, equipment and time range. Frequently requested room metadata and opening hours may be cached. The application can scale horizontally by adding application instances without changing the domain model.

The design avoids requiring every search request to call the legacy inventory database or facilities calendar. Those systems will be synchronised by background adapters, so the search path remains predictable.

The trade-off is that synchronised data may be slightly stale. The product owner must define the acceptable freshness of inventory and calendar data. Reservation creation will perform an authoritative conflict check against the CLRS reservation store rather than trusting a search result.

#### QR-3: Security

Authentication is represented by an inbound authentication port. The SAML adapter validates assertions from the university identity provider and maps them to a CLRS user and role. Application services perform authorisation checks, so access control is not dependent on a particular HTTP framework.

Staff operations will create audit records through an audit port. Audit records will contain the staff identity, action, target resource, timestamp, outcome and correlation ID, but not unnecessary personal information. General application logs will use pseudonymous user identifiers or one-way request identifiers rather than names, email addresses or SAML assertions.

The trade-off is additional implementation and testing around identity mapping, role changes and audit completeness.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Libraries, opening hours, equipment categories, room metadata and calendar mappings will be configuration data rather than hard-coded branches. Adding a library will therefore require a configuration and data migration or import, not a code change. The inventory and facilities adapters will use configured endpoints and campus identifiers.

The trade-off is that configuration becomes a controlled product artefact. Invalid configuration could affect an entire campus, so it requires schema validation, review and deployment checks.

#### QR-5: Testability

The domain core will expose operations such as:

- `checkAvailability`
- `createReservation`
- `modifyReservation`
- `cancelReservation`
- `createBlockBooking`
- `calculateDailyUsage`

These operations will receive time, user, room and reservation data through interfaces or in-memory repositories. Tests can use fake implementations of outbound ports. Consequently, rules such as the three-hour daily limit, overlap prevention, staff block-booking precedence and 48-hour notice can be tested without a database or network.

The trade-off is that the team must maintain explicit interfaces and mapping code between domain objects and persistence models. This is more design work than directly placing rules in controllers or database queries.

#### QR-6: Operability

A modular monolith is suitable for a two-person team. It has one application build, one main deployment pipeline and fewer distributed-system failure modes than microservices. Container images will be immutable and deployments will use a versioned database migration process. The previous image remains available for rollback, and the deployment process will be rehearsed to complete rollback within ten minutes.

The trade-off is less independent scaling and deployment. Reporting workloads, for example, share the application and database with reservation traffic. This can be mitigated using read replicas, scheduled report generation or separate worker processes if measurements show a problem.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives

**Method A — Layered monolith:**  
This would be simple to deploy and understand, and it would support QR-6 well. However, traditional layers often allow business rules to become coupled to controllers, ORM models or database concerns. It provides weaker protection for QR-5 and makes replacement or testing of SAML, iCal and legacy database integrations less explicit. Hexagonal architecture retains the operational benefits of a monolith while enforcing stronger dependency boundaries.

**Method B — Microservices:**  
Separate reservation, inventory, notification and reporting services could provide independent scaling and fault isolation. However, the system would require service discovery, authentication between services, distributed tracing, deployment coordination and more complex data consistency. Reservation conflict checking and block-booking overrides would be harder to make atomic. These costs are inappropriate for QR-6 and the two-person operating team at the initial scale. Microservices may be considered later if independent scaling becomes measurable.

**Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS:**  
An event log and projections would naturally support fast searches, kiosk updates and asynchronous notifications. It could improve QR-1 and the ten-second kiosk requirement. However, event ordering, replay, eventual consistency, projection recovery and operational support add significant complexity. A search result could temporarily lag behind a reservation command, and reporting would need projection-management processes. For the first release, an indexed relational read model plus an outbox is sufficient. Full CQRS may be introduced if performance or kiosk scale requires it.

---

## 3. Structure

### 3.1 Container/component diagram

```text
+------------------+       +------------------+
| Student/Staff UI |       | Kiosk clients    |
+--------+---------+       +--------+---------+
         | HTTPS                   | HTTPS/SSE or polling
         v                         v
+------------------------------------------------------+
|                 CLRS Application                    |
|                                                      |
|  HTTP/SAML Adapters                                  |
|       |                                              |
|       v                                              |
|  Inbound Use-Case Ports                              |
|       |                                              |
|       v                                              |
|  Application Services                                |
|   - Search rooms                                     |
|   - Manage reservations                              |
|   - Manage block bookings                            |
|   - Manage rooms/opening hours                       |
|   - Generate reports                                 |
|       |                                              |
|       v                                              |
|  Domain Core                                         |
|   - Reservation rules                                |
|   - Conflict checking                                |
|   - Daily usage limit                                |
|   - Block-booking precedence                         |
|       |                                              |
|       v                                              |
|  Outbound Ports                                      |
|   - Reservation repository                           |
|   - Inventory provider                               |
|   - Calendar provider                                |
|   - Notification provider                            |
|   - Audit sink                                       |
|   - Kiosk update publisher                           |
|                                                      |
|  Outbox/worker: kiosk updates and reminders          |
+----------+------------------+------------------------+
           |                  | 
           v                  v
+------------------+  +-----------------------------+
| CLRS PostgreSQL  |  | External-system adapters    |
| reservations,    |  | SAML IdP                   |
| rooms, audits,   |  | iCal facilities feeds      |
| outbox           |  | Legacy PostgreSQL inventory|
+------------------+  | Email/push provider        |
                      +-----------------------------+
```

The application is one deployable unit, although background workers may run as a separate process from the same image. All dependencies point inward toward the domain and application layers. The domain core does not depend on adapters.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: search available rooms

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates the request format and invokes the search inbound port.
3. The application service checks the authenticated user context and validates the time window.
4. The service calls the inventory, opening-hours and reservation repository ports.
5. The repository uses indexed CLRS data containing synchronised room metadata and reservations. It excludes rooms whose capacity or equipment does not match, rooms outside opening hours and rooms with overlapping reservations or block bookings.
6. The adapter maps domain results to a response containing room ID, campus, capacity, equipment and available time.
7. Metrics record the request duration, result count and status code, without recording personal data.

The search result is advisory. When a user submits a reservation, the application performs a new transactional conflict check to prevent two users reserving the same room based on stale search results.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk schedule updates

1. A reservation, modification, cancellation or block booking is committed through the reservation application service.
2. The transaction writes the change and an outbox message containing the room ID and schedule version.
3. A worker publishes the update to connected kiosk clients using server-sent events or makes it available to the polling endpoint.
4. Each kiosk stores the complete last-known schedule and its version locally.
5. On receiving a newer version, the kiosk replaces its cached schedule and displays the current and next reservation.
6. If the kiosk cannot connect, it continues displaying the cache and clearly shows its last refresh time.
7. The target is that at least 99% of kiosk changes are visible within ten seconds. Retries and an update backlog metric identify failures.

---

## 4. Quality Plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

**Unit tests:**  
The domain core will have the largest test suite. Tests will cover:

- Reservation overlap and boundary-time rules.
- Three-hour-per-day limit.
- Create, modify and cancel permissions.
- Recurring block bookings.
- 48-hour notice requirement.
- Block bookings overriding affected student reservations.
- Opening-hour validation.
- Equipment and capacity matching.
- Time zones, daylight-saving changes and month boundaries.

These tests use in-memory entities and fake clocks, repositories and event publishers. They directly satisfy QR-5.

**Application-service tests:**  
Using fake outbound ports, these tests verify orchestration, transaction behaviour, authorisation, idempotency, audit creation and outbox creation. Examples include rejecting unauthenticated users, auditing staff actions and ensuring a failed notification does not undo a committed reservation.

**Adapter and integration tests:**  
Containerised PostgreSQL tests will verify schema constraints, indexes, transactions, optimistic locking or unique conflict constraints, migrations and report queries. Adapter tests will cover SAML assertion validation, role mapping, iCal parsing, inventory synchronisation and notification-provider behaviour. Network failures, malformed feeds and expired credentials will be included.

**Contract tests:**  
Contracts will define the HTTP API, error codes and event/outbox schemas. Consumer-oriented tests will verify that web clients and kiosks can rely on response fields, schedule versions and cache behaviour. The SAML and notification integrations will use provider test environments where available.

**End-to-end tests:**  
A small stable suite will run against a deployed test environment. It will authenticate test student and staff accounts, search, reserve, modify and cancel a room, create a block booking, verify an audit record and confirm a kiosk update. It will also test offline kiosk behaviour and reminder scheduling.

**Performance and resilience tests:**  
A load test will simulate 2,000 concurrent users at semester-start traffic levels, with particular focus on search p95 being below 400 ms. Tests will include cache-disabled and normal operating modes. Resilience tests will disconnect iCal, the inventory database, notification delivery and kiosk connections to verify graceful degradation.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use short-lived feature branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer where practical.

Continuous integration gates are:

1. Formatting, static analysis and dependency vulnerability checks.
2. Domain and application unit tests.
3. Adapter and database integration tests.
4. API and contract tests.
5. Build of an immutable versioned container image.
6. Deployment to a temporary test environment.
7. End-to-end smoke tests.
8. Performance checks on scheduled builds and before major releases.

A failed gate prevents merging. Database migrations must be backward compatible during rolling deployment: add new structures first, deploy compatible code, migrate data, then remove obsolete structures in a later release.

Production deployment will use a rolling or blue-green approach with health checks. The previous container image and configuration will be retained. A release is considered successful only after smoke tests, error-rate checks and reservation-conflict checks pass.

Rollback will be initiated if health checks fail, error rate exceeds the agreed threshold or reservation correctness is compromised. The process is:

1. Stop promotion of the new version.
2. Route traffic to the previous version or redeploy its image.
3. Confirm application and database health.
4. Verify search and reservation smoke tests.
5. Record the incident and preserve logs.

A rollback rehearsal will be performed before launch and must complete within ten minutes to satisfy QR-6.

### 4.3 Observability

**Logging:**  
Structured logs will include timestamp, severity, service version, operation, status, duration, correlation ID and campus/room identifiers where appropriate. Staff audit records will include actor role, action, target, result and timestamp. Logs will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, session tokens or reservation notes containing PII. Access to audit logs will be restricted.

**Metrics for QR-1:**

- Availability and health-check success by application instance.
- HTTP 5xx rate and request failure rate.
- Database connection failures and transaction rollback rate.
- SAML authentication failure rate.
- Outbox age, retry count and dead-letter count.
- Kiosk update delay from reservation commit to client acknowledgement.
- Number of kiosks offline and age of each kiosk’s last successful update.
- iCal and inventory synchronisation success and freshness.

Alerts will fire for five consecutive minutes of elevated 5xx responses, failed health checks, a growing outbox, kiosk updates exceeding ten seconds, or synchronised data exceeding its agreed freshness limit. Monthly availability will be calculated during opening hours; the operational objective is stricter than 99.5% to provide margin.

**Metrics for QR-2:**

- Search request count and latency percentiles, especially p50, p95 and p99.
- Search latency separated by campus and cache-hit status.
- Database query latency and slow-query count.
- Active users, request rate and connection-pool utilisation.
- CPU, memory and database resource usage.

An alert will trigger if search p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten minutes under normal traffic, or if load testing shows failure to meet the 2,000-concurrent-user acceptance target. Dashboards will show latency alongside traffic and resource saturation so that alerts are actionable.

---

## 5. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Likelihood / impact | Measurable trigger | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legacy inventory database is unavailable or has inconsistent room data. | Medium / High | Two consecutive synchronisations fail, or more than 1% of room records fail validation. | Store a timestamped local synchronised copy; validate imports; retry with backoff; alert staff; define a manual correction process. |
| Facilities iCal feeds are delayed, malformed or contain conflicting events. | Medium / Medium | Feed age exceeds four hours, parser rejects more than 1% of events, or duplicate/conflicting events appear. | Isolate feed parsing in an adapter; retain the last valid feed; quarantine invalid events; alert operations; confirm authoritative conflict policy with the product owner. |
| Concurrent requests create double reservations. | Medium / High | Any production incident shows overlapping confirmed reservations, or concurrency tests produce one incorrect result. | Enforce transactional conflict checks and database constraints; use idempotency keys; run race-condition integration tests; monitor overlap-detection reports. |
| Search does not meet the 400 ms p95 target at semester start. | Medium / High | Load test exceeds 400 ms p95 with 2,000 users, or production p95 exceeds 350 ms for ten minutes. | Add composite indexes and read caching; precompute availability data where appropriate; profile slow queries; scale application instances and database resources. |
| Kiosk updates exceed the ten-second requirement. | Medium / High | More than 1% of updates take over ten seconds, or outbox age exceeds 30 seconds. | Use an outbox with retry and idempotent schedule versions; support polling as a fallback; persist local kiosk cache; alert on stale kiosks and backlog growth. |
| SAML configuration or role mapping is incorrect. | Medium / High | Authentication failure rate exceeds 2% for known test users, or a staff test action lacks the expected role/audit record. | Test against the identity provider before release; use explicit role mapping; provide a break-glass operational account process; never bypass authentication in production. |
| Notification provider failure causes missed reminders. | Medium / Medium | Delivery failure exceeds 5%, or a reminder remains queued within ten minutes of its scheduled send time. | Use an outbox and retry policy; make notification delivery asynchronous; record delivery status; provide email fallback where permitted. |
| Configuration-only campus onboarding is error-prone. | Medium / Medium | A new-campus dry run requires code changes or configuration validation reports any missing mandatory field. | Define a versioned configuration schema; validate in CI and at startup; create an onboarding checklist and dry-run import; require peer review. |
| Two-person team cannot safely operate the system. | Medium / High | Rollback rehearsal exceeds ten minutes, or an on-call task requires undocumented manual steps. | Automate deployment, backups, health checks and rollback; maintain runbooks; rehearse incidents; keep the initial deployment as a modular monolith. |

---

## 6. Open Questions for the Product Owner

1. What is the authoritative source when CLRS, the facilities calendar and the legacy inventory database disagree?
2. How fresh must room inventory and iCal data be for the search results to be considered valid?
3. When a block booking overrides student reservations, what notification and refund or dispute policy applies?
4. Does “48 hours’ notice” mean 48 hours before the first affected reservation, each occurrence, or the block-booking creation time?
5. What time zone and daylight-saving rules apply to reservations across campuses?
6. Are kiosks permitted to use server-sent events, or must they use polling only?
7. What is the expected maximum number of kiosk clients and the expected semester-start request profile?
8. Which staff roles may manage rooms, create overrides and export reports?
9. What retention period and access policy apply to audit records and utilisation reports?
10. Which email and push notification providers are approved, and what delivery guarantees are required?
11. What information may appear on a kiosk, particularly concerning user names or reservation titles?
12. What is the required backup recovery-point objective and recovery-time objective for the reservation database?

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the existing study-room reservation tool used across three university libraries. Students and staff will search for rooms, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks located outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities calendars supplied through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The system must support reservation limits, conflict detection, staff overrides with 48 hours’ notice, utilisation reporting and kiosk updates.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify the complete implementation or detailed user-interface design. The main architectural goals are:

* reliable reservation and conflict rules;
* availability search with predictable performance;
* graceful kiosk operation during network failures;
* secure authentication and staff auditing;
* onboarding of additional campuses through configuration;
* testability of business rules without infrastructure; and
* deployment and rollback procedures manageable by a two-person team.

The selected primary style is **hexagonal architecture**, implemented as a modular monolith. The system will initially be packaged as one deployable application artifact, with API and background-worker processes using the same codebase and release version.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C — Hexagonal architecture**, with a framework-independent reservation domain at the centre. The application will be separated into domain logic, application use cases, ports and infrastructure adapters.

The system will use:

* a relational database owned by CLRS for reservations, campus configuration, opening hours, audit records and report data;
* read-only adapters for the legacy inventory database and facilities iCal feeds;
* a SAML identity adapter;
* an outbox table for reliable delivery of reservation-change notifications;
* a kiosk update channel using server-sent events (SSE), with polling as a fallback;
* a background worker for reminders, calendar synchronisation, report generation and outbox delivery; and
* a kiosk client that stores the last-known schedule locally.

The API and worker may run as separate processes for operational reasons, but both are built and released as one versioned application. This avoids the operational overhead of independently deployed microservices in the first release.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation rules are the most important business logic: time-overlap detection, the three-hour daily limit, staff block-booking precedence and the 48-hour notice rule. These rules will be implemented in pure domain objects and services that depend only on in-memory values and abstractions. They will not call a database, HTTP client or SAML provider. Unit tests can therefore execute the rules without a database or network.

For example, an application service receives a reservation command, loads relevant reservations through a port, invokes the domain policy, and persists the result through another port. The domain policy can be tested independently using fake values and deterministic clocks.

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A modular monolith has fewer network and deployment failure points than a distributed microservice system. The reservation database will have automated backups, health checks and a highly available managed deployment where available. Kiosks will cache their most recent valid schedule and display its timestamp when disconnected. Reservation changes will be written to an outbox in the same database transaction as the reservation, preventing a successful reservation from being lost before kiosk or notification processing.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability search will use indexes on campus, room attributes and reservation time ranges. A dedicated availability query adapter will avoid loading the complete domain object graph for every search. Frequently requested room metadata and opening-hour configuration may be cached with short expiry. The architecture allows performance-sensitive read queries to be optimised without changing the reservation domain.

A load test will validate p95 search latency below 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users. Search results will be paginated and limited to the requested time window.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
SAML authentication is isolated behind an identity-provider port and adapter. The application will accept only authenticated identities and will derive staff permissions from approved SAML attributes or a controlled staff-role mapping. Staff operations will create immutable audit records containing actor identifier, action, target type and timestamp. Application logs will use opaque request and entity identifiers rather than names, email addresses or SAML assertions.

The hexagonal boundary also makes it possible to substitute a test identity adapter without weakening production authentication.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus, library, room, equipment, opening-hour and calendar-source information will be configuration data rather than hard-coded branches. Adding a library will involve creating configuration records, importing its inventory and configuring its calendar source. Generic adapters will handle all campuses. Campus-specific integration differences, if unavoidable, will be isolated behind adapter implementations rather than spread through the domain.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A single release artifact is simpler for a two-person team to build, deploy, monitor and roll back than several independently versioned services. Database migrations will be backward-compatible and run separately before application activation. Releases will use a rolling or blue/green deployment, depending on the hosting platform. The previous application version will remain available until health checks pass, allowing rollback within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simpler to start and would also support QR-6. It was not selected because conventional layers often allow business rules to become coupled to web frameworks, ORM entities and database details. That would make QR-5 weaker: tests of reservation rules could require database setup or mocking infrastructure.

A layered monolith could achieve similar results if carefully designed with dependency inversion, but that design would effectively introduce the ports-and-adapters principles selected here. The chosen architecture makes those boundaries explicit. The trade-off is additional interfaces, adapters and structural discipline for a small first-release team.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. This might help QR-2 if search traffic greatly exceeded transactional traffic. They would also provide stronger isolation between failures.

However, microservices introduce network calls, distributed tracing, service discovery, multiple deployment pipelines and cross-service consistency problems. A reservation change would need to propagate reliably to kiosk, notification and reporting services. These costs conflict with QR-6 and increase the risk of missing QR-1 during partial failures. Microservices also make end-to-end and contract testing more important and operationally expensive. The first release does not have enough scale or team capacity to justify that complexity.

The selected design gives up independent service scaling and process isolation. If later measurements show that search or reporting requires separate scaling, the ports and application boundaries provide a path to extract a module.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

Event-driven CQRS would be well suited to kiosk updates, reminders and high-volume search projections. An event log could provide an excellent audit trail and allow read models to scale independently.

The costs are eventual consistency, event-schema versioning, replay and projection-recovery mechanisms. A user could create a reservation successfully but see stale search results until projections catch up. This complicates conflict handling and operational diagnosis. An event broker and event-log platform would also increase the deployment burden under QR-6.

The chosen design uses a limited transactional outbox and asynchronous workers, but not a full event-sourced or CQRS architecture. It gives up the scalability and replayability of a complete event-driven design in exchange for simpler consistency and operations.

---

## 3. Structure

### 3.2 Components

**HTTP/API adapter.**  
Exposes endpoints such as:

* `GET /rooms`;
* `POST /reservations`;
* `PATCH /reservations/{id}`;
* `DELETE /reservations/{id}`;
* `POST /block-bookings`;
* `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule`; and
* `GET /reports/utilisation`.

It validates request shape, maps authentication information and converts application results into HTTP responses. A reservation conflict returns HTTP 409.

**Application use cases.**  
Use cases include SearchAvailability, CreateReservation, ModifyReservation, CancelReservation, CreateBlockBooking, GetKioskSchedule and ExportUtilisationReport. They coordinate ports and transactions but do not contain infrastructure-specific code.

**Domain core.**  
The domain contains Reservation, BlockBooking, Room, TimeWindow, OpeningHours and policies such as ReservationConflictPolicy and DailyLimitPolicy. It enforces:

* no overlapping reservations for a room;
* no reservation exceeding three hours per day per user;
* valid opening hours;
* staff block-booking precedence;
* 48 hours’ notice for affected student reservations; and
* valid modification and cancellation permissions.

The domain uses an injected clock so time-dependent rules can be tested deterministically.

**Ports and adapters.**

* `IdentityPort` authenticates users and provides roles.
* `ReservationRepository` stores and retrieves reservation data.
* `RoomInventoryPort` reads room and equipment information.
* `FacilitiesCalendarPort` imports external calendar information.
* `NotificationPort` sends email or push reminders.
* `KioskSchedulePort` publishes or retrieves current room schedules.
* `AuditPort` records staff actions.

The PostgreSQL adapters, SAML adapter, iCal adapter and notification provider are replaceable infrastructure implementations.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. The client sends campus, capacity, equipment and time-window parameters to `GET /rooms`.
2. The API adapter authenticates the user through the SAML session and validates the parameters.
3. The SearchAvailability use case loads campus configuration and room data through `RoomInventoryPort`.
4. The availability query obtains opening hours and existing reservations through read-optimised repository queries.
5. The query excludes rooms whose attributes do not match, whose opening hours do not cover the requested interval, or whose reservations overlap the interval. Block bookings are treated as unavailable.
6. The API returns available rooms and relevant metadata.

The query uses database indexes and avoids invoking the full domain aggregate for every room. The create-reservation use case still performs an authoritative transactional conflict check, because search results may become stale between search and booking.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk update

1. A reservation, modification, cancellation or block booking is committed to the CLRS database.
2. The same transaction writes a room-specific change record to the outbox.
3. The worker reads the outbox and updates the kiosk schedule cache, then publishes a change notification through SSE.
4. The kiosk receives the new schedule and stores it locally with a version and timestamp.
5. If SSE fails, the kiosk polls the schedule endpoint. If the server or network is unavailable, it displays the locally stored schedule and clearly shows that it is last known.
6. Monitoring records the time from reservation commit to kiosk acknowledgement. The target is less than ten seconds for at least 99% of changes.

Outbox records are idempotent, using a unique event/change identifier so retries do not create duplicate updates.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

**Unit tests.**  
Unit tests cover the framework-independent domain core and application use cases with in-memory repositories and fake clocks. Important examples include:

* overlapping and adjacent reservation intervals;
* the three-hour daily limit;
* recurring block-booking expansion;
* 48-hour notice calculations;
* opening-hours validation;
* modification and cancellation permissions;
* campus configuration rules; and
* kiosk schedule version handling.

These tests directly satisfy QR-5 because they require neither a database nor a network.

**Adapter and integration tests.**  
Database integration tests run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance. They verify transaction boundaries, unique constraints, time-range queries, indexes, migrations, outbox atomicity and rollback behaviour. Adapter tests verify SAML response handling, iCal parsing, legacy inventory queries and notification-provider integration.

Concurrency tests will issue simultaneous reservation requests for the same room and time window. Exactly one conflicting reservation must succeed.

**Contract tests.**  
Contracts will define API request and response schemas, error codes, authentication expectations and kiosk schedule versions. Consumer-driven tests will verify that the browser and kiosk clients continue to work with the API. Provider contracts will cover the notification adapter and any external identity or calendar assumptions. These tests are particularly important because the kiosk may be updated on a slower release cycle than the server.

**End-to-end tests.**  
A small suite will run in a production-like environment using a test SAML identity provider. It will cover login, search, create/modify/cancel, staff block booking, conflict responses, kiosk refresh and reminder scheduling. End-to-end tests will not attempt to cover every business-rule combination; those combinations belong in unit tests.

**Performance and resilience tests.**

* Load test availability search with 2,000 concurrent users and verify p95 below 400 ms.
* Test reservation writes under concurrent conflict.
* Disconnect kiosks and verify last-known schedule behaviour.
* Stop the worker and verify that outbox records remain pending and are processed after restart.
* Simulate unavailable SAML, iCal, legacy inventory and notification services.
* Test restore from database backup and rollback of the application version.

CI will publish test results and fail the build on critical test failures, security findings or performance-regression thresholds.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer where practical. CI gates are:

1. formatting, static analysis and type checks;
2. unit tests;
3. adapter and database integration tests;
4. contract tests;
5. dependency and container vulnerability scans; and
6. a smoke test of the deployable artifact.

The application is built once into an immutable versioned container. Deployment proceeds to staging, where migrations and end-to-end tests run. Production deployment uses a blue/green or rolling approach with health checks for API, database connectivity, worker heartbeat and outbox processing.

Database migrations must be expand-and-contract migrations: add compatible schema first, deploy code, migrate data if necessary, and remove obsolete fields only in a later release. This prevents rollback from being blocked by an incompatible schema.

Rollback is performed by directing traffic to the previous application version and stopping the faulty worker. The release process includes a documented one-command rollback and a pre-release backup. The target is completion within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6. Feature flags will allow risky functions, such as a new notification provider, to be disabled without a full redeployment.

### 4.3 Observability

Logs will be structured and correlated using a request ID and reservation-change ID. Logs may include campus, room identifier, operation, outcome, latency and error category. They must not include names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions or other PII. Staff audit records are stored separately with controlled access and retention.

Metrics include:

* API request count, error rate and latency by endpoint;
* availability-search p50, p95 and p99 latency;
* reservation conflict rate;
* database connection, lock and query latency;
* worker heartbeat and queue/outbox depth;
* age of the oldest outbox item;
* kiosk SSE connection count and polling rate;
* kiosk schedule update latency;
* number and age of kiosks using last-known data;
* reminder success, failure and retry counts; and
* uptime during configured library opening hours.

Alerts include:

* monthly availability projection approaching the 99.5% QR-1 budget;
* search p95 above 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal or load-test traffic;
* five-minute API error rate above 2%;
* any outbox item older than 30 seconds;
* kiosk update latency above ten seconds for more than 1% of changes over fifteen minutes;
* a kiosk remaining offline or on stale data for ten minutes; and
* worker heartbeat missing for two minutes.

Synthetic probes will periodically perform an authenticated search and a test kiosk schedule read. The service-level report will distinguish opening-hours availability from overnight maintenance.

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students can search for rooms, create or change reservations, cancel reservations and receive reminders. Library staff can manage rooms and opening hours, create recurring block bookings and export utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities’ iCal feeds and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release is intended to be operated by a two-person team, so the architecture must avoid unnecessary operational complexity.

This document covers the first-release architecture, component responsibilities, quality plan, delivery approach, observability and major risks. It does not specify implementation-level code or a complete database schema.

The main architectural concerns are reservation consistency, fast availability searches, reliable kiosk updates, secure authentication and auditing, configuration-based onboarding of new libraries, and rapid recovery from failed deployments.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Selected style

The selected primary architectural style is **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented as a modular monolith with a framework-independent reservation domain core.

The system will be deployed as one application initially. Its business rules will be isolated from web frameworks, databases and external services through ports and adapters.

The core domain will contain concepts such as:

- User and staff permissions
- Room and campus
- Reservation
- Recurring block booking
- Opening hours
- Reservation conflicts
- Daily three-hour user limit
- Forty-eight-hour block-booking notice rule

The application layer will implement use cases such as:

- Search availability
- Create, modify and cancel reservation
- Create block booking
- Synchronise room and calendar data
- Generate utilisation reports
- Publish reservation-change notifications

Ports will define interfaces required by the core, for example:

- `ReservationRepository`
- `RoomCatalogue`
- `CalendarProvider`
- `IdentityProvider`
- `NotificationSender`
- `KioskUpdatePublisher`
- `AuditWriter`
- `Clock`

Adapters will implement those ports for HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email/push providers, the kiosk channel and the application database.

This choice gives the domain rules independence from infrastructure and directly satisfies **QR-5**: reservation rules can be tested using in-memory repositories, fake clocks and fake external ports without a database or network.

### 2.2 Rationale against quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A single deployable is simpler for a two-person operations team to monitor and restart. The application can run with at least two instances behind a load balancer, avoiding a single process failure. External integrations are isolated by adapters and scheduled synchronisation jobs. If the iCal feed or legacy inventory database is unavailable, the last successful local copy is used with a freshness indicator. Kiosks retain their most recent schedule locally and display it with an “offline/last updated” status when the CLRS connection fails.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability searches will use the CLRS database’s indexed local room and reservation data rather than querying the legacy inventory database synchronously for every request. Search queries will be indexed by campus, time range, capacity and equipment. Frequently used room metadata may be cached. The application can be scaled horizontally without changing the domain model. A load test will verify p95 below 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is represented by an `IdentityProvider` port, with a SAML adapter handling assertions and mapping users to roles. Authorisation is enforced in the application layer rather than only in the controller. Staff actions produce audit records containing actor identifier, action, target type/identifier, timestamp and result. Application logs use opaque correlation IDs and do not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions or reservation notes containing PII.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific settings are stored in configuration: campus identifier, opening hours, time zone, rooms, equipment, kiosk mappings, calendar feed and notification settings. Adding a library therefore requires configuration and data synchronisation rather than a code change. The core uses campus-independent concepts and does not contain conditions such as `if campus == LibraryA`.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The domain core depends only on ports and injected services. Tests can use an in-memory reservation repository, fake identity provider and deterministic clock. Conflict detection, recurring bookings, cancellation, the daily three-hour limit and the 48-hour notice rule can therefore be tested quickly and deterministically.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
The modular monolith has one deployable artifact, one primary runtime and one main database, which is appropriate for a two-person team. Immutable container images and a blue/green or rolling deployment allow the previous version to be restored within ten minutes. Database changes will be backwards compatible so that either application version can run during rollback.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would also be simple to deploy and might provide lower initial development cost. However, conventional layered designs often allow business rules to become coupled to controllers, ORM models or database transactions. That would make **QR-5** harder to satisfy and make changes to external integrations more risky.

The selected hexagonal design gives up some simplicity in exchange for explicit ports, adapters and dependency injection. It requires more interfaces and initial design effort than a basic layered monolith. This cost is justified because CLRS has several external systems and strict reservation rules.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They could also isolate failures between those capabilities. However, they would introduce service discovery, multiple deployments, distributed tracing, inter-service contracts, network failures and more complicated data consistency. These costs conflict with **QR-6**, since only two people operate the system.

Separating reservation and search into services could also make conflict checking and read consistency more difficult. Microservices are therefore rejected for the first release. The hexagonal modules are designed so that a high-load module could be extracted later if measurements justify it. The trade-off is less independent scaling in the first release.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would naturally support fast search projections and kiosk updates. Events could also support notifications and reporting. However, eventual consistency would complicate reservation conflicts, block-booking overrides and user-visible confirmation. It would require event replay, projection monitoring, idempotency and recovery procedures.

The selected architecture gives up some of the scalability and natural fan-out of CQRS. Instead, it uses a transactional database for authoritative reservations and a transactional outbox for reliable asynchronous kiosk and notification updates. This provides much of the decoupling benefit without making reservation creation eventually consistent. The outbox is an implementation technique, not the system’s primary event-driven/CQRS style.

### 3.2 Main components

- **HTTP/API adapter:** Exposes endpoints for rooms, reservations, block bookings, kiosks and reports. It performs request validation but does not implement reservation policy.
- **SAML adapter:** Validates SAML responses and creates an authenticated user context containing an opaque university user ID and role.
- **Application layer:** Coordinates use cases, transactions and ports.
- **Domain core:** Applies reservation rules independently of infrastructure.
- **CLRS database:** Stores authoritative reservations, campus configuration, synchronised room data, audit records and outbox entries.
- **Search/read cache:** Stores query-friendly room and availability information. It is rebuilt from authoritative data if necessary.
- **Outbox publisher:** Reliably delivers reservation-change messages after the reservation transaction commits. Messages contain room ID, change type, version and timestamp, but no unnecessary PII.
- **Kiosk adapter:** Delivers updates by server-sent events or polling. Each kiosk stores the last-known schedule locally.
- **Synchronisation adapters:** Import room data from the legacy PostgreSQL database and calendar events from iCal feeds. Imports are idempotent and record source freshness.
- **Reporting component:** Computes monthly utilisation from reservation and opening-hour data, using a read-only reporting query or generated export.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&from=&to=` to the HTTP adapter.
2. The SAML-authenticated user context is passed to the application use case.
3. The application validates the time window and campus configuration.
4. The search port queries indexed local room and reservation data. It does not make a synchronous call to the legacy database.
5. The domain/application logic excludes rooms that are unavailable because of existing reservations, block bookings, facilities events or closed opening hours.
6. Results are returned with room capacity, equipment, campus and available time information.
7. If synchronised external data is stale beyond an agreed threshold, the response includes a degraded-data indicator and an alert is raised for operators.

Reservation creation performs a final authoritative conflict check in a database transaction. Search results are therefore advisory and cannot create a race-condition-based double booking.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden by a block booking.
2. The domain operation commits the reservation change and an outbox message in the same database transaction.
3. The publisher reads the outbox and sends a room-specific update to the kiosk adapter.
4. Connected kiosks receive the update through server-sent events. Kiosks that do not maintain a connection poll `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` using the schedule version.
5. The kiosk replaces its local schedule only when the received version is newer.
6. The target is that the update reaches and is rendered by the kiosk within ten seconds. If the kiosk or network is offline, it displays its last-known schedule and the time it was retrieved.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit and domain tests

The largest test suite will target the framework-independent domain core. These tests use in-memory ports and a fake clock.

They will cover:

- Overlapping reservations and concurrent conflict scenarios
- Three-hour daily limit per user
- Create, modify and cancel rules
- Staff versus student permissions
- Recurring block bookings
- Forty-eight-hour notice and override behaviour
- Opening-hours validation
- Campus configuration
- Time zones and daylight-saving transitions
- Idempotent processing of repeated commands

These tests directly satisfy QR-5 and should run on every commit.

#### Application-service tests

Application tests will use fake adapters to verify:

- Correct port invocation
- Transaction boundaries
- Audit records for staff operations
- Outbox entry creation
- Notification scheduling 15 minutes before a reservation
- Appropriate HTTP outcomes, including `409 Conflict`
- Behaviour when external data is stale or unavailable

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests will use containerised or test instances of the CLRS database to verify:

- Database schema and indexes
- Transactional conflict protection
- Repository queries
- Outbox locking and retry behaviour
- Search performance for representative data
- Import from sample iCal feeds
- Read-only access to the legacy PostgreSQL schema
- SAML assertion mapping using a test identity provider

External services will be stubbed in normal CI. A scheduled integration environment will test against approved SAML, calendar and notification sandboxes.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will be maintained for:

- The HTTP API
- SAML attribute and role mapping
- iCal parsing assumptions
- Notification provider requests
- Kiosk schedule format and version semantics

The kiosk client and server must agree on schedule versions, timestamps and offline behaviour. Contract tests prevent a server change from silently breaking deployed kiosks.

#### End-to-end tests

A small stable suite will run against a production-like environment:

1. Authenticate as a student.
2. Search for a room.
3. Create a reservation.
4. Confirm the reservation appears in search and on the kiosk.
5. Modify and cancel it.
6. Authenticate as staff and create a block booking.
7. Verify audit output and notification scheduling.

End-to-end tests will not replace unit tests because they are slower and more environment-dependent.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

Before release:

- Load-test availability search with 2,000 concurrent users and verify p95 under 400 ms.
- Test reservation contention for the same room.
- Disconnect kiosks and confirm last-known schedules remain visible.
- Stop notification and calendar dependencies and verify retries and graceful degradation.
- Run dependency, static-analysis and authentication/authorisation security scans.
- Verify that representative logs contain no PII.

### 4.2 Delivery and rollback

Development will use short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires:

- Successful compilation and formatting
- Unit/domain tests
- Application and adapter tests
- Static analysis and dependency scanning
- API contract tests
- Database migration validation
- No critical security findings
- Coverage of all changed reservation rules

A merge to `main` builds an immutable, versioned container image and deploys automatically to a test environment. Release requires approval after integration, end-to-end and performance checks.

Database migrations must follow an expand-migrate-contract process:

1. Add backwards-compatible schema changes.
2. Deploy application code that can work with both old and new schema.
3. Migrate or backfill data.
4. Remove obsolete schema only in a later release.

Production deployment will use two instances behind a load balancer. A new version is first deployed to one instance and checked using health probes and smoke tests. Traffic is then shifted gradually. The old image remains available.

Rollback is triggered by failed smoke tests, elevated error rate, SLO breach or operator decision. Traffic is shifted back to the previous image, while database changes remain backwards compatible. A rehearsed rollback procedure and pre-pulled images target restoration within ten minutes.

Structured logs will include:

- Operation name
- Campus and room identifiers where appropriate
- Outcome and error category
- Duration
- External dependency name and latency

Logs will exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, notification content and other PII. Staff audit records are kept separately from diagnostic logs and have controlled access.

#### Metrics

For **QR-1**, measure:

- Successful request availability during opening hours
- HTTP 5xx and timeout rate

- SAML authentication failure rate
- iCal and inventory synchronisation success/freshness
- Outbox backlog size and oldest message age

- Number of kiosks displaying stale schedules
- Notification delivery success rate

For **QR-2**, measure:

- Search request count
- Search p50, p95 and p99 latency
- Database query latency
- Cache hit ratio
- Request rate and concurrent requests
- CPU, memory, connection pool and database lock utilisation

#### Tracing and dashboards

Distributed/request tracing will connect an HTTP request to its database query, outbox message and kiosk update without recording PII. Dashboards will show availability, search latency, external dependency health and kiosk freshness by campus.

#### Alerts

Alerts include:

- Monthly availability budget projected below 99.5%
- Five-minute search p95 above 400 ms during opening hours
- Search error rate above 1% for five minutes
- Outbox oldest message above 30 seconds, critical above two minutes
- Any kiosk update latency above ten seconds at sustained levels
- Synchronised inventory or iCal data older than the agreed maximum

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing room-reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

The scope includes the reservation API, domain rules, persistence, external-system adapters, kiosk update mechanism, notifications, reporting and operational processes. It excludes implementation details of the university identity provider, replacement of the inventory database, and physical kiosk hardware.

The primary architectural style selected is **hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a single deployable application with separate background workers where appropriate. This provides a framework-independent reservation domain while avoiding the operational complexity of a microservice or fully event-sourced system.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture.

The core reservation domain will contain the business rules and will not depend on HTTP, databases, SAML libraries, email providers or network clients. Application services will coordinate use cases through explicit ports. Infrastructure adapters will implement those ports for PostgreSQL, SAML, iCal, notifications and kiosk delivery.

The first release will be deployed as one versioned application image with horizontally scalable instances. A scheduler or worker process may run from the same codebase for reminders, iCal synchronisation and reports. This preserves the simplicity of a small-team deployment while keeping the domain independent from technical infrastructure.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
This is the strongest reason for the decision. Reservation rules will be implemented as pure domain services and entities. For example, checking the three-hour daily limit, detecting overlapping reservations, applying a block booking and validating the 48-hour notice rule can be tested using in-memory objects. Tests do not require a database, HTTP server or external identity provider. Database and network concerns are accessed only through ports, so adapters can be replaced with test doubles.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication and authorisation are represented by an inbound security port. The SAML adapter translates an identity-provider assertion into a trusted application user and role. The domain and application layer receive a user identity and permissions rather than handling SAML details. Staff operations pass through an audit port, ensuring that actions such as creating a block booking or changing opening hours generate audit records. Logging policies at the adapter and application boundaries will redact personal data.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific information will be represented as configuration: campus identifier, opening hours, time zone, room-inventory mapping and facilities-calendar endpoint. The domain will operate on a `Campus` value rather than hard-coded campus names. Adding a new library therefore requires configuration and data provisioning, not a source-code change. The architecture also permits a new identity, notification or calendar adapter without changing the reservation rules.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
The architecture allows the search use case to use a read-optimised availability repository rather than querying the legacy inventory database for every request. Inventory and calendar data can be synchronised into CLRS-managed tables. Indexes on campus, capacity, equipment and time ranges will support the search query. The API can run multiple application instances behind a load balancer, while caching relatively stable room metadata. The 400 ms p95 target will be verified through load testing at 2,000 concurrent users.

**QR-1 — Availability and graceful kiosk degradation.**  
A single deployable is simpler to operate than several independently failing services. At least two application instances will be used during opening hours, with health checks and automatic replacement of unhealthy instances. PostgreSQL will use managed backups and high-availability facilities where available. Kiosk clients will persist their last successful schedule locally. If the server or network is unavailable, the kiosk will display that schedule with its last-updated time instead of becoming blank.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
Hexagonal architecture does not require a large distributed platform. A two-person team can build, deploy and monitor one application image and one primary database. Immutable images, automated migrations, health checks and a blue-green or canary deployment will support rollback within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would also be simple to deploy and could meet the initial scale requirement. It was rejected as the primary style because conventional layered designs often allow application and domain logic to become coupled to ORM models, controllers and infrastructure. That would weaken QR-5 and make changes to SAML, iCal or the legacy database more invasive.

The selected design gives up some of the straightforwardness of a conventional layered monolith. Ports, adapters and dependency inversion require more initial design and more interfaces. However, it retains the monolith’s operational simplicity while improving isolation and testability.

#### Method B — Microservices

Separate reservation, inventory, notification and reporting services could allow independent scaling and deployment. For example, search could scale separately from reporting. However, microservices would introduce network failures, distributed tracing, service discovery, multiple deployment pipelines and more complex data consistency. Correctly preventing two concurrent reservations would be more difficult if reservation state were distributed. These costs conflict with QR-6 and the two-person operational model.

By not choosing microservices, CLRS gives up independent service-level scaling and deployment. This is acceptable because the expected load is substantial but bounded, and horizontal scaling of the application is simpler for the first release. Service boundaries can still be introduced later if measured bottlenecks justify them.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would naturally support kiosk projections, notifications, reports and rapid search reads. It could also provide a strong historical record of reservation changes. However, it introduces eventual consistency between command handling and read models. A user could search a stale projection immediately after a booking, and conflict handling would require careful event-log concurrency control. Operating an event broker, replaying projections and diagnosing delayed events also increases complexity.

The selected architecture gives up the scalability and replayability benefits of a central event log. Instead, it will use database transactions for authoritative reservation changes and a lightweight update mechanism for kiosks. This provides stronger immediate consistency for reservation conflicts and is more appropriate for the first release. An outbox table may be added as an implementation technique for reliable asynchronous notifications, without making event-driven CQRS the primary style.

### 3.2 Main components

- **HTTP/API adapter:** exposes endpoints such as `/rooms`, `/reservations`, `/block-bookings` and `/reports`. It validates request shape, obtains the authenticated user and maps application results to HTTP responses.
- **Authentication adapter:** consumes SAML assertions and maps them to a user ID, staff/student role and permitted attributes.
- **Application layer:** coordinates transactions, permissions, repositories, notifications and audit records.
- **Domain core:** implements reservation invariants, including overlap prevention, the three-hour daily limit, staff block-booking precedence and notice rules.
- **Reservation repository adapter:** uses PostgreSQL transactions and constraints to ensure that conflicting reservations cannot be committed concurrently.
- **Inventory and calendar adapters:** synchronise room attributes, opening hours and external calendar data into CLRS-managed tables.
- **Kiosk adapter:** provides a schedule endpoint and server-sent events (SSE), with clients polling every five seconds as a fallback.
- **Notification worker:** finds upcoming reservations and sends reminders through email or push providers.
- **Reporting component:** calculates or exports monthly utilisation from reservation and opening-hours data.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search available rooms

1. A user requests `GET /rooms?campus=C1&capacity=6&from=...&to=...`.
2. The HTTP adapter verifies the SAML session and creates a search command containing the user identity and search criteria.
3. The application service validates the time window and calls the room-search port.
4. The repository queries the local room and availability tables. It filters by campus, capacity and equipment, then excludes rooms with overlapping student reservations, block bookings, external calendar closures or outside-opening-hours periods.
5. Appropriate indexes and a read-optimised availability representation allow the query to meet the QR-2 target.
6. The adapter returns available rooms and relevant room information. It does not expose personal data about other users’ reservations.

The legacy inventory database and iCal feeds are synchronised asynchronously. A failed synchronisation is visible operationally and does not make every search dependent on an external network request.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. When a reservation, cancellation, modification or staff block booking commits successfully, the application service records a room-schedule update in the same transaction or in a reliable outbox record.
2. The kiosk update adapter publishes an invalidation or updated schedule for the affected room.
3. Connected kiosks receive the update through SSE. Kiosks also poll the schedule endpoint every five seconds, so a missed push is recovered quickly.
4. The target is that 99% of changes reach the kiosk within ten seconds.
5. Each kiosk stores the most recent valid schedule locally. If it cannot reach CLRS, it displays the cached schedule, its timestamp and an offline indicator. On reconnection it fetches the current schedule and replaces the cache.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

The domain core will have extensive unit tests without a database or network, satisfying QR-5. Tests will cover:

- overlapping reservations;
- the three-hour-per-day user limit;
- creation, modification and cancellation permissions;
- recurring block bookings;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- block bookings overriding student reservations;
- opening-hours validation;
- time zones and daylight-saving transitions;
- equipment and capacity filtering;
- idempotency of repeated commands.

Table-driven tests and property-based tests will check combinations of time windows and reservation sequences. Application services will use fake ports to test transaction coordination, authorisation, audit generation and notification scheduling.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance. They will verify:

- schema migrations;
- indexes and availability queries;
- transaction boundaries;
- uniqueness and overlap protection under concurrent booking attempts;
- repository mappings;
- outbox delivery;
- report calculations.

Test containers will be used in CI so that tests do not depend on a developer’s local database.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will be defined for every external boundary:

- SAML assertion fields, roles and failure cases;
- iCal parsing and time-zone behaviour;
- read-only inventory database queries;
- email and push notification requests;
- kiosk schedule JSON and SSE events;
- public HTTP response codes, including `409 Conflict` for reservation conflicts.

Where real systems are unavailable, provider simulators will be used. Changes to an adapter or API contract must cause CI failure before merging.

#### End-to-end tests

A small set of end-to-end tests will run against a deployed test environment:

1. authenticate as a student and search for a room;
2. create, modify and cancel a reservation;
3. attempt a conflicting reservation;
4. create a staff block booking;
5. confirm a kiosk receives the updated schedule;
6. generate a utilisation report;
7. verify a reminder is queued.

End-to-end tests will not replace unit and integration tests because they are slower and less diagnostic.

#### Non-functional testing

- Load testing will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users, with realistic search patterns and a smaller percentage of booking writes. The release gate is search p95 below 400 ms under the target workload.
- Failure tests will stop an application instance, interrupt an iCal feed and disconnect a kiosk. The system must continue serving through another instance, report stale integration data, and display the kiosk’s last-known schedule.
- Security testing will include dependency scanning, SAST, authentication bypass tests, authorisation tests, input validation and checks that PII is not emitted in application logs.
- Deployment rehearsal will measure rollback time and require a completed rollback in less than ten minutes.

### 4.2 Delivery

The team will use trunk-based development with short-lived branches and pull requests. Every pull request must pass:

- compilation and static analysis;
- formatting and linting;
- unit, integration and contract tests;
- migration validation;
- dependency and security scans;
- minimum agreed code-coverage thresholds for the domain;
- API compatibility checks.

A merge to the main branch produces an immutable container image. Deployment proceeds automatically to a test environment, followed by smoke tests and load-test checks for release candidates.

Production deployment will use a canary or blue-green approach:

1. apply backward-compatible database changes first;
2. deploy the new application image alongside the existing version;
3. route a small percentage of traffic to the new version;
4. check error rate, latency, reservation conflicts and health probes;
5. increase traffic if the metrics remain within thresholds.

Configuration for campuses, integrations and feature flags will be external to the image. Secrets will be stored in a secret manager, not in source control.

Rollback consists of routing traffic to the previous image and disabling the new feature flag. Database migrations must be expand-and-contract migrations so that the previous image remains compatible. The rollback procedure will be documented, automated and rehearsed monthly. The target is a completed application rollback within ten minutes, supporting QR-6.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will include:

- timestamp, severity and correlation ID;
- endpoint and operation name;
- campus and room identifier where appropriate;
- outcome and error category;
- latency;
- external dependency name and response status;
- deployment version.

Logs will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, session tokens or reservation descriptions. User identifiers will be salted or irreversibly hashed where correlation is necessary. Staff audit records will be separate from operational logs and will contain the minimum required actor, action, target, timestamp and result.

#### Metrics

For QR-1:

- successful and failed requests by endpoint;
- application availability during opening hours;
- HTTP 5xx rate;
- database connection saturation and query failures;
- SAML, iCal and notification-provider failure rates;
- kiosk connection status;
- percentage of kiosk updates delivered within ten seconds;
- age of each kiosk’s last successful schedule refresh;
- number of kiosks displaying stale/offline schedules.

For QR-2:

- search request count;
- search p50, p95 and p99 latency;
- latency by campus and result size;
- concurrent requests;
- database query duration;
- CPU, memory, connection-pool and cache utilisation.

#### Alerts

Alerts will include:

- availability below the monthly 99.5% budget or a five-minute 5xx rate above 2%;
- search p95 above 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under meaningful traffic;
- database CPU above 80% for ten minutes or connection-pool exhaustion;
- more than 1% of kiosk updates exceeding ten seconds over five minutes;
- any kiosk with no successful refresh for fifteen minutes during opening hours;
- iCal or inventory synchronisation failure for three consecutive runs;
- notification queue age exceeding five minutes;
- failed deployment health checks or abnormal reservation-conflict rates.

Dashboards will show service health, search performance, integration freshness and kiosk state by campus.

## 5. Risks and mitigations

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Measurable trigger | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Concurrent reservations create double bookings | Medium | High | Any confirmed overlapping reservation in a concurrency test or production audit | Use domain validation plus PostgreSQL transaction isolation/overlap constraints; run concurrent booking tests; return `409 Conflict` on failed commit |
| Search performance fails at semester start | Medium | High | Search p95 exceeds 400 ms in the 2,000-user load test or for ten production minutes | Use indexed local availability tables, cache room metadata, profile queries, scale application instances and pre-warm caches |
| SAML integration is delayed or changes unexpectedly | Medium | High | Test identity-provider integration unavailable for more than two scheduled test cycles, or contract tests fail | Agree an early SAML contract, use a provider simulator, isolate SAML behind an adapter and perform an integration spike before core development |
| iCal or inventory data becomes stale or unavailable | High | Medium | Synchronisation fails three times or data age exceeds 30 minutes | Store a timestamped local copy, retry with backoff, alert operators, expose data freshness and define a product policy for stale availability |
| Kiosks do not refresh within ten seconds | Medium | High | More than 1% of updates exceed ten seconds during testing or production | Use SSE plus five-second polling fallback, maintain an outbox, instrument update latency and cache the last-known schedule locally |
| Reminder delivery is late or duplicated | Medium | Medium | More than 1% of reminders are delivered after the start time or duplicate delivery exceeds 0.1% | Use an idempotent notification job, durable queue/outbox, provider delivery status and retry with a deduplication key |
| A deployment or migration cannot be rolled back | Low/Medium | High | Rollback rehearsal exceeds ten minutes or previous version fails after migration | Use immutable images and expand-and-contract migrations; rehearse rollback monthly; retain the previous image and database backup |
| PII is accidentally written to logs | Medium | High | Automated log scan detects an email, name or token pattern | Central redaction middleware, structured logging allow-list, secret scanning, security tests and restricted log access |
| Two-person team is overloaded by scope | Medium | Medium | Any milestone slips by more than one week or more than three unresolved high-priority defects remain | Prioritise FR-1 to FR-5 for first release, defer low-value report features if necessary, automate CI/deployment and review scope weekly with the product owner |
| Campus-specific rules require code changes | Medium | Medium | Onboarding a test campus requires a pull request rather than configuration/data changes | Define a campus configuration schema, validate it at startup and include a new-campus onboarding test in CI |
