## 5. Trade-off Ledger

This section records technical and project risks, including accumulated technical debt referred to as **design entropy**. Likelihood and impact are assessed as Low, Medium or High. Triggers are measurable conditions that require action.

| Risk | Likelihood / impact | Measurable trigger | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legacy inventory database is slow, unavailable or changes schema. | Medium / High | Inventory sync fails twice in 24 hours, schema validation fails, or query p95 exceeds 1 second. | Use a read-only adapter and local synchronised room catalogue. Add schema checks, timeouts, alerting and an agreed contact with the inventory owner. Search continues using the last valid catalogue. |
| Reservation race conditions create double bookings. | Medium / High | Any duplicate room/time reservation is found in testing or production, or conflict tests fail. | Enforce database constraints/transaction isolation, perform conflict checks inside the transaction, and add concurrency tests with at least 100 competing reservation attempts. |
| SAML integration or role mapping is misunderstood. | Medium / High | More than 1% of authentication attempts fail in staging, or any student can access a staff operation. | Use provider test fixtures, contract tests and explicit role-mapping review. Deny by default and provide an emergency staff-access runbook. |
| Kiosk updates exceed the ten-second requirement. | Medium / Medium | More than 1% of measured reservation changes take over ten seconds to reach the kiosk, or outbox age exceeds five minutes. | Use transactional outbox events, idempotent worker processing, room-specific updates and polling fallback. Kiosks retain and display the last-known schedule. |
| Semester-start traffic causes search latency or outage. | High / High | Load test p95 exceeds 400 ms, error rate exceeds 1%, or database CPU exceeds 75% at expected load. | Index time-range queries, cache room metadata, tune connection pools, scale application instances and run a 2,000-concurrent-user test before release. |
| Recurring block-booking and notice rules are ambiguous. | Medium / High | Product examples contradict one another, or acceptance tests cannot determine expected behaviour for an override. | Obtain written product-owner decisions, encode examples as acceptance tests, and prevent implementation until conflict semantics are approved. |
| Notification provider failure causes missed reminders. | Medium / Medium | Provider failure rate exceeds 5%, queue age exceeds five minutes, or delivery receipts fall below the agreed threshold. | Queue reminders through the worker, retry with backoff, make delivery idempotent, monitor provider status and expose an operational report of failed reminders. |
| Two-person team lacks capacity for operations and support. | Medium / High | More than two unresolved priority-one operational tasks exist, or planned work slips by two iterations. | Keep the deployment small, automate CI/CD, create runbooks, rotate on-call responsibility and defer non-essential features. |
| Configuration-only campus onboarding becomes hidden code. | Medium / Medium | A new-campus change requires a source-code change or more than one deployment-specific exception. | Define a validated configuration schema, add sample campus fixtures and make onboarding a contract/integration test. |
| Accumulated technical debt increases design entropy. | Medium / Medium | Critical modules exceed agreed complexity thresholds, duplicated adapter logic exceeds 10%, or test coverage of domain rules falls below 95%. | Maintain an explicit debt register, reserve 15% of each iteration for cleanup, refactor before adding more integrations and review architecture boundaries quarterly. |

The main deliberate trade-off is accepting a modular monolith rather than independent services. This reduces operational risk now but means that a defect or resource exhaustion in the application could affect several functions simultaneously. Health isolation, bounded background-worker concurrency and feature flags reduce this exposure. If measured traffic or team growth later justifies service separation, the ports provide seams for extraction.

# CS 3410 Software Engineering — Assignment 2  
## Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms, create or modify reservations, cancel reservations and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities iCal feeds and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release is expected to be deployed and operated by a two-person team, so the architecture should avoid unnecessary operational complexity.

This document defines the architecture, component structure, testing approach, delivery process, observability strategy and risk mitigations for the first release. It covers the reservation, search, kiosk, notification and reporting capabilities, but not the implementation details of the external identity provider, facilities system or legacy database.

The principal quality objectives are high availability during opening hours, responsive availability searches under semester-start load, secure authentication and auditing, configuration-only onboarding of new campuses, database-independent testing of reservation rules, and rollback within ten minutes.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture** as its primary architectural style.

The system will contain a framework-independent domain core surrounded by application services, ports and external adapters. The first release will be delivered as a small number of deployable components, preferably one API deployment and one worker deployment using the same codebase and release artifact. This preserves operational simplicity while allowing asynchronous work such as reminders and kiosk-update publication.

The domain core will own reservation rules, including:

- time-window validation;
- room and equipment eligibility;
- the three-hour daily user limit;
- conflict detection;
- recurring block-booking precedence;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- reservation modification and cancellation rules.

The domain will not directly depend on HTTP, PostgreSQL, SAML libraries, iCal parsing libraries or messaging infrastructure.

### 2.2 Rationale against quality requirements

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
Hexagonal architecture provides the strongest fit for the requirement that reservation rules be testable without a database or network. The domain core receives required data through interfaces such as `ReservationRepository`, `RoomCatalog`, `Clock` and `NotificationPublisher`. Unit tests can provide in-memory fakes and a fixed clock. Conflict detection and daily-limit rules can therefore be tested quickly and deterministically without starting PostgreSQL or contacting SAML.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is implemented by an inbound SAML adapter. The adapter validates the SAML response and maps it to an internal user identity and roles. Application services then authorise operations such as staff block bookings. A separate audit port records staff actions. This prevents security concerns from being scattered through domain code. Logging policies can also be applied at the adapter and application-service boundaries so that user identifiers, email addresses and other PII are excluded from ordinary logs.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific information—opening hours, time zone, room metadata, equipment and facilities-feed locations—will be held in configuration and the room catalogue. The application service uses a `CampusConfiguration` port rather than hard-coded campus branches. Adding a fourth library should therefore involve configuration, data migration or administration—not a code change. External systems are also isolated behind adapters, which limits the impact of changes to SAML, iCal or the legacy inventory database.

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
The main API can remain stateless and run with at least two instances behind a load balancer. Database transactions protect reservation consistency while health checks and rolling deployment support availability. The kiosk adapter stores the last successfully retrieved schedule locally on the kiosk. If the API or network is temporarily unavailable, the kiosk continues showing the last-known schedule and indicates its age. This directly supports graceful degradation.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability searches use a read-oriented repository with indexed room, campus, capacity and time-range data. Frequently requested room metadata and opening-hour configuration can be cached. Because the API is stateless, additional instances can be added during semester start. Performance testing will use 2,000 concurrent users and measure p95 latency, rather than relying only on average response time.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
Hexagonal architecture does not require a distributed service mesh, multiple service databases or complex event infrastructure. A two-person team can deploy a small API and worker using container images and managed PostgreSQL. Health checks, versioned migrations, feature flags and an immutable previous release support rollback within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and could satisfy QR-6 initially. It would also provide straightforward transactions for reservations. However, conventional layered designs often allow application and domain code to become coupled to persistence and web frameworks. That would make QR-5 weaker and make external integration changes more invasive.

A layered monolith remains a possible deployment shape, but hexagonal architecture is preferred because it explicitly protects the domain from infrastructure. The trade-off is that ports, adapters and dependency inversion introduce more concepts and initial design effort.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices would allow notification, reporting and reservation workloads to scale independently. A failure in reporting might also be isolated from reservation creation. However, the first release has a two-person operations team. Multiple services would introduce service discovery, independent deployments, distributed tracing, network failures, API versioning and potentially distributed transactions.

Reservation creation and conflict checking should be strongly consistent. Splitting those operations across services could make QR-1 and correctness harder to guarantee. Microservices would also increase deployment and rollback complexity, conflicting with QR-6. The system gives up independent service scaling and failure isolation by not choosing microservices, but avoids excessive operational overhead at the current scale.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS projections would be attractive for FR-1 and FR-4. Search and kiosk views could be served from optimised read models, and events could naturally trigger reminders and kiosk updates. However, projections are eventually consistent. A student could search successfully and immediately receive stale availability, or a kiosk could temporarily show an old schedule. Additional work would be required for event ordering, replay, idempotency, projection recovery and reconciliation.

This design therefore gives up the scalability and decoupling benefits of a full event-driven system. Instead, CLRS will use a transactional outbox and lightweight asynchronous worker where useful, without making CQRS or an event log the primary architecture.

The diagram shows logical boundaries rather than mandatory separate deployments. The API and worker may initially be deployed as two processes from the same versioned container image.

### 3.2 Main components

- **HTTP/API inbound adapter:** Implements the REST interface and converts HTTP requests into application commands and queries.
- **SAML authentication adapter:** Validates SAML assertions and maps claims to an internal identity, campus access and staff role.
- **Application services:** Coordinate use cases, authorisation, transactions and ports. Examples include `CreateReservation`, `ModifyReservation`, `CreateBlockBooking`, `SearchAvailability` and `GetKioskSchedule`.
- **Domain core:** Contains reservation entities, value objects, policies and invariants. It has no database or network dependency.
- **Persistence adapter:** Stores reservations, block bookings, users, campuses and outbox messages in CLRS PostgreSQL.
- **Inventory adapter:** Reads room metadata from the legacy PostgreSQL database.
- **Facilities-calendar adapter:** Imports and normalises iCal closures and external bookings.
- **Notification adapter:** Sends reminders through email or push providers.
- **Kiosk adapter:** Publishes change notifications or serves schedules for kiosk polling. Each kiosk retains a local last-known copy.
- **Reporting adapter:** Generates monthly campus utilisation exports from read-only reporting queries.
- **Observability adapter:** Exports metrics, traces and sanitised structured logs.

Reservation writes use a database transaction. A uniqueness or exclusion constraint on room/time intervals is the final protection against concurrent double booking. The application checks business rules before writing, and conflicting writes return HTTP 409.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=C1&capacity=4&from=...&to=...`.
2. The SAML adapter validates the session and supplies the internal user identity.
3. The API adapter maps the request to a `SearchAvailability` query.
4. The query service obtains campus configuration and room data through ports.
5. The persistence and inventory adapters provide rooms, existing reservations, block bookings, opening hours and relevant facilities closures.
6. The search service filters by campus, capacity and equipment, then removes rooms whose requested interval overlaps an existing reservation, block booking or closure.
7. Indexed queries and cached room/configuration data support QR-2. The API returns available rooms and a correlation ID, but no PII.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

When a reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden:

1. The reservation application service commits the change and an outbox message in one transaction.
2. The worker reads the outbox message and publishes a room-specific update or invalidates the kiosk schedule cache.
3. Kiosks receive a push update or poll the schedule endpoint.
4. The target kiosk retrieves the current and next reservation and stores it locally with a timestamp.
5. The normal target is that the display is updated within ten seconds of the committed reservation change.
6. If the kiosk cannot reach CLRS, it displays the locally stored schedule, marks it “last updated at” and retries with backoff.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application policies using fakes for all ports. They will test:

- overlapping and adjacent reservations;
- three-hour daily limits;
- modification and cancellation permissions;
- recurring block-booking expansion;
- block bookings overriding student reservations;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- opening-hour and closure rules;
- campus configuration;
- time-zone and daylight-saving transitions.

A fixed `Clock` port will make reminder and notice calculations deterministic. These tests directly satisfy QR-5 and should run on every commit.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Adapter tests will verify:

- PostgreSQL mappings, constraints and transaction behaviour;
- iCal parsing and handling of malformed feeds;
- SAML assertion validation and role mapping;
- email/push provider requests;
- kiosk polling or push protocols;
- migration scripts and indexes.

Tests will use disposable containers or a dedicated test environment rather than production systems. A concurrency integration test will attempt simultaneous reservations for the same room and verify that at most one succeeds.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will define stable interfaces between CLRS and external dependencies. They will cover the expected SAML claims, iCal formats, inventory schema, notification payloads and kiosk schedule response. Consumer-driven contracts will ensure that API changes do not break kiosk clients or staff reporting tools.

#### End-to-end tests

A small set of end-to-end tests will run against a deployed test environment:

- SAML login followed by room search;
- student reservation and cancellation;
- conflicting reservations;
- staff block booking;
- reservation change reaching the kiosk;
- reminder creation;
- report export.

End-to-end tests will not attempt to cover every reservation-rule combination; those combinations belong in unit tests.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

A load test will simulate 2,000 concurrent users at semester-start traffic proportions, with a stated target of availability-search p95 below 400 ms. It will also monitor error rate and database saturation.

Resilience tests will stop a worker, temporarily disconnect a kiosk and make the iCal feed unavailable. Expected behaviour is queued processing, last-known kiosk display and recovery without duplicate notifications.

Security tests will include SAML signature and replay validation, role-boundary tests, authorisation checks, dependency scanning, secret scanning and verification that logs contain no email addresses, names or raw SAML assertions.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development will use short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. Every pull request must pass:

- compilation and formatting checks;
- unit and domain tests;
- adapter/integration tests;
- contract tests;
- static analysis;
- dependency and secret scanning;
- database migration validation.

A merge to `main` produces an immutable versioned container image. Deployment proceeds automatically to a test environment, followed by smoke tests and the performance test suite on release candidates.

Production deployment will use a rolling or blue-green strategy with health checks. Database changes must be backward-compatible: add new structures first, deploy code, migrate data, and remove old structures only in a later release. Feature flags will permit risky functionality such as kiosk push delivery to be disabled without rollback.

Before deployment, the team records the current image tag and database migration version. If smoke tests fail, error rates increase, or the availability/performance SLO is breached, traffic is returned to the previous image. Rollback will be rehearsed monthly and must complete within ten minutes. The worker must be idempotent so that rolling back does not duplicate reminders or kiosk updates.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests receive a correlation ID. Structured logs will record timestamps, operation names, campus and room identifiers where non-sensitive, outcome, latency, status code, deployment version and correlation ID. Logs will not include names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation notes or raw request bodies. Staff audit records are separate, access-controlled and contain the staff subject identifier, action, target resource, timestamp and result.

Metrics include:

- opening-hours API availability and successful/failed health checks;
- HTTP error rate by endpoint;
- search p50, p95 and p99 latency;
- active users and request rate;
- database connection-pool utilisation and query latency;
- reservation conflict rate;
- outbox queue depth and oldest message age;
- reminder delivery success and failure;
- kiosk update propagation latency;
- kiosk last-contact age and percentage using last-known data;
- iCal and inventory adapter failure rates.

Alerts will include:

- monthly or rolling availability burn rate threatening 99.5%;
- search p95 above 400 ms for five consecutive minutes under meaningful traffic;
- search error rate above 2% for five minutes;
- outbox oldest message older than two minutes;
- more than 1% of kiosks not contacting the service for five minutes;
- kiosk reservation-change propagation p95 above ten seconds;
- database storage, CPU or connection usage above 80%.

Dashboards will distinguish an unavailable CLRS service from a disconnected kiosk. Synthetic probes will search availability and retrieve a kiosk schedule during library opening hours.

This section records risks, mitigations and accumulated technical debt, referred to as **design entropy**. Likelihood and impact are assessed qualitatively, while triggers are measurable and actionable.

# Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS)  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel reservations. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservations.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems:

- the university identity provider using SAML;
- facilities calendars through iCal feeds; and
- the read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.

The first release includes reservation management, availability search, staff block bookings, kiosk schedules, reminders and utilisation reports. It does not replace the identity provider, facilities calendar or inventory database.

The principal design constraints are high availability during opening hours, fast availability searches at semester start, secure authentication and auditing, configuration-only onboarding of new libraries, database-independent reservation-rule testing, and deployment and rollback by a two-person operations team.

The design therefore prioritises a small operational footprint and a framework-independent domain model over independent service scaling. The proposed architecture is a **hexagonal modular monolith**: the reservation domain is isolated behind ports, while HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, notification and kiosk integrations are replaceable adapters.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C — Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith with one deployable application and one relational database.

The system will contain a framework-independent domain core surrounded by application use cases and inbound and outbound ports. Infrastructure concerns such as HTTP, authentication, persistence, messaging and external integrations will be implemented as adapters.

The application may use an internal asynchronous event dispatcher and an outbox table for kiosk updates and reminders. This is an implementation technique within the hexagonal architecture; CLRS will not adopt full event-driven CQRS as its primary style.

### 2.2 Rationale and quality requirements

#### QR-1: Availability

A single deployable reduces operational failure points compared with multiple independently deployed services. The application can run with at least two instances behind a load balancer, while PostgreSQL uses automated backups and a standby or managed high-availability configuration.

Kiosk schedules will be stored in a local kiosk cache. A kiosk receiving no response from CLRS will continue to display its last-known valid schedule, together with a visible “last updated” timestamp. The kiosk client will retry using exponential backoff. This satisfies the graceful-degradation requirement even when the application or network is temporarily unavailable.

External systems will not be placed synchronously on the critical reservation path unless necessary. For example, an iCal failure will mark external data as stale rather than preventing users from viewing locally known rooms. Notifications will be processed asynchronously so a mail-provider outage does not make reservation creation unavailable.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability searches will use an indexed local database representation of rooms, equipment, opening hours, external calendar exclusions and reservations. Search does not need to query the legacy inventory database or iCal feeds synchronously. Appropriate indexes will be created on campus, capacity, equipment and reservation time ranges.

The target is p95 search latency below 400 ms under a 2,000-concurrent-user load test. Stateless application instances can be scaled horizontally, and frequently repeated room metadata may be cached. A modular monolith avoids the network hops and distributed-query overhead that could make a simple search slower in a microservices architecture.

#### QR-3: Security

SAML is isolated behind an identity-provider adapter. The application receives a validated authenticated principal and role claims rather than allowing domain logic to depend on SAML libraries. Authorisation policies are enforced in application use cases, including the distinction between student and staff operations.

Staff actions will generate audit records containing actor identifier, action, target, timestamp, outcome and correlation ID. Application logs will use pseudonymous user identifiers or hashed internal IDs and will exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens and reservation descriptions that could contain PII. Logging and audit storage will be separate so audit completeness is not dependent on ordinary debug logging.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

A new library will be represented by configuration containing its campus identifier, opening hours, room mapping, timezone, equipment vocabulary, calendar feed and kiosk settings. The application will not contain campus-specific conditional code.

External systems are also replaceable through ports. For example, a second inventory source can be implemented as another inventory adapter without changing reservation rules. This supports future campus onboarding and integration changes while keeping the domain model stable.

#### QR-5: Testability

Reservation rules will be implemented as pure domain services and value objects. They will accept domain data and a clock or policy object rather than directly accessing a database, HTTP client or framework. Consequently, rules such as the three-hour daily limit, overlapping reservations, opening hours, block-booking precedence and 48-hour notice can be tested with in-memory objects and fake ports.

This directly satisfies the requirement that reservation rules be testable without a database or network.

#### QR-6: Operability

One versioned application artifact and a single primary database are suitable for a two-person team. Deployment can use a container image and automated database migrations. Backward-compatible migrations allow a new application version to run temporarily alongside the previous version.

A blue-green or rolling deployment will be used. The previous container image remains available, and rollback consists of routing traffic back to the previous version. The rollback procedure will be rehearsed and must complete within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would have similar deployment simplicity and could meet QR-6. It would also be a reasonable fallback if the team has limited experience with ports and adapters.

It was not selected because ordinary layered designs commonly allow presentation or persistence concerns to leak into application and domain code. That would make QR-5 weaker and make replacing SAML, iCal or the legacy inventory integration more expensive. Hexagonal boundaries make these dependencies explicit and enforceable.

The trade-off is additional interfaces, mapping code and architectural discipline. For a small application, this can appear more complex than a conventional layered structure.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They would isolate failures and allow separate technology choices. However, they introduce service discovery, inter-service authentication, distributed tracing, deployment coordination and data consistency problems.

Creating a reservation and updating the kiosk read path would require reliable cross-service communication. This increases the risk of stale schedules and makes QR-6 harder for a two-person team. It also makes end-to-end and contract testing more extensive. CLRS does not currently have independently scaling workloads or organisational teams that justify these costs.

The system gives up independent service deployment and fine-grained scaling by choosing a monolith. Horizontal scaling of the complete application is accepted for the first release.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

Event-driven CQRS would naturally support kiosk projections, notifications and reporting. An event log could provide strong history and replay capabilities. It may become appropriate if reporting volume, integration count or audit requirements grow substantially.

It was not selected because event logs, projections, replay, idempotency and eventual consistency introduce significant complexity. Availability search and reservation conflict rules require a clear authoritative transactional state. A delayed projection could show a room as available immediately after another user reserves it. Full CQRS would also increase operational burden and complicate QR-6.

CLRS gives up the scalability and replay benefits of a complete event-driven design. Instead, it uses a transactional outbox and small asynchronous consumers for non-critical updates, retaining reliable reservation transactions without making every read eventually consistent.

The domain core contains entities and policies for `Room`, `Reservation`, `BlockBooking`, `OpeningHours` and `UserReservationQuota`. It does not import HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL drivers, iCal parsers or notification SDKs.

Representative inbound use cases are:

- `SearchAvailableRooms`;
- `CreateReservation`;
- `ModifyReservation`;
- `CancelReservation`;
- `CreateBlockBooking`;
- `GetKioskSchedule`; and
- `ExportUtilisationReport`.

Representative outbound ports are:

- `ReservationRepository`;
- `RoomCatalogue`;
- `ExternalCalendarAvailability`;
- `NotificationSender`;
- `KioskSchedulePublisher`;
- `AuditWriter`; and
- `Clock`.

The application uses a transaction when changing reservations. The reservation and corresponding outbox event are committed atomically. A worker later processes the event, updates the kiosk cache and sends notifications. Events include unique IDs, and consumers are idempotent so retries do not duplicate effects.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. A browser sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&from=&to=` to the HTTP adapter.
2. The adapter authenticates the request through the SAML session and validates campus, time and capacity parameters.
3. The `SearchAvailableRooms` use case calls the `RoomCatalogue` and availability query ports.
4. The search adapter queries the locally indexed CLRS database, combining room attributes, opening hours, reservations, block bookings and synchronised external-calendar exclusions.
5. The application returns only rooms satisfying campus, capacity, equipment and time-window constraints.
6. If an external feed is unavailable, its last successful synchronised data is used and its age is recorded. The response or operational dashboard can indicate that external data is stale.
7. Search results are read-only and do not require the reservation domain to open a network connection to an external system. This supports the QR-2 latency target.

Reservation creation performs a new authoritative transaction after search. The domain rechecks conflicts and the three-hour daily limit, preventing a race in which two users reserve the same room after seeing the same search result. A conflict returns HTTP 409.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk schedule

1. A kiosk calls `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` initially and then polls every five seconds, or maintains an optional server-sent-events connection.
2. The HTTP adapter retrieves the room’s schedule from the kiosk cache.
3. When a reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden by a block booking, the transaction writes an outbox event.
4. The worker consumes the event and updates the affected room’s kiosk schedule.
5. The kiosk receives the update through server-sent events or observes it on the next poll. The expected propagation time is below ten seconds.
6. If CLRS or the network is unavailable, the kiosk displays its last-known schedule and timestamp. It must not display the schedule as current when it is operating from stale data.
7. A scheduled reconciliation job compares recent reservation changes with kiosk-cache versions and repairs missed updates.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application use cases with fake ports. They will test:

- overlapping reservations and conflict detection;
- the three-hour daily user limit;
- modification and cancellation permissions;
- opening-hour restrictions;
- recurring block bookings;
- 48-hour block-booking notice;
- block-booking precedence;
- timezone and daylight-saving transitions;
- idempotent event processing; and
- reminder selection 15 minutes before start.

These tests run without a database or network and are the primary evidence for QR-5. Boundary-value and property-based tests will be used for time windows and recurring bookings.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will run the PostgreSQL repository, migrations, indexes, transaction boundaries and outbox using containerised PostgreSQL. They will verify that simultaneous reservation attempts result in at most one successful reservation and that reservation and outbox records commit atomically.

Adapters for iCal, SAML metadata/claims handling, the legacy PostgreSQL database and notification provider will be tested against representative fixtures and controlled test instances. Failure, timeout, malformed-feed and retry behaviour will be included.

#### Contract tests

The HTTP API will have consumer-facing contracts covering request validation, authentication requirements, response schemas, HTTP 409 conflicts and kiosk schedule versioning. Adapter contracts will define the interfaces used by the application, including notification idempotency and inventory synchronisation.

External-provider contracts will be tested against mocked provider specifications. SAML certificates and iCal feed formats will be checked in a staging environment before release.

#### End-to-end tests

A small critical-path suite will run in a production-like environment:

1. SAML login;
2. search for a room;
3. create a reservation;
4. verify a conflicting reservation is rejected;
5. modify and cancel the reservation;
6. create a staff block booking;
7. verify kiosk propagation;
8. generate a utilisation report; and
9. verify reminder dispatch through a test notification provider.

End-to-end tests will not attempt to cover every domain rule; that responsibility belongs to unit tests. This keeps the suite reliable and fast.

#### Non-functional tests

Before semester start, load tests will simulate 2,000 concurrent users, with realistic search and reservation mixtures. The release gate is p95 availability-search latency below 400 ms and an error rate below 1%.

Failure-injection tests will stop an application instance, delay the iCal source, interrupt notification delivery and disconnect a kiosk. Acceptance criteria include continued service through one application-instance failure, kiosk last-known display, retry without duplicate notifications and successful reconciliation.

Security testing will include dependency scanning, SAST, authentication and authorisation tests, audit verification, log-redaction tests and OWASP-style API checks.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development will use short-lived branches merged into `main` through pull requests. Each pull request requires:

- successful compilation and formatting;
- unit, integration and contract tests;
- static analysis and dependency vulnerability scanning;
- database migration validation;
- container image creation; and
- review by the other team member where practical.

`main` must remain deployable. A release candidate is deployed automatically to staging, where end-to-end, smoke and migration tests run. Production deployment requires an explicit approval and a recorded version.

The application will use immutable versioned container images. Database migrations must be backward-compatible: additive schema changes are deployed first, followed by application use, and destructive changes are postponed until the old version is no longer required.

Production deployment will use a rolling or blue-green strategy:

1. create a database backup or confirm the latest valid backup;
2. deploy the new image to a small canary instance;
3. run health checks and smoke tests;
4. monitor error rate, search p95 and reservation conflicts;
5. route traffic to the new version; and
6. retain the previous image for immediate rollback.

Rollback is performed by routing traffic to the previous image and disabling the new worker if necessary. The runbook will be tested in staging and measured from decision to restored service; the target is under ten minutes.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests carry a correlation ID. Logs will record timestamp, severity, component, operation, result, latency, correlation ID and non-PII technical identifiers. Audit records will separately record staff actions. No names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens or free-text PII will be logged.

Metrics include:

- monthly opening-hours availability;
- successful and failed health checks;
- HTTP 5xx rate;
- availability-search p50, p95 and p99 latency;
- concurrent requests;
- database connection-pool utilisation;
- reservation conflict rate;
- outbox age and failure count;
- kiosk-cache age and update latency;
- percentage of kiosks using last-known data;
- iCal synchronisation age and failure count;
- notification queue age and delivery failure rate; and
- deployment and rollback duration.

Alerts will include:

- opening-hours availability below the 99.5% monthly objective or an urgent burn-rate threshold;
- search p95 above 400 ms for five consecutive minutes under normal load;
- search error rate above 1% for five minutes;
- kiosk update propagation above ten seconds for more than 1% of changes;
- any kiosk cache older than a defined threshold, such as five minutes;
- outbox events older than two minutes;
- failed database health checks; and
- repeated authentication or authorisation failures.

A dashboard will show QR-1 and QR-2 directly, with links from alerts to correlated logs and traces.

## 5. Trade-off Ledger

This section records risks, mitigations and the design entropy created by accepted compromises. **Design entropy** means accumulated technical debt and weakening of architectural consistency over time.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Measurable trigger | Mitigation |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Legacy inventory schema or permissions change | Medium | High | A synchronisation job fails twice in 24 hours, or schema validation differs from the approved contract | Isolate the read-only adapter, maintain schema fixtures, use a service account with read-only access, cache the last valid catalogue and agree a legacy-system change notice process |
| iCal feeds are delayed, malformed or unavailable | High | Medium/High | Feed age exceeds 15 minutes or three consecutive synchronisations fail | Validate and version feed parsing, retain last successful data, expose feed age, alert operations and provide a manual staff override for urgent closures |
| Reservation race causes double booking | Medium | High | Any invariant test or production reconciliation finds overlapping confirmed reservations | Use database transactions and exclusion/locking constraints, recheck rules during creation, run concurrency tests and perform periodic conflict reconciliation |
| Kiosk updates exceed the ten-second requirement | Medium | High | More than 1% of changes take over ten seconds, or outbox age exceeds two minutes | Use transactional outbox events, idempotent workers, five-second polling fallback, kiosk version numbers, cache reconciliation and alerting |
| SAML configuration or certificate expiry interrupts login | Medium | High | Staging validation fails, certificate expires within 30 days, or authentication failures exceed 2% | Monitor metadata and certificate expiry, support overlapping certificates, test SAML in staging and maintain a documented emergency configuration procedure |
| Search performance fails at semester start | Medium | High | Load test p95 is at least 400 ms, or production p95 exceeds 400 ms for five minutes | Use local indexed data, query plans, caching and horizontal application scaling; conduct capacity tests before release and define a load-shedding policy for non-critical reports |
| Notification provider outage causes missed reminders | Medium | Medium | Queue age exceeds five minutes or delivery failure rate exceeds 5% | Process notifications asynchronously, retry with idempotency keys, record failures, provide alternative email/push routing and communicate notification limitations to users |
| Two-person team cannot operate the system reliably | Medium | High | Any on-call procedure requires undocumented specialist knowledge or rollback rehearsal exceeds ten minutes | Keep one deployable, automate deployment and backups, maintain runbooks, use dashboards and rehearse restore and rollback monthly |
| Configuration-only campus onboarding becomes code-specific | Medium | Medium | A new-campus change requires a source-code change or more than one deployment | Use schema-validated campus configuration, configuration review tests and a sample fourth-campus onboarding exercise before release |
| Accumulated technical debt increases design entropy | Medium | Medium/High | More than three direct domain-to-infrastructure imports, more than 10% of domain tests require containers, or two successive releases bypass architecture review | Enforce dependency rules in CI, reserve one sprint capacity allocation per release for debt reduction, record exceptions in this ledger and review entropy metrics at each release |

The main accepted trade-off is that the modular monolith does not independently scale reporting, notifications and search. This is acceptable for the first release but should be revisited if load tests or production metrics show materially different scaling requirements. The internal outbox is deliberately limited: it provides reliable asynchronous side effects without committing the project to the operational complexity of a complete event-log and CQRS platform.

## 1. Context and Scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the existing study-room reservation tool used across three university libraries. Students and staff will search for rooms, create and manage reservations, receive reminders, and view room schedules through kiosks. Library staff will manage room information, opening hours and recurring block bookings, and export utilisation reports.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities calendars supplied through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. Reservation rules include a maximum of three hours per day per user and staff block bookings that can override student reservations with at least 48 hours’ notice.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify implementation-level code. The design prioritises reliable reservation rules, testability, simple operations for a two-person team, graceful kiosk degradation, and the ability to onboard a new campus through configuration rather than code changes.

The proposed architecture is a **hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith. The domain core remains independent of databases, networks and frameworks. External systems are accessed through explicit ports and adapters.

---

## 2. Architectural Decision

### 2.1 Selected style: Method C — Hexagonal Architecture

CLRS will use **hexagonal architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture. The reservation domain and application use cases will be isolated from delivery mechanisms and external infrastructure.

The system will initially be deployed as one modular application, but its internal modules will have clear boundaries:

- Reservation domain
- Room and availability domain
- Staff block-booking management
- Notification scheduling
- Kiosk schedule delivery
- Reporting
- Authentication and authorisation
- Integration adapters

The domain core will communicate with infrastructure only through interfaces, or **ports**. Database repositories, SAML integration, iCal import, notification providers and kiosk delivery mechanisms will be implemented as adapters.

This choice provides the following benefits.

#### QR-1: Availability

A modular monolith has fewer independently failing runtime components than a microservices or event-driven deployment. It can be deployed and monitored as one service by the two-person operations team. The reservation database will use transactions and constraints to prevent conflicting bookings.

Kiosks will use a local cache containing the most recently retrieved schedule. If the CLRS API or network is unavailable, the kiosk displays the last-known schedule with its retrieval time and an “offline” indicator. A kiosk adapter can poll the schedule endpoint using conditional requests, reducing unnecessary traffic.

The architecture does not automatically guarantee 99.5% availability. It supports that target by reducing operational complexity, using health checks, database backups, redundant application instances where practical, and a tested rollback procedure.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability search will have a dedicated application use case and repository port. The persistence adapter can use indexed queries over room attributes, opening hours and reservations. Frequently used room metadata and imported calendar information can be cached.

Because the application is not split into several synchronous services, a search request avoids multiple network hops. This makes it easier to achieve the p95 target of under 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users. Performance tests will validate the complete deployment and identify database or query bottlenecks before semester start.

#### QR-3: Security

Authentication is represented by an inbound security port and implemented by a SAML adapter. The adapter validates SAML assertions and creates an internal user identity containing only the information required by CLRS. Role checks are performed in application use cases rather than being left solely to the user interface.

Staff actions produce audit records through an audit port. Audit records contain the actor’s internal identifier, action, target resource, timestamp and outcome, but not unnecessary personal information. Application logs use opaque correlation IDs and reservation or room IDs rather than names, email addresses or SAML assertions. Passwords and SAML tokens are never logged.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Campus-specific values will be stored in configuration, including:

- Campus identifier and display name
- Opening hours and holiday calendars
- Room-inventory source
- Facilities iCal feed
- Notification settings
- Kiosk configuration
- Time zone and reporting settings

The domain uses campus identifiers and configuration objects rather than hard-coded campus logic. Therefore, adding a fourth library should require configuration, data loading and operational verification, rather than a code change.

#### QR-5: Testability

Reservation rules are implemented in framework-independent domain services. They accept domain objects and a repository abstraction rather than directly accessing PostgreSQL or a network. Unit tests can therefore verify:

- Three-hour daily limits
- Overlapping reservations
- Modification and cancellation permissions
- Staff block-booking precedence
- The 48-hour notice requirement
- Opening-hour restrictions
- Recurring booking expansion
- Time-zone and daylight-saving behaviour

These tests run with in-memory fakes and no database, network or external identity provider.

#### QR-6: Operability

A modular monolith is more suitable than multiple independently deployed services for a two-person team. It requires fewer deployment pipelines, dashboards, runtime credentials and failure modes. A versioned container image and backward-compatible database migration strategy allow a release to be deployed gradually and rolled back within ten minutes.

The trade-off is that the whole application may need to be deployed when one module changes. This is acceptable for the first release because the operational simplicity is more valuable than independent service scaling.

### 2.2 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be straightforward to build and deploy. It would also offer the same single-deployment operational advantages as the proposed design.

However, traditional layered designs often allow application and domain code to depend directly on framework or persistence classes. That would weaken QR-5 because reservation rules could become difficult to test without PostgreSQL. It would also make external integrations harder to replace and could encourage campus-specific logic to spread across presentation, service and persistence layers.

Hexagonal architecture retains the monolith’s deployment simplicity while providing stronger dependency boundaries. The cost is additional interfaces, adapters and design discipline.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notification and reporting. For example, search could be scaled during semester start while reporting remained at a lower capacity. Independent services could also be deployed separately.

The disadvantages are significant for this release:

- Reservation consistency would cross service boundaries.
- Availability search might require calls to inventory and reservation services.
- Network failures and partial deployments would make QR-1 harder to achieve.
- Contract, integration and end-to-end testing would be more extensive.
- Deployment, monitoring and incident response would be difficult for a two-person team.
- Rollback within ten minutes would be harder if several services and schemas changed together.

Microservices are therefore rejected for the first release. The internal modular boundaries leave open the possibility of extracting a service later if measured load or team size justifies it.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log could provide highly scalable read models for availability searches and kiosks. Events could also naturally trigger reminders, audit processing and reporting projections.

However, event-driven consistency introduces complexity into the most important workflow: deciding whether a reservation is valid. A user may search a slightly stale read model and then receive a conflict when submitting the reservation. Kiosk updates may also be delayed by failed consumers or projection lag. Event replay, schema evolution, idempotency and operational recovery would increase the burden under QR-6.

The selected design may use a small internal event or outbox mechanism for notifications and kiosk invalidation, but the primary system of record and reservation decision remain synchronous and transactionally consistent. Full CQRS is deferred.

### 2.3 Decision summary

Hexagonal architecture is selected because it combines:

- Testable business rules
- Strong integration boundaries
- Simple initial deployment
- Consistent reservation transactions
- Configuration-based campus onboarding
- A path to future scaling without prematurely adopting distributed systems

The main sacrifice is that the first release does not provide independent deployment or scaling of every capability. This is considered an appropriate trade-off for the stated requirements and team size.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: Search availability

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=...&capacity=...&from=...&to=...`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates syntax, obtains the authenticated user context and invokes the `SearchAvailableRooms` use case.
3. The use case validates the time window and campus configuration.
4. The room repository port obtains configured room metadata from the inventory adapter or cache.
5. The reservation repository port retrieves reservations overlapping the requested time window.
6. The availability domain service applies opening hours, equipment, capacity, facilities-calendar exclusions and reservation conflicts.
7. The use case returns a result containing available rooms and relevant attributes.
8. The HTTP adapter maps the result to JSON.

Search queries use indexes on campus, room, start time and end time. Room metadata and imported iCal data may be cached, but reservation creation always rechecks conflicts transactionally.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: Kiosk refresh

1. A kiosk requests `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` using a device-specific credential.
2. The kiosk application use case reads the current and next reservation from the schedule repository port.
3. The response includes a schedule version, retrieval timestamp and cache-control information.
4. The kiosk polls at an interval below ten seconds or uses a long-polling endpoint. A reservation change invalidates the room’s schedule cache and increments its version.
5. The kiosk updates its local schedule when the version changes.
6. If the request fails, the kiosk continues showing its local last-known schedule, clearly labelled with its age and offline state.
7. When connectivity returns, the kiosk retrieves the newest version.

The target is that 99% of reservation changes produce a visible kiosk update within ten seconds under normal operating conditions. Monitoring records the change-to-kiosk-update latency.

## 4. Quality Plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests cover the framework-independent domain core and application use cases. They use in-memory fakes for repository and audit ports. Important cases include:

- A user cannot exceed three reservation hours per day.
- Overlapping reservations are rejected.
- A modification cannot create a conflict.
- A user cannot modify or cancel another user’s reservation.
- Staff-only operations reject student identities.
- Block bookings override student bookings only when the 48-hour requirement is satisfied.
- Opening hours and campus-specific configuration are enforced.
- Recurring bookings handle boundaries and daylight-saving transitions.
- Reminder times are calculated correctly.

These tests directly satisfy QR-5. They run on every commit and should be deterministic and fast.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests verify real adapters and infrastructure:

- PostgreSQL repository queries, constraints and transactions
- Database migrations and rollback compatibility
- Cache invalidation and outbox processing
- iCal parsing and malformed-feed handling
- Inventory adapter access to the read-only PostgreSQL database
- SAML assertion validation using a test identity provider
- Email and push provider adapters
- Kiosk schedule retrieval and conditional requests

Test databases and sandbox identity/provider accounts will be used. External production systems will not be called by CI.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will be defined for:

- HTTP API responses and error codes
- SAML claims and role mapping
- iCal feed formats
- Inventory adapter queries and expected schema
- Notification provider requests
- Kiosk schedule response fields

Consumer-driven or schema-based contract tests ensure that an adapter change does not silently break the application. In particular, a reservation conflict must remain represented consistently as HTTP 409.

#### End-to-end tests

A small suite will exercise complete user journeys in a staging environment:

1. Authenticate through the test SAML provider.
2. Search for an available room.
3. Create a reservation.
4. Verify that the room is no longer available.
5. Modify and cancel the reservation.
6. Create a staff block booking and verify affected reservations.
7. Confirm kiosk schedule updates.
8. Trigger a reminder using a controlled clock.
9. Generate a utilisation report.

End-to-end tests will cover critical paths rather than every business-rule combination, since exhaustive domain coverage belongs in unit tests.

#### Performance and resilience tests

A load test will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users, with representative search filters and realistic reservation data. The release gate is p95 search latency below 400 ms, with error rate below 1%.

Resilience tests will stop the application temporarily, disconnect kiosks, delay the iCal feed and make the notification provider unavailable. The expected behaviour is graceful kiosk degradation, safe retrying and no duplicate reservations or notifications.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use trunk-based development with short-lived branches and pull requests. Every pull request requires:

- Successful compilation and static analysis
- Unit tests
- Integration tests
- Contract tests
- Security and dependency scanning
- Database migration validation
- Code review by another team member
- API compatibility checks

A staging deployment is created automatically from the main branch. End-to-end and performance tests run before production release.

Production deployment will use an immutable versioned container image. The database schema will follow an expand-and-contract approach:

1. Add backward-compatible schema changes.
2. Deploy application code compatible with both old and new fields.
3. Migrate or backfill data.
4. Remove obsolete fields only in a later release.

This prevents rollback from being blocked by an incompatible database migration.

The deployment sequence is:

1. Build and scan the image.
2. Deploy to staging.
3. Run smoke and end-to-end tests.
4. Take or verify a recent database backup.
5. Deploy one production instance.
6. Run health checks and a synthetic reservation/search transaction.
7. Gradually route traffic to the new version.
8. Monitor error rate, latency and reservation conflicts.

Rollback uses the previous immutable image and can be initiated by the on-call engineer. The previous image remains available locally in the deployment registry. Automated health checks and a scripted rollback procedure will be tested during release rehearsal. The target is restoration of the previous application version within ten minutes.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will include:

- Timestamp
- Severity
- Correlation ID
- Request or job type
- Campus and room identifiers where necessary
- HTTP status
- Duration
- Error category
- Application version

Logs will not include names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions or other unnecessary PII. Staff audit records are separate from diagnostic logs and contain only the minimum required audit fields.

#### Metrics

The service will measure:

- Successful and failed requests
- Search p50, p95 and p99 latency
- Search request rate
- HTTP 5xx and timeout rates
- Database connection pool use
- Database query latency
- Cache hit rate
- Reservation conflict rate
- SAML authentication failures
- iCal feed freshness and parsing failures
- Notification queue depth and delivery failures
- Kiosk update latency
- Number and age of kiosks using stale schedules
- Application instance health
- Backup success and restore-test results

#### Alerts

Alerts will include:

- Monthly opening-hours availability forecast below 99.5%
- Any sustained 5xx rate above 1% for five minutes
- Search p95 above 400 ms for ten minutes during opening hours
- Search p99 above 1 second
- Database saturation above 80% for ten minutes
- Kiosk change-to-update latency above ten seconds for 1% or more of changes
- Kiosk cache age above fifteen minutes
- Notification queue items older than five minutes
- SAML authentication failure rate above an agreed threshold
- Failed backup or failed health check

A synthetic monitor will periodically authenticate with a test account, search for a designated test room and retrieve a kiosk schedule. Availability calculations will exclude planned maintenance but include unplanned opening-hours downtime.

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing room-reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms, create, modify and cancel reservations, while library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems: the university identity provider using SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The principal engineering challenges are enforcing reservation rules consistently, preventing double bookings, providing fast availability searches during semester-start demand, and remaining operable by a two-person team.

This document selects **Method C: Hexagonal Architecture** as the primary architectural style. The proposed system is a modular monolith with a framework-independent domain core and explicit ports and adapters for databases, identity, calendars, notifications and kiosk delivery. The design addresses all six quality requirements:

- **QR-1:** 99.5% availability during opening hours and graceful kiosk degradation.
- **QR-2:** Availability-search p95 below 400 ms for 2,000 concurrent users.
- **QR-3:** SAML authentication, staff audit records and no PII in logs.
- **QR-4:** New libraries configurable without code changes.
- **QR-5:** Reservation rules testable without a database or network.
- **QR-6:** Deployment by two people and rollback within ten minutes.

The design covers the first release and does not specify the implementation of the external identity provider, facilities calendar, inventory database or email/push providers.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Selected style: Hexagonal Architecture

CLRS will use **Hexagonal Architecture**, also known as Ports and Adapters. The domain and application logic will be independent of web frameworks, database technology and external services.

The architecture will be deployed initially as a **single modular application**. Its internal modules will include:

1. Identity and access control
2. Availability search
3. Reservation management
4. Block-booking management
5. Kiosk schedule delivery
6. Notifications
7. Reporting
8. Campus and room configuration

The domain core will contain entities and policies such as:

- `Reservation`
- `BlockBooking`
- `Room`
- `OpeningHours`
- `ReservationPolicy`
- `Availability`
- `UserRole`

Example ports include:

- `IdentityProvider`
- `ReservationRepository`
- `AvailabilityRepository`
- `RoomInventory`
- `FacilitiesCalendar`
- `NotificationSender`
- `AuditWriter`
- `KioskSchedulePublisher`
- `Clock`

Adapters will implement these ports:

- SAML identity adapter
- PostgreSQL reservation adapter
- Legacy inventory database adapter
- iCal synchronisation adapter
- Email and push notification adapters
- HTTP/REST API adapter
- Kiosk polling or server-sent-events adapter
- Metrics, audit and structured logging adapters

The database adapter will enforce transactional conflict protection in addition to domain validation. For example, reservation creation will use a transaction and an appropriate time-range uniqueness or exclusion constraint so that concurrent requests cannot create overlapping reservations for the same room.

### 2.2 Rationale against quality requirements

#### QR-1: Availability and graceful degradation

A modular monolith has one primary deployment and fewer network hops than a distributed microservice solution. This reduces operational failure points and is appropriate for a two-person team.

The kiosk adapter will maintain a local last-known schedule containing the current and next reservations. Kiosks will continue displaying this schedule when the CLRS endpoint or campus network is unavailable. The display will show the timestamp of the last successful refresh so that stale data is visible rather than misleading.

The application will use health checks, multiple application instances and a managed database with backups. These measures support the 99.5% monthly availability target.

#### QR-2: Availability-search performance

Availability searches will use a local, indexed availability store rather than querying the legacy inventory database and iCal feeds synchronously for every request. Background adapters will periodically synchronise room metadata, opening hours and external calendar blocks into this store.

The search use case will be read-oriented and can be scaled by adding application instances. Indexes will cover campus, capacity, equipment and time ranges. Frequently repeated searches may use a short-lived cache. This avoids making the 400 ms p95 target dependent on the latency of external systems.

A performance test environment will reproduce 2,000 concurrent users and measure p95 latency separately for cache hits, normal indexed searches and synchronisation periods.

#### QR-3: Security

Authentication is isolated behind the `IdentityProvider` port. The SAML adapter validates assertions and maps university identities to internal user IDs and roles. Application use cases receive an authenticated principal rather than handling SAML details themselves.

Staff operations pass through an authorization policy and generate tamper-resistant audit events. Normal application logs contain correlation IDs, operation names, status codes and timing data, but not names, email addresses, SAML assertions or reservation descriptions. User identifiers in diagnostics are pseudonymous.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Campus-specific properties will be configuration data rather than code. Configuration will include:

- Campus and library identifiers
- Room metadata and equipment
- Opening hours and holidays
- iCal feed locations
- Kiosk-to-room mappings
- Notification settings
- Reporting time-zone rules

Adding a library will therefore involve loading validated configuration and connecting its feeds. The application will reject invalid configuration at startup or during controlled configuration deployment.

#### QR-5: Testability

The reservation rules will be implemented in the framework-independent domain core. A use case can be tested with in-memory repositories, a fake clock and fake external ports. It will not require a database, network, SAML provider or notification service.

Rules such as the three-hour daily limit, overlapping reservations, cancellation, staff overrides and the 48-hour notice requirement can therefore be tested quickly and deterministically.

#### QR-6: Operability

A single deployable application is easier for two people to build, monitor and release than several independently deployed services. Releases will use immutable container images and automated database migration checks. A previous image can be redeployed quickly, supporting rollback within ten minutes.

The design does not require a distributed event broker, service mesh or complex multi-service tracing platform. Asynchronous work such as notifications and kiosk updates can be implemented using an outbox table and a worker process, while remaining within the same deployable product.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simpler to understand and deploy. It would also provide good performance and low operational overhead. However, traditional layered designs often allow application code to depend directly on framework and persistence details. That would make QR-5 harder to satisfy and could make integrations difficult to replace or test.

Hexagonal Architecture retains the operational advantages of a monolith while enforcing stronger boundaries. The trade-off is additional interfaces, dependency-injection configuration and design discipline.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They would also isolate some failures and allow separate technology choices. However, CLRS is a relatively small first release, and microservices would introduce network failures, distributed authentication, contract versioning, deployment coordination and more complex observability.

They would make QR-6 more difficult for a two-person team. Reservation consistency would also be harder if reservation, inventory and block-booking data were split across services. CLRS gives up independent service scaling and fault isolation in favour of simpler deployment and transactional consistency.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would suit kiosk updates, reporting and high-volume search. Events could provide an effective history of reservation changes and allow read models to scale independently.

However, CQRS introduces eventual consistency. A newly created reservation might not immediately appear in the search or kiosk projection, which complicates FR-4 and conflict handling. Event replay, schema evolution, duplicate delivery and projection recovery would also add operational complexity.

CLRS will use a small outbox and asynchronous worker for notifications and kiosk invalidation, but it will not make a distributed event log and CQRS the primary style. This gives up some scalability and event-replay capability but better supports QR-5, QR-6 and immediate reservation consistency.

The database and external systems are accessed only through adapters implementing application ports. The domain core does not import HTTP, SQL, SAML or provider-specific libraries.

### 3.2 FR-1 availability search walkthrough

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates syntax, obtains the authenticated principal through the SAML adapter and applies role-based access rules.
3. The availability search use case validates the time window and constructs a search request.
4. The search port queries the indexed local availability store. Room metadata comes from synchronised inventory data; external facilities blocks and CLRS reservations are incorporated into the indexed availability data.
5. The domain policy excludes rooms that are unavailable because of capacity, equipment, opening hours, facilities blocks, student reservations or staff block bookings.
6. The adapter returns matching rooms and availability information.

Synchronisation is asynchronous and records feed freshness. If a feed is stale beyond its permitted threshold, the system marks affected results as potentially stale and raises an operational alert rather than silently treating old data as current.

### 3.3 FR-4 kiosk schedule walkthrough

1. When a reservation, cancellation or block booking changes, the reservation use case commits the change and writes an outbox record in the same database transaction.
2. A worker processes the outbox record and invalidates or updates the affected room’s kiosk schedule.
3. Kiosks use conditional polling with an `ETag` or may maintain a server-sent-events connection. A changed schedule is returned immediately; unchanged schedules produce a lightweight response.
4. The target is that at least 99% of changes reach the kiosk within ten seconds.
5. Each kiosk stores the last successful schedule locally. If it loses connectivity, it continues displaying the cached schedule, labels it with its last refresh time and retries with backoff.
6. Reprocessing an outbox record is idempotent, so duplicate delivery cannot create duplicate reservations or notifications.

- Notification scheduling

A fake `Clock`, fake repositories and fake notification port ensure the tests require no database or network. This directly satisfies QR-5. Boundary-value and property-based tests will be used for time intervals and daily limits.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will verify real adapters and infrastructure:

- PostgreSQL transactions and overlap constraints
- Database migrations
- Availability indexes
- Outbox atomicity
- iCal parsing and synchronisation
- Legacy PostgreSQL read-only access
- Kiosk cache and ETag behaviour
- Email/push provider adapter
- Configuration loading for a new campus

Test databases will be created per pipeline run and seeded with anonymised data.

#### Contract tests

Consumer/provider contracts will be defined for:

- HTTP API clients and the CLRS API
- Kiosk clients and kiosk schedule responses
- SAML assertion mapping
- iCal feed assumptions
- Notification provider requests

Contract tests will detect incompatible changes before deployment. The SAML integration will use representative signed test assertions, without using production identities.

#### End-to-end tests

A small number of browser and kiosk scenarios will run against a deployed test environment:

1. User signs in through SAML.
2. User searches for a room.
3. User reserves an available room.
4. A second user receives a conflict response.
5. Staff creates a block booking.
6. The affected kiosk receives the updated schedule within ten seconds.
7. A reminder is scheduled and sent through a test notification provider.
8. Staff exports a utilisation report.

End-to-end tests will not attempt to duplicate the full unit-test suite; their purpose is to verify the complete deployed path.

#### Non-functional and security testing

Load tests will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users at semester-start traffic levels. The acceptance criterion is availability-search p95 below 400 ms, with error rate below 1%.

Security tests will include dependency scanning, static analysis, authentication bypass tests, authorization tests, injection tests and verification that known PII values do not appear in application logs. Audit records will be checked for staff actions, actor role, action, target resource, timestamp and outcome.

### 4.2 Delivery

The team will use short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. `main` must always be releasable. Feature flags will be used for incomplete user-visible features rather than long-lived branches.

Every pull request must pass:

- Compilation and formatting checks
- Static analysis
- Unit tests
- Integration tests
- Contract tests
- Dependency and container vulnerability scans
- Database migration validation
- Coverage thresholds for domain and application modules

A nightly pipeline will run full end-to-end and load tests.

Deployments will use an immutable versioned container image. The pipeline will deploy first to a staging environment, run smoke tests, and then perform a rolling production deployment. Database migrations must be backward-compatible with both the current and previous application version.

For rollback, the previous container image remains available. If health checks, error rates or latency regress after deployment, the operator redeploys the previous image using the deployment platform. Rollback is practised monthly and must complete within ten minutes. Changes to irreversible database schemas require a separate migration plan and are not included in the fast rollback path.

#### Logs

Structured logs will include:

- Timestamp
- Severity
- Correlation/request ID
- Endpoint or use-case name
- HTTP status or domain outcome
- Duration
- Campus and room IDs where needed
- External dependency name and latency
- Deployment version

Logs will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions or raw request bodies. User identifiers will be hashed or replaced with an internal non-PII identifier.

Staff actions will be recorded separately in an append-only audit store. Audit records will include actor ID, role, action, affected resource, timestamp, reason where required and success/failure.

#### Metrics

The system will measure:

- Availability percentage during defined opening hours
- HTTP 5xx rate and request error rate
- Search request count and p50/p95/p99 latency
- Search latency by campus and response-cache status
- Database connection pool usage
- Database query latency
- Synchronisation success, failure and feed age
- Outbox backlog and oldest outbox age
- Kiosk update propagation latency
- Number of kiosks using stale schedules
- Notification success and failure rates

#### Alerts

Alerts will include:

- Monthly availability burn rate indicating risk of falling below 99.5%
- Any five-minute 5xx rate above 1%
- Availability-search p95 above 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal load
- Database latency or connection saturation above 80% for ten minutes
- Outbox oldest age above 30 seconds or backlog above 1,000 records
- More than 1% of kiosk updates exceeding ten seconds
- Any kiosk remaining offline for 15 minutes
- iCal or inventory feed age exceeding its agreed threshold

A synthetic search and kiosk-change monitor will run continuously from each campus. These probes measure the requirements from outside the application rather than relying only on internal health checks.
