## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application policies. They will test:

- Reservation overlap and conflict detection
- Three-hour daily limit
- Create, modify and cancel rules
- Ownership and staff authorisation
- Recurring block bookings
- The 48-hour notice rule
- Opening hours and time-zone boundaries
- Equipment and capacity filtering
- Idempotency and duplicate command handling

Repositories, clocks and notification ports will be replaced by in-memory fakes. This directly satisfies QR-5 because reservation rules run without a database or network. Unit tests must run on every pull request, with branch coverage targets for domain rules, particularly boundary cases.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will use containerised PostgreSQL and verify:

- Transactional reservation creation
- Database constraints preventing overlapping reservations
- Migration correctness
- Query indexes and availability filtering
- Outbox insertion and retry behaviour
- Read-model synchronisation
- Persistence of audit records

These tests will also verify that a failed notification or kiosk delivery does not roll back a successful reservation transaction.

#### Contract tests

Contract tests will protect boundaries with external systems and clients:

- HTTP/OpenAPI contracts for web and kiosk endpoints
- SAML claims, role and expiry assumptions
- iCal parsing and time-zone behaviour
- Legacy inventory database schema and read-only access
- Email/push provider request and response formats
- Kiosk schedule payloads and schedule-version semantics

External provider sandbox environments will be used in scheduled CI jobs. Consumer-driven contracts will ensure that API changes do not silently break kiosk clients.

#### End-to-end tests

A small number of end-to-end tests will run against a deployed test environment. They will verify:

- SAML login followed by a room search
- Successful reservation and conflict response
- Staff block-booking workflow
- Reservation change appearing on the kiosk
- Reminder job producing a notification
- Monthly report export

End-to-end tests will not attempt to cover every rule; that responsibility belongs to unit and integration tests. This keeps the suite reliable and sufficiently fast for continuous delivery.

#### Non-functional testing

- Load tests will simulate 2,000 concurrent users and confirm search p95 below 400 ms.
- Soak tests will run during a representative opening-hours period.
- Failure tests will disconnect kiosks, stop notification delivery and make external feeds unavailable.
- Security tests will check SAML validation, privilege escalation, injection, secrets handling and PII leakage.
- Rollback drills will measure whether the previous release can be restored within ten minutes.

### 4.2 Delivery

The team will use short-lived feature branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires review by the other team member where practical.

CI gates will include:

1. Formatting, static analysis and dependency vulnerability checks.
2. Unit tests and coverage threshold.
3. Integration tests with PostgreSQL.
4. Contract tests.
5. Build of the production container.
6. Migration compatibility checks.
7. A smoke test against the deployment artifact.

Changes that fail required gates cannot merge. Main-branch builds deploy automatically to a non-production environment. Production deployment requires an approval after smoke tests and a review of database migration risk.

Database migrations must be expand-and-contract migrations: add compatible structures first, deploy code that supports both versions, migrate data, and remove old structures only in a later release. This makes rollback safer.

Production deployment will use a blue-green or rolling strategy with health checks. The previous image and configuration will be retained. If error rate, reservation conflict anomalies, kiosk update delay or search latency exceeds the agreed thresholds, the team can switch traffic to the previous version. The rollback runbook will be practised before release and must complete within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will include:

- Timestamp, severity and correlation/request ID
- Operation and endpoint
- Campus and room identifiers where appropriate
- Outcome and error category
- Duration
- Schedule version for kiosk events
- External dependency name and response category

Logs will not include names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens or free-text personal data. User references will be pseudonymous. Staff audit records will be stored separately with controlled access and will include actor ID, action, target, timestamp and result.

#### Metrics

For QR-1:

- Successful and failed requests by endpoint
- Application availability during configured opening hours
- Database connection and transaction failure rates
- External feed and SAML dependency failures
- Outbox backlog size and age
- Kiosk update latency
- Number and duration of kiosk offline states
- Percentage of kiosks serving last-known schedules

For QR-2:

- Search request count and latency histogram
- Search p50, p95 and p99 latency
- Concurrent requests
- Database query duration
- Cache hit ratio
- CPU, memory and connection-pool utilisation

#### Alerts

Alerts will be actionable and tied to service-level objectives:

- Opening-hours availability below the equivalent of 99.5% monthly budget
- Search p95 above 400 ms for five consecutive minutes under meaningful traffic
- Search error rate above 2% for five minutes
- Outbox oldest item above 30 seconds, indicating risk to the ten-second kiosk objective
- More than 1% of kiosk updates exceeding ten seconds over a rolling 15-minute period
- Database connection saturation above 80% for ten minutes
- External inventory or iCal data older than the agreed freshness limit

A dashboard will show current availability, latency, dependency health, deployment version and kiosk status. Alerts will identify the likely failing component and link to the rollback or recovery runbook.

# CS 3410 Software Engineering — Assignment 2  
## Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities calendar iCal feeds and the read-only legacy PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release will provide the HTTP API, web interface, kiosk endpoint, notification processing and staff reporting functions. The architecture must support reliable reservation rules, rapid searching, secure staff administration and straightforward operation by a two-person team.

This document selects a primary architecture, explains the trade-offs against the alternatives, defines the component structure, and specifies the testing, delivery, observability and risk-management plan for implementation in Assignment 3.

The design focuses on the stated functional requirements FR-1 to FR-6 and quality requirements QR-1 to QR-6. Database technology, cloud provider, notification vendor and exact user-interface design remain open unless specified in this document.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a **modular monolith** with one deployable application and separate background workers where operationally necessary.

The central domain core will contain framework-independent reservation rules and use-case logic. External systems will be accessed through ports, with adapters for HTTP, PostgreSQL, SAML, iCal, email/push notifications and kiosk delivery.

The reservation domain will be the system of record for reservations. A relational database will provide transactional consistency and constraints preventing overlapping reservations. Search data may use indexed database tables or a read-optimised view, but reservation creation will always be validated against the authoritative domain and transaction.

This combines the testability and isolation benefits of hexagonal architecture with the operational simplicity of a small deployment.

### 2.2 Rationale against quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A single modular monolith has fewer network hops and fewer independently failing services than a microservice system. It can be deployed as multiple application instances behind a load balancer, while sharing a highly available database. The kiosk adapter stores the latest successful schedule locally and displays it with a timestamp when the network or CLRS is unavailable. This fulfils graceful degradation to a last-known schedule.

Hexagonal boundaries also allow external dependencies such as SAML, iCal and notification providers to fail independently. For example, a temporary notification outage need not prevent reservations from being created; notifications can be retried asynchronously.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability search is handled by a dedicated application use case and indexed read queries. Room attributes, campus, opening hours and reservation intervals will have appropriate indexes. Since the application is not split into several synchronous services, a search request avoids API-gateway and service-to-service latency. Horizontal application scaling and connection pooling will support the target of p95 below 400 ms for 2,000 concurrent users.

A load test will validate the design at semester-start traffic levels. If search becomes the dominant bottleneck, the search port can later be backed by a dedicated read store without changing the domain core.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
SAML authentication is implemented as an inbound adapter. The domain and application layers receive a verified user identity and roles rather than handling SAML directly. Staff-only commands are authorised by application policies and produce audit records through an audit port. Logs use a correlation ID and technical identifiers but exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions and other PII.

Centralising the application also makes it easier to apply common authentication, authorisation, input validation and audit policies consistently.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus, library, room, equipment, opening-hours and calendar settings are represented as configuration or managed data. The application uses a campus identifier rather than hard-coded campus-specific branches. Onboarding a new library should therefore involve adding configuration, importing room data and validating integration settings, without changing application code.

Adapters isolate differences in iCal feeds, inventory schemas and notification providers. A new campus-specific feed can be supported by configuring an existing adapter or adding an adapter without changing reservation rules.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation rules are placed in a framework- and database-independent domain core. For example, the three-hour daily limit, overlap detection, opening-hours validation, staff block-booking rules and 48-hour notice rule can be tested using in-memory objects and fake ports. Unit tests do not require a database, SAML provider or network.

The application layer can be tested with fake repositories and notification ports. Integration tests can separately verify real adapters and database transactions.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A modular monolith is appropriate for a two-person operational team. There is one main application artifact, one deployment pipeline and one rollback target rather than several independently versioned services. Database migrations will be backward-compatible, and deployment will use a rolling or blue-green strategy. A previous container image can be redeployed within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would also be easy to deploy and could meet basic availability and operational requirements. However, conventional layered systems often allow business rules to become coupled to controllers, ORM models or database queries. That would make QR-5 weaker: testing reservation rules could require database setup.

Layering also does not by itself define how to isolate SAML, iCal and notification failures. Hexagonal ports make those boundaries explicit. The selected design gives up some of the simplicity of a purely conventional layered codebase in exchange for stricter dependency direction and additional interfaces.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They could also isolate failures and allow teams to deploy components separately. However, CLRS has a two-person team and QR-6 requires simple deployment and rollback. Microservices would introduce service discovery, API versioning, distributed tracing, multiple deployment units, network failure modes and potentially distributed transaction problems during reservation creation.

A reservation operation spanning reservation, inventory and notification services could produce inconsistent outcomes unless carefully designed with sagas or events. Microservices are therefore rejected for the first release. The modular structure preserves a future extraction boundary if scale or team size justifies it. The trade-off is less independent scaling and fault isolation than Method B.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and event-driven projections would be attractive for FR-4 because kiosk and search read models could be updated from reservation events. It would also support asynchronous notifications and audit history. However, event propagation introduces eventual consistency. A kiosk or search result could temporarily show a reservation change that is not yet reflected in the authoritative reservation decision. Meeting the ten-second kiosk target would require monitoring projection lag and handling duplicate, missing or out-of-order events.

An event log, replayable projections and separate read models would also increase operational complexity for the small team. The selected design will still publish domain events after successful commits and process notifications asynchronously, but it will not make the entire system event-sourced or CQRS-based. The trade-off is less natural horizontal scaling for read models and less built-in historical replay.

The domain core depends on abstractions such as `ReservationRepository`, `RoomCatalog`, `Clock`, `NotificationSender` and `AuditWriter`. Concrete database, identity, calendar and notification implementations are outside the core.

The CLRS database contains reservations, campus configuration, audit records, an outbox of committed events and the latest kiosk schedule cache. The outbox ensures that notification and kiosk-update work is not lost after a successful reservation transaction.

### 3.2 FR-1 availability search walkthrough

1. The user sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=`.  
2. The HTTP adapter validates syntax, authenticates the SAML session/token and creates a `SearchAvailability` command containing a user identity and search criteria.  
3. The application layer checks that the requested time window is valid and calls the `RoomCatalog` and availability ports.  
4. The inventory adapter reads room capacity and equipment from the synchronised legacy inventory representation. iCal closures and opening hours are applied through the availability component.  
5. The database query uses campus, capacity, equipment and time-range indexes to exclude overlapping student or staff bookings.  
6. The response is returned without contacting notification services. Search is read-only and can be cached briefly where safe.  
7. Reservation creation does not trust a previous search result. It repeats the conflict check inside a database transaction and uses an exclusion constraint or equivalent locking strategy to prevent two concurrent users reserving the same room.

### 3.3 FR-4 kiosk schedule walkthrough

1. A kiosk requests `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule`, or maintains a server-sent-event/polling connection.  
2. After a successful reservation, modification, cancellation or block-booking operation, the application writes the change and an outbox event in the same transaction.  
3. A kiosk-update worker consumes the event, calculates the current and next schedule, and updates the kiosk cache.  
4. Kiosks poll at a suitable interval, such as five seconds, or receive a push notification. The endpoint returns the schedule version and update timestamp.  
5. The target is that the change reaches the kiosk within ten seconds.  
6. If the kiosk cannot contact CLRS, it displays the cached schedule and clearly indicates its last update time. The kiosk never invents a new booking while offline.  
7. Retries are idempotent using the room ID and schedule version. Monitoring measures event-to-kiosk propagation latency.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application policies:

- reservation overlap detection;
- maximum three hours per user per day;
- opening-hours validation;
- equipment and capacity rules;
- modification and cancellation ownership;
- recurring staff block bookings;
- 48-hour notice and override rules;
- time-zone and daylight-saving boundaries;
- idempotency and duplicate commands.

Tests use in-memory entities, fake repositories and a controllable clock. They require no database or network, directly satisfying QR-5. Target: at least 90% line coverage for domain code and full branch coverage for critical reservation policies.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance and verify:

- transaction boundaries;
- overlapping-booking constraints under concurrent requests;
- migrations;
- reservation and outbox atomicity;
- report queries;
- kiosk-cache updates;
- inventory synchronisation;
- iCal parsing and time-zone handling.

External dependencies will use sandbox services or recorded test fixtures. These tests confirm that adapters correctly implement the ports.

#### Contract tests

Contract tests will protect integrations:

- SAML attribute and role mapping;
- expected iCal feed structure;
- legacy PostgreSQL schema and read-only access;
- notification-provider request and retry semantics;
- HTTP response schemas, including `409 Conflict`.

Provider contracts or representative fixtures will run in CI. Any change to an external integration must update and pass its contract tests.

#### End-to-end tests

A small critical-path suite will run in a staging environment:

1. authenticate through a SAML test identity;
2. search for a room;
3. create a reservation;
4. verify a conflicting reservation receives `409`;
5. modify and cancel the reservation;
6. create a staff block booking;
7. verify the kiosk schedule changes;
8. verify a notification is queued;
9. generate a staff utilisation report.

The suite will avoid testing every domain rule through the UI; those rules belong in fast unit tests.

#### Non-functional tests

A performance test will generate 2,000 concurrent users with realistic search distributions and confirm search p95 below 400 ms, with error rate below 1%. A resilience test will stop notification, iCal and inventory dependencies independently and verify that reservations and cached kiosk schedules behave as designed. A deployment rehearsal will demonstrate rollback within ten minutes.

Security testing will include dependency scanning, static analysis, authentication bypass tests, authorisation tests, audit verification and checks that PII is not emitted in logs.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use trunk-based development with short-lived branches and mandatory pull requests. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer, passing automated checks and a linked requirement or defect.

The CI pipeline will include:

1. formatting and linting;
2. static analysis and dependency vulnerability scanning;
3. unit tests;
4. integration and contract tests;
5. build of an immutable container image;
6. migration compatibility checks;
7. staging end-to-end tests;
8. performance smoke tests.

The main branch produces a versioned container image. Deployment uses backward-compatible expand-and-contract database migrations:

- add new schema elements first;
- deploy code that supports old and new fields;
- migrate data;
- remove obsolete fields only in a later release.

Production deployment will use a rolling or blue-green strategy with health checks. Feature flags will allow risky functions, such as push kiosk updates, to be disabled without a redeployment.

Before deployment, the team records the current image version, migration version and rollback command. If health checks fail, error rate rises, or latency breaches the defined threshold, traffic is returned to the previous image. Rollback will be rehearsed at least once per release cycle and must complete within ten minutes. Irreversible database changes are prohibited in the same release as the code depending on them.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will contain timestamp, severity, service version, correlation ID, operation, campus identifier, room identifier where necessary, result and duration. They will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation notes or other PII.

Security audit records, stored separately with restricted access, will record staff actor ID, action, target entity, timestamp, result and reason. Audit retention and access will follow university policy.

#### Metrics

For QR-1:

- successful and failed request counts by endpoint;
- uptime during configured opening hours;
- HTTP 5xx rate;
- database availability and connection-pool exhaustion;
- SAML, iCal, inventory and notification adapter failure rates;
- outbox backlog and retry count;
- kiosk heartbeat success rate;
- percentage of kiosks using cached schedules;
- reservation event-to-kiosk update latency;
- percentage of kiosk updates completed within ten seconds.

For QR-2:

- search request latency p50, p95 and p99;
- concurrent request count;
- search timeout and error rate;
- database query latency;
- cache hit rate;
- CPU, memory, connection-pool and database resource usage.

#### Alerts and dashboards

Alerts will include:

- monthly availability burn rate indicating that 99.5% availability may be missed;
- sustained 5xx rate above 2% for five minutes;
- search p95 above 400 ms for ten minutes during opening hours;
- search p99 above 1 second;
- kiosk update SLO below 99% within ten seconds over a fifteen-minute window;
- any kiosk offline for fifteen minutes;
- outbox backlog older than two minutes;
- database replication or storage warnings;
- repeated SAML failures.

A dashboard will show current and monthly SLO compliance, latency by endpoint and dependency health. Alerts will include runbook links and identify whether rollback, scaling or dependency escalation is required.

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel reservations. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservations.

CLRS must integrate with three external systems: the university identity provider through SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and the read-only legacy room-inventory PostgreSQL database. The first release will be a centrally deployed web application with kiosk clients.

This design focuses on the architecture and quality plan rather than full implementation. The design prioritises:

- reliable reservation rules and prevention of conflicting bookings;
- fast room availability searches during semester-start demand;
- secure authentication and staff auditing;
- configuration-based onboarding of additional libraries;
- testability of reservation rules without databases or networks; and
- simple deployment and rapid rollback by a two-person operations team.

The proposed solution is a **hexagonal architecture implemented as a modular monolith**. The domain and application logic remain independent of frameworks, databases and external services. Adapters provide HTTP, persistence, SAML, iCal, notifications and kiosk integration.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Selected style

The selected primary style is **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a single deployable modular monolith.

The system will be divided into modules such as:

- Reservations;
- Rooms and opening hours;
- Block bookings;
- Notifications;
- Reporting; and
- Identity and audit.

The central domain core contains reservation entities, value objects and business rules. It communicates with the outside world through ports. Inbound ports expose use cases such as `SearchAvailability`, `CreateReservation`, `ModifyReservation`, `CancelReservation` and `CreateBlockBooking`. Outbound ports abstract repositories, identity verification, calendar imports, notification delivery and time.

Adapters implement those ports. For example, a REST controller is an inbound adapter, while PostgreSQL repositories, the SAML client, the iCal importer and an email provider are outbound adapters.

The monolith will use one transactional reservation database. Availability searches can use indexed tables and a derived availability table or cache, while reservation creation remains protected by a database transaction and a definitive conflict check.

### 2.2 Rationale and quality trade-offs

#### QR-1: Availability

A modular monolith has fewer independently failing network components than a microservice system. The reservation API, search API and kiosk schedule API can be deployed together and monitored as one service. Database replication, health checks and multiple application instances can support the 99.5% opening-hours availability target.

Kiosks will store the last successfully retrieved schedule locally, including its retrieval timestamp. If the CLRS API or kiosk network is unavailable, the display will show the last-known schedule with an “offline” indicator rather than becoming blank. Kiosk requests will be read-only and separated from reservation writes so heavy searches or notification processing do not unnecessarily prevent schedule reads.

Hexagonal boundaries also permit external systems to be replaced or temporarily bypassed. For example, an iCal adapter can cache the most recent successful feed rather than making every user request depend on the facilities calendar.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability searches are read-heavy and can be optimised without changing domain rules. The search adapter will use database indexes on campus, room capacity, equipment and reservation time ranges. Frequently requested room metadata and opening hours can be cached. Search results will not call SAML, iCal or the legacy inventory database synchronously; those sources will be synchronised or cached by background adapters.

A performance budget will target a p95 below 400 ms under 2,000 concurrent users. Multiple stateless application instances can be added behind a load balancer. A modular monolith is sufficient for the expected first-release scale and avoids the additional latency of several service-to-service calls.

The trade-off is that all modules share a deployment and potentially a database. A poorly optimised reporting query could affect reservation traffic. This will be mitigated through read-only reporting connections, query limits, scheduled report generation and resource monitoring.

#### QR-3: Security

The SAML integration is isolated behind an identity port and adapter. Controllers receive a verified user identity and roles; the domain does not need to understand SAML assertions. Staff-only use cases perform explicit authorisation checks and write audit records.

The application will use structured logs containing request IDs, operation names, status codes and non-identifying internal IDs. Names, email addresses, SAML assertions and other PII will not be logged. Audit records will be separate from operational logs and will record the staff actor’s internal identifier, action, target resource, timestamp and outcome.

A single application boundary simplifies security review and deployment. However, the monolith has a larger blast radius than isolated services: a vulnerability in one module could affect the whole application. Dependency scanning, least-privilege database access, secure headers, central authentication and regular penetration testing will reduce this risk.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Library, campus, room, equipment and opening-hour information will be represented as configuration and data rather than hard-coded conditionals. A new library can therefore be onboarded by adding authorised configuration, room data, calendar-feed details and kiosk registrations.

Adapters isolate campus-specific integration details. For example, different iCal feed formats can be handled by adapter configuration or a feed-specific adapter without changing reservation rules. The modular structure prevents campus-specific code from spreading through the domain.

The compromise is that configuration must be validated carefully. Invalid opening hours, duplicate room identifiers or an incorrect calendar mapping could cause operational errors. Configuration changes will therefore use schema validation, review, an audit trail and a staging preview.

#### QR-5: Testability

The reservation domain will be framework-independent. Rules such as the three-hour daily limit, time-window validity, room eligibility, conflict detection, cancellation and 48-hour block-booking notice will be implemented as pure domain services or entities.

Tests can instantiate the domain using in-memory objects and a fake clock. No database, HTTP server, SAML provider or network is required. This directly satisfies QR-5 and allows fast, comprehensive unit testing.

Hexagonal ports also make external failures testable. Fake repositories can simulate conflicts, unavailable calendar feeds and notification failures. Contract tests can verify that adapters conform to the interfaces expected by the application core.

#### QR-6: Operability

A single deployable application is appropriate for a two-person team. It requires fewer repositories, pipelines, dashboards, service credentials and operational procedures than microservices. The application will be packaged as an immutable container and deployed using a rolling or blue-green strategy.

Database changes will use backward-compatible migrations. The previous application version will remain available during deployment, and rollback will consist of switching traffic to the previous image. The rollback procedure will be rehearsed and must complete within ten minutes.

The trade-off is reduced independent scaling. For example, reporting cannot be deployed separately from reservations. This is acceptable for the first release; module boundaries preserve a future extraction path if operational evidence justifies it.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives

#### Method A: Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and could meet QR-6. It would also provide reasonable performance and availability. However, conventional layers often allow domain logic to depend gradually on persistence or web frameworks. That would make QR-5 weaker and make integrations harder to replace. The selected hexagonal structure retains the deployment simplicity of a monolith while enforcing stronger dependency direction.

#### Method B: Microservices

Microservices would allow reservation, notification, inventory and reporting to scale and deploy independently. They might isolate failures and allow teams to work independently.

For this project, the costs outweigh those benefits. A two-person team would need to operate multiple services, service discovery or gateway configuration, distributed tracing, separate deployment pipelines and cross-service authentication. Reservation consistency would be harder if data were distributed. Network failures would threaten QR-1, and service calls could make QR-2 harder to achieve. Microservices would also increase rollback complexity and make QR-6 less achievable. The system’s current scale does not justify this operational burden.

#### Method D: Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and event-driven projections would be strong for kiosk updates, search read models, audit history and high read scalability. Events could notify kiosks and reminders asynchronously.

However, event propagation introduces eventual consistency. A reservation might not appear in the search or kiosk projection immediately, complicating the ten-second kiosk requirement and making conflict feedback less direct. Event replay, schema evolution, idempotency, dead-letter queues and operational recovery would be substantial for a first release. The selected design may publish application events internally and use an outbox for notifications, but it does not make event-driven CQRS the primary architecture.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. The client sends campus, capacity, equipment and time-window parameters to `GET /rooms`.
2. The REST adapter validates syntax and converts the request into a `SearchAvailability` command.
3. The application service reads room metadata, opening hours and reservations through outbound ports.
4. The search query uses indexed reservation time ranges and room attributes. Cached room and opening-hour data may be used.
5. The domain service excludes rooms that are closed, lack the requested equipment or overlap an existing reservation or block booking.
6. The adapter returns available rooms and times to the client.

The search path does not synchronously contact SAML, iCal or the legacy database. Authentication is validated at the application boundary, while external data is synchronised and cached. This supports the QR-2 latency target and prevents external outages from making searches unavailable.

Reservation creation repeats the definitive conflict check inside a database transaction. Search results are therefore advisory; the create operation returns `409 Conflict` if another reservation has claimed the room.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A kiosk calls `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` initially and periodically thereafter.
2. The kiosk stores the returned schedule, version and retrieval timestamp locally.
3. When a reservation changes, the application commits the change and publishes a room-specific update through an internal update publisher.
4. A kiosk can receive the update through server-sent events or short polling. The target is that the new schedule is available within ten seconds.
5. If the kiosk cannot contact CLRS, it continues displaying its last-known schedule, marks itself offline and retries with backoff.
6. The schedule endpoint returns only the current and next reservation information required by the display.

The update event is published after the reservation transaction commits. An outbox record prevents a successful database change from losing its kiosk update or notification work.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application services. Representative cases include:

- reservations cannot overlap;
- a user cannot exceed three hours per day;
- reservations must fall within opening hours;
- room capacity and equipment requirements are enforced;
- users may modify or cancel only permitted reservations;
- staff block bookings follow the 48-hour notice rule;
- block bookings override student reservations according to the agreed policy;
- recurring booking expansion is correct across time zones and daylight-saving changes; and
- reminder times are calculated as 15 minutes before the start.

The tests use in-memory repositories, fixed clocks and fake notification ports. They require no database or network, satisfying QR-5. Boundary-value and property-based tests will be used for time intervals and daily-hour calculations.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will verify adapters and persistence:

- repository queries against a disposable PostgreSQL instance;
- transaction isolation and concurrent reservation conflicts;
- database indexes and migration scripts;
- iCal parsing and synchronisation;
- SAML assertion mapping and role extraction;
- outbox processing and retry behaviour; and
- kiosk schedule retrieval and cache headers.

The legacy inventory database will be represented by a controlled test database or approved read-only test instance.

#### Contract tests

Contract tests will define stable interfaces between the application and external providers. They will verify:

- SAML response claims and staff-role mappings;
- supported iCal feed formats;
- email/push notification request and retry semantics;
- kiosk API response schema and version handling; and
- REST status codes, including `401`, `403`, `409` and validation errors.

Provider contracts will run in CI where test environments are available and in scheduled integration jobs otherwise.

#### End-to-end tests

A small critical-path suite will run against a deployed test environment:

1. authenticate through a SAML test identity;
2. search for a room;
3. create a reservation;
4. verify a conflicting reservation is rejected;
5. modify and cancel the reservation;
6. create a staff block booking;
7. verify the kiosk schedule changes; and
8. verify an audit record and notification job are created.

The suite will avoid testing every business-rule combination, since those cases belong in unit tests.

#### Non-functional tests

Before release, the team will run:

- load tests with 2,000 concurrent users, with realistic search distributions;
- performance tests verifying search p95 below 400 ms;
- failure tests for database, iCal, notification and kiosk-network outages;
- deployment and rollback rehearsals targeting less than ten minutes;
- security scanning of dependencies and containers; and
- a test confirming that generated logs contain no PII.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use short-lived feature branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires code review and passing CI. CI gates will include formatting, static analysis, unit tests, integration tests, contract tests, dependency vulnerability scanning and migration validation.

Merges to `main` produce a versioned container image and deploy automatically to a test environment. A release candidate requires successful end-to-end and load-smoke tests. Production deployment will use blue-green or rolling deployment with health checks and a smoke test before traffic is switched.

Database migrations must be backward-compatible with both the current and previous application versions. Destructive changes will be performed only in a later release.

The previous container image and configuration will be retained. If smoke tests fail, error rates increase, or the performance SLO is breached, the operator will switch traffic back to the previous version. Rollback runbooks will be documented and rehearsed monthly. The target is a completed application rollback within ten minutes. Backups and point-in-time recovery will protect data; application rollback will not automatically undo committed reservations.

### 4.3 Observability

Operational telemetry will use metrics, structured logs and distributed traces.

Metrics include:

- successful and failed request counts by endpoint;
- opening-hours availability percentage;
- application health-check success;
- database connection-pool utilisation;
- reservation transaction conflicts;
- kiosk schedule update latency;
- number and age of stale kiosks;
- iCal synchronisation success and age of last successful feed;
- notification queue depth and delivery delay;
- search latency p50, p95 and p99; and
- active concurrent users.

QR-1 dashboards will show monthly uptime during opening hours, API error rate, database health, stale kiosk count and dependency failures. Alerts will trigger on:

- projected monthly availability below 99.5%;
- sustained elevated 5xx responses;
- no successful iCal synchronisation within an agreed threshold;
- a kiosk schedule older than the permitted freshness period; and
- notification or outbox queues exceeding their threshold.

QR-2 dashboards will show availability-search latency segmented by campus and response status. Alerts will trigger if p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal load, or if database CPU, locks or connection pools approach defined capacity limits.

They will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, free-text user data or reservation details that constitute PII. Audit logs will be access-controlled and retained separately.

# Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS)  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing room-reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students can search for rooms, create or change reservations, cancel reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff can manage rooms and opening hours, create recurring block bookings, and export utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release must provide reliable operation during opening hours, fast availability searches during semester-start demand, secure authentication and auditing, configuration-based onboarding of new campuses, independently testable reservation rules, and rapid deployment and rollback by a two-person operations team.

This document defines the architecture for the first release and the associated testing, delivery, observability, and risk-management plan. It does not specify the implementation of every feature or the detailed user-interface design.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Selected style: Hexagonal architecture

The primary architectural style will be **hexagonal architecture**, also called ports-and-adapters architecture. CLRS will initially be delivered as a modular monolith with a framework-independent domain core. The core will contain reservation policies and use cases, while external systems will be accessed through explicit ports implemented by adapters.

The main principle is that business rules do not depend directly on HTTP, PostgreSQL, SAML, iCal, email, push notifications, or kiosk protocols.

The system will contain:

- **Domain core**
  - Reservation, room, opening-hours, block-booking and user concepts.
  - Policies for conflicts, three-hour daily limits, modification, cancellation, and 48-hour block-booking notice.
  - No database, network, framework, or identity-provider dependencies.

- **Application services**
  - Search availability.
  - Create, modify, and cancel reservations.
  - Create recurring block bookings.
  - Import facilities schedules.
  - Generate utilisation reports.
  - Schedule reminders.
  - Publish room-schedule changes.

- **Inbound adapters**
  - REST/JSON API for web clients and staff tools.
  - Kiosk API and Server-Sent Events (SSE) endpoint.
  - Scheduled jobs for imports and reminders.

- **Outbound ports and adapters**
  - Reservation repository backed by the CLRS database.
  - Availability-search repository backed by indexed reservation and room data.
  - SAML authentication adapter.
  - iCal import adapter.
  - Read-only legacy inventory adapter.
  - Email/push notification adapter.
  - Audit-log adapter.
  - Kiosk update publisher.

The monolith may use an internal transactional outbox for reliable notification and kiosk-update delivery. This is an implementation mechanism within the hexagonal system, not a separate externally deployed microservice architecture.

### 2.2 Rationale and quality trade-offs

#### QR-1: Availability

A single deployable application is simpler for a two-person team to operate and reduces network dependencies between services. Database transactions can enforce reservation conflict rules atomically. Health checks, connection pooling, timeouts, and retry policies will protect the application from temporary failures in external integrations.

Kiosk schedules will be cached locally in the kiosk browser or device. Each successful response contains the schedule, a version, and a retrieval timestamp. If the kiosk loses connectivity, it displays the last-known schedule with an “offline” indicator rather than becoming blank. The application will use SSE for rapid updates, with polling as a fallback.

The trade-off is that a monolith is a larger failure domain than independently deployed services. A defect in one module could affect the whole application. This risk is mitigated by modular boundaries, automated tests, health checks, and staged deployment.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability search will use a dedicated indexed read structure rather than repeatedly querying the legacy inventory database. Relevant room attributes and reservation intervals will be stored in the CLRS database and indexed by campus, capacity, equipment, and time range. Frequently requested room metadata may also be cached.

The application can be horizontally scaled behind a load balancer if semester-start traffic requires it. Stateless HTTP handling allows additional instances to be added without changing the domain model.

The trade-off is that search data may be briefly stale while iCal or inventory imports run. Reservation creation remains authoritative and performs a final transactional conflict check, so a stale search result cannot create double bookings. Load testing will verify p95 search latency below 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users.

#### QR-3: Security

SAML authentication is isolated behind an identity port and adapter. Application services receive a trusted user identity and roles rather than processing SAML details throughout the system. Staff actions pass through an audit port. Audit records contain user identifier, role, action, target entity, result, and timestamp, but not unnecessary personal data.

Structured application logs will contain correlation IDs, campus, room ID, operation, status, and latency. They will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions, or other PII.

The trade-off is that centralising authentication in one application means a CLRS outage affects all user operations. This is acceptable for the first release because authentication still depends on the university identity provider regardless of deployment style. Short-lived operational caches may support graceful handling of transient SAML metadata failures, but they will not bypass authentication.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Campus-specific information such as campus identifier, opening hours, room attributes, time zone, notification settings, and iCal feed locations will be configuration data. The core application will use the same policies for all campuses. A new campus should therefore require configuration, data migration or import, and operational setup, not a code change.

Adapters isolate campus-specific integration differences. For example, different iCal feed formats can be handled by an adapter or mapping configuration without changing reservation rules.

The trade-off is that configuration becomes a potential source of errors. Configuration will be schema-validated, reviewed, version-controlled, and checked in a staging environment before activation.

#### QR-5: Testability

The reservation domain will use dependency inversion. For example, the reservation service depends on ports such as `ReservationRepository`, `RoomCatalog`, `Clock`, and `NotificationPublisher`. Unit tests can provide in-memory fakes and a fixed clock. They therefore test conflict detection, daily limits, block-booking notice, opening-hours rules, and cancellation without a database or network.

This directly satisfies QR-5 and reduces the cost of testing the most important business rules.

#### QR-6: Operability

A modular monolith has one main application artifact, one release pipeline, and fewer runtime components than a microservice solution. It can be deployed by a two-person team using an immutable container image and a managed database. Database migrations will be backward-compatible and run separately from application activation.

Blue-green or canary deployment will keep the previous version available. If health checks or key metrics fail, traffic can be switched back to the previous image within ten minutes.

The trade-off is that individual features cannot be deployed independently. This is acceptable for the first release because the team is small and operational simplicity has higher priority than independent service scaling.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives

#### Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be easy to understand and deploy. It would likely perform well and have low operational complexity. However, if domain code is allowed to depend directly on persistence or web frameworks, reservation rules become difficult to test without a database, weakening QR-5. It also provides weaker protection against integration concerns spreading through the codebase. Hexagonal architecture retains the deployment simplicity of a monolith while giving stronger dependency boundaries.

#### Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications, reporting, and reservations. They would isolate some failures and permit independent deployment. However, they introduce service discovery, network failures, distributed tracing, multiple deployment pipelines, data ownership decisions, and more operational work. A two-person team would have difficulty meeting QR-6 while maintaining consistent reservation transactions. Distributed reservation and block-booking rules would be more complex to test and operate. Microservices may be reconsidered when scale or team size justifies them.

#### Event-driven architecture with CQRS

Event-driven CQRS would naturally support kiosk updates, notification processing, audit history, and highly scalable search projections. It would also allow read and write models to scale separately. However, it introduces eventual consistency, event-schema management, replay and projection recovery, and more complicated debugging. A user could search for a room immediately before a projection reflects a new booking. Although the final command could still enforce consistency, the design would be unnecessarily complex for the first release. The selected design can use an outbox and internal notifications, leaving a future path toward event-driven projections if required.

### 3.2 FR-1: Search availability walkthrough

1. The client sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=`.
2. The REST adapter validates syntax, authenticates the user through the SAML-backed session, and maps the request to a `SearchAvailability` command.
3. The application service queries the availability repository through a port.
4. The repository uses indexed CLRS room and reservation data. It excludes rooms whose opening hours, facilities closures, student reservations, or staff block bookings overlap the requested interval.
5. Results are returned with room ID, campus, capacity, equipment, and available time information.
6. The application records request duration and outcome using a correlation ID, without logging PII.

The search result is not the final authority for booking. When a reservation is created, the domain service and database transaction re-check the conflict and daily three-hour limit.

### 3.3 FR-4: Kiosk update walkthrough

1. A kiosk requests `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` and receives the current and next reservations, schedule version, and retrieval timestamp.
2. The kiosk opens an SSE connection for its room. If SSE is unavailable, it polls at a configured interval.
3. When a reservation, cancellation, modification, or block booking is committed, the application writes an outbox record in the same transaction.
4. The worker publishes a room-specific update. The kiosk fetches the latest schedule and replaces its cached schedule.
5. The target is that the update is visible within ten seconds of the committed change.
6. If the kiosk is offline, it continues showing its last-known schedule, clearly marked with its age and offline status. On reconnection it retrieves the latest version.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application services using fakes for all ports. Important cases include:

#### Integration tests

- Database migrations and rollback compatibility.
- Report aggregation.

Tests will also exercise the adapters against controlled test doubles for email, push, SAML metadata, iCal feeds, and the legacy database.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will be maintained for external boundaries:

- Two users attempt the same room simultaneously; exactly one succeeds.
- Staff creates a block booking and affected student reservations are handled correctly.
- A reservation change reaches a kiosk.
- A reminder is generated.
- Staff exports a utilisation report.

End-to-end tests will run in staging on every release candidate. They will not replace the faster domain and integration tests.

#### Non-functional tests

- Load tests will simulate 2,000 concurrent users searching at semester-start patterns. The release gate is p95 below 400 ms under the agreed test environment.
- Failure-injection tests will stop the SAML provider, iCal feed, notification provider, database connection, and kiosk network.
- Security tests will check authorization, SAML validation, audit completeness, injection resistance, secrets handling, and absence of PII in logs.
- Deployment rehearsals will measure rollback time, with a target of less than ten minutes.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use trunk-based development with short-lived branches and pull requests. Every change requires review by the second engineer or designated reviewer.

CI gates will include:

1. Formatting, linting, and static analysis.
2. Unit tests with a required coverage threshold for the domain core.
3. Integration and migration tests.
4. Contract tests.
5. Dependency and container vulnerability scans.
6. API/schema compatibility checks.
7. Performance smoke tests on search.
8. Build of a versioned immutable container image.

The deployment process is:

1. Merge to main creates a versioned image.
2. Deploy the image to staging.
3. Run contract, end-to-end, smoke, and selected load tests.
4. Deploy using blue-green or canary release.
5. Run health checks and compare error rate, search latency, database health, and kiosk update delay.
6. Promote only if metrics remain within thresholds.

Database changes will use an expand-migrate-contract approach. The new application version must initially work with both the old and new schema where necessary. Destructive changes occur only after the previous version is no longer required.

Rollback consists of routing traffic to the previous image and disabling the new version. The previous image and configuration remain available. Rollback will be rehearsed at least once before production and measured against the QR-6 ten-minute requirement.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logging

Structured logs will include:

- Timestamp and severity.
- Correlation/request ID.
- Operation and endpoint.
- Campus and room ID where appropriate.
- Result code and latency.
- Dependency name and failure category.
- Deployment version.

Logs will exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions, tokens, reservation text, and other PII. Staff audit records will be stored separately with controlled access and retention.

#### Metrics

For QR-1:

- Successful and failed requests by endpoint.
- Application availability during configured opening hours.
- HTTP 5xx rate and timeout rate.
- Database connection failures and transaction failures.
- SAML authentication failure rate.
- Outbox backlog and oldest outbox message age.
- Kiosk connection status and last successful refresh.
- Kiosk schedule age and update propagation latency.

For QR-2:

- Search request count and latency histogram.
- p50, p95, p99 search latency.
- Search error and timeout rate.
- Database query duration, connection-pool saturation, CPU, memory, and cache hit rate.
- Concurrent requests and load-balancer queue time.

#### Alerts and dashboards

Alerts will include:

- Monthly opening-hours availability forecast below 99.5%.
- Search p95 above 400 ms for 15 consecutive minutes or in two consecutive five-minute windows.
- Search error rate above 1% for five minutes.
- Database saturation above 80% for ten minutes.
- Outbox backlog above 100 messages or oldest message above two minutes.
- Any kiosk update latency approaching ten seconds, with a warning at eight seconds.
- More than 5% of kiosks offline for ten minutes.

A production dashboard will show current and monthly availability, search percentiles, dependency health, kiosk freshness, and deployment version. Synthetic checks will periodically authenticate through a test SAML account and search a known campus.

# CS 3410 Software Engineering — Assignment 2  
## Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the existing study-room reservation tool used across three university libraries. Students and staff will search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel bookings. Library staff will manage opening hours, rooms and recurring block bookings. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems: the university identity provider using SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. It must also provide reminders, utilisation reports and reliable kiosk updates.

This document defines the architecture for the first release and the quality plan that will guide implementation. The design focuses on the six stated quality requirements: availability, performance, security, modifiability, testability and operability. It does not specify detailed user-interface designs, vendor selection or the final visual design of kiosk screens.

The recommended architecture is a **hexagonal architecture with a modular application core**. The reservation rules remain independent of databases, networks and web frameworks. External systems are connected through ports and adapters. This provides strong testability and makes it possible to add campuses through configuration rather than code changes, while avoiding the operational overhead of multiple independently deployed services.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture.

The central application core contains the domain model and use cases. It communicates with the outside world through interfaces, or ports. Adapters implement those ports for HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email/push providers and kiosk communication.

The first release will be deployed as a modular application rather than as several independently deployed services. Internally, the modules will be separated into reservation, room catalogue, notifications, reporting, kiosk and administration areas. This preserves clear boundaries without introducing unnecessary distributed-system complexity.

The reservation database will be the authoritative source for reservations. Search data may be cached or maintained in locally indexed tables, but creating or changing a reservation will always recheck availability against the authoritative reservation store in a transaction.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

#### QR-1 — Availability

A modular monolith has fewer runtime components than a microservice or event-driven solution. There is one primary application deployment and one transactional database, reducing the number of network calls and independently failing services. This is appropriate for a small two-person operations team.

Kiosks will use a kiosk-specific read endpoint and retain the last successfully retrieved schedule locally. If the network or CLRS is unavailable, the kiosk will show the cached schedule with its retrieval timestamp and an “offline” indicator. When connectivity returns, it refreshes automatically. This directly supports graceful degradation.

The application will use health checks, database connection pooling and multiple application instances behind a load balancer. Database backups and restore tests will be part of operations.

#### QR-2 — Performance

The search use case will read from a locally indexed room and availability representation rather than repeatedly querying the read-only legacy inventory database or remote iCal feeds. Indexes will cover campus, capacity, equipment and time ranges. Frequently requested room metadata can be cached.

The reservation creation path is separate from the search path. Search can be optimised for read throughput, while reservation commands perform the authoritative conflict check. This separation prevents search traffic from weakening reservation consistency.

The target is p95 search latency below 400 ms under a load of 2,000 concurrent users. The design supports horizontal scaling of the application while retaining a shared database. If performance testing shows that the database is the bottleneck, a read replica or dedicated search index can be introduced behind the existing outbound search port without changing the domain core.

#### QR-3 — Security

Authentication is isolated behind an `IdentityProvider` port. A SAML adapter validates assertions from the university identity provider and maps users to application identities and roles. The application core receives an authenticated user context rather than dealing directly with SAML details.

Authorisation is enforced in the application use cases, not only in the user interface. For example, only staff roles can create block bookings or export reports. Staff actions produce audit records containing the actor identifier, action type, target resource and timestamp.

Application logs will contain correlation IDs, operation names and outcomes, but not names, email addresses, SAML assertions, reservation descriptions or other unnecessary PII. Identifiers will be pseudonymised or represented by internal IDs. Audit records will be access-controlled separately from ordinary diagnostic logs.

#### QR-4 — Modifiability

Campus, library, room and opening-hour information will be represented as configuration and managed data. Adding a campus will require adding its identifier, time zone, opening hours, facilities-calendar source and room-inventory mapping. The code will not contain campus-specific conditionals.

External integrations are adapters behind ports. For example, a new calendar source can implement the calendar port without changing reservation rules. This limits the impact of changes to infrastructure or supplier systems.

#### QR-5 — Testability

The domain core has no dependency on HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal or external notification services. Reservation rules are expressed as pure use-case and domain logic. Tests can supply in-memory implementations of ports.

For example, a `CreateReservation` use case can receive an in-memory room repository and reservation repository. Tests can verify the three-hour daily limit, overlapping reservations, block-booking overrides and authorisation without starting a database or network service. This directly satisfies QR-5 and makes the most important business rules fast and deterministic to test.

#### QR-6 — Operability

A single primary deployable is simpler for a two-person team to build, monitor and recover than four independently deployed microservices. Releases will use an immutable container image and a backward-compatible database migration process. The previous image remains available so that rollback can be performed quickly.

A rolling or blue-green deployment will be used, depending on the hosting platform. A rollback runbook will be tested during staging and must restore the previous application version within ten minutes. Feature flags can disable non-critical functions such as report generation or push notifications without disabling core reservations.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be easy to deploy and may be sufficient for QR-6. However, conventional layered designs often allow application and domain code to depend directly on frameworks and database repositories. That would make QR-5 weaker because reservation rules become difficult to execute without infrastructure.

It would also make external integration details spread through the application layer. Hexagonal architecture provides the same deployment simplicity while enforcing stronger dependency boundaries. The trade-off is a small amount of additional interface and adapter code.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They would also isolate failures more strongly if designed and operated well. However, they introduce service discovery, API versioning, distributed tracing, deployment coordination, inter-service authentication and possible distributed transaction problems.

Reservation and block-booking operations require consistent conflict handling. Splitting this logic across services could make correctness harder to guarantee. Microservices would therefore increase operational risk for a two-person team and make QR-6 harder to meet. The design gives up independent service scaling and independent release schedules in exchange for simpler operations and transactional consistency.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would be attractive for kiosk updates, notifications, reporting and high-volume search. Reservation events could update read models asynchronously. However, this introduces eventual consistency: a search or kiosk projection might temporarily show outdated availability immediately after a reservation. Additional event replay, idempotency, ordering and projection-recovery mechanisms would be required.

This design gives up the scalability and natural event distribution of CQRS. Instead, the selected architecture uses transactional reservation updates plus an outbox and background worker for reliable notifications and kiosk invalidation. This provides asynchronous side effects without making the core reservation decision eventually consistent.

The worker can run as a separate process from the same image if required, but it shares the same codebase and deployment version.

### 3.2 Main components

- **HTTP/API adapter:** Implements endpoints such as `/rooms`, `/reservations`, `/block-bookings`, `/kiosk` and `/reports`. It validates request shape and converts requests into application commands.
- **SAML adapter:** Authenticates users and maps university attributes to internal user IDs and roles.
- **Application use cases:** Coordinate operations such as search, create reservation, cancel reservation, create block booking, export report and refresh kiosk data.
- **Domain core:** Contains entities and rules for rooms, reservations, recurring block bookings, opening hours and daily user limits.
- **Reservation repository adapter:** Reads and writes authoritative reservation data in PostgreSQL. It uses transactions and database constraints to prevent overlapping bookings.
- **Catalogue and calendar adapters:** Import room metadata and facilities closures into locally managed tables or cache.
- **Outbox and worker:** Records notification and kiosk-update events in the same transaction as a reservation change. A worker processes them asynchronously and retries failed delivery.
- **Kiosk adapter:** Provides polling or server-sent events. Kiosks retain the last-known schedule locally.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=C1&capacity=6&equipment=display&from=...&to=...`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates the time range and obtains the authenticated user context.
3. The search use case queries the indexed local catalogue and availability data.
4. The search logic filters rooms by campus, capacity and equipment, then excludes:
   - existing student reservations;
   - staff block bookings;
   - facilities closures and unavailable periods;
   - rooms outside opening hours.
5. Results are returned with room identifiers and available time information.
6. The response is instrumented with a correlation ID and latency metric.

Search is an optimisation path and may use a cache or read model. When a user submits a reservation, the command path performs a final authoritative conflict check in a database transaction. Therefore, a stale search result cannot create a double booking.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A kiosk authenticates using a device credential and requests `/kiosk/{roomId}/schedule`.
2. The kiosk receives the current and next reservation plus a version or last-modified timestamp.
3. The kiosk polls periodically, or maintains a server-sent-event connection where supported.
4. When a reservation is created, changed, cancelled or overridden, the transaction writes an outbox item for the affected room.
5. The worker publishes an invalidation to the kiosk adapter. The next poll or push message causes the kiosk to fetch the new schedule.
6. The target is that 95% of kiosk updates are visible within ten seconds of a successful reservation change.
7. If the kiosk loses connectivity, it displays its last-known schedule, the age of that schedule and an offline indicator. It does not claim that the cached schedule is current.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit and domain tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application use cases. Important cases include:

- overlapping and adjacent reservations;
- the three-hour daily limit;
- modification and cancellation ownership;
- staff permissions;
- recurring block bookings;
- the required 48-hour notice;
- opening hours and facilities closures;
- campus configuration;
- reminder timing;
- invalid time zones and daylight-saving transitions.

These tests use in-memory repositories and fake ports. They run on every commit and should form the majority of the test suite. They demonstrate QR-5 because no database or network is needed.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests will run against containerised PostgreSQL and test:

- transaction boundaries;
- unique and exclusion constraints for conflicting reservations;
- migrations;
- query indexes;
- outbox insertion and retry behaviour;
- report generation;
- catalogue synchronisation from representative inventory data.

External systems will generally be replaced by test doubles. A small scheduled integration environment will test the real SAML sandbox, iCal feeds and notification provider.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will specify the HTTP request and response formats, status codes and error structures. They will cover the public API, kiosk endpoint, SAML attribute mapping and notification provider interface.

Examples include confirming that a reservation conflict returns HTTP 409, unauthenticated requests return HTTP 401, and unauthorised staff operations return HTTP 403. Kiosk clients will be tested against the endpoint contract to avoid breaking deployed devices.

#### End-to-end tests

A small number of end-to-end tests will run through the browser/API, authentication test flow, database and worker. They will cover:

- searching and reserving an available room;
- rejecting a conflicting reservation;
- modifying and cancelling a reservation;
- staff creation of a block booking;
- kiosk update after a reservation change;
- reminder generation;
- report export.

End-to-end tests will not attempt to cover every business-rule combination; that responsibility belongs to unit tests.

#### Non-functional tests

Before release, load tests will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users, with realistic search filters and a smaller proportion of reservation commands. The acceptance target is search p95 below 400 ms, with error rate and database saturation also recorded.

Failure-injection tests will stop the application’s connection to iCal, the notification provider and the kiosk push channel. Kiosks must continue showing cached schedules. Security tests will check SAML validation, role enforcement, session expiry, injection attacks, access control and PII leakage in logs.

### 4.2 Delivery and rollback

The team will use short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. Every pull request requires:

- compilation and static analysis;
- unit tests;
- integration tests;
- API contract tests;
- dependency and container vulnerability scanning;
- database migration validation;
- formatting and coverage checks;
- review by the other team member.

The pipeline builds one immutable, versioned container image. Migrations must be backward compatible: additive schema changes are deployed first, followed by application changes, and destructive changes are delayed until old versions are no longer used.

Deployment proceeds to a staging environment, followed by smoke tests and a controlled production rollout. Health checks include application readiness, database connectivity and outbox-worker health. The previous image and configuration are retained.

If smoke tests fail, error rates increase, or key latency thresholds are breached, traffic is returned to the previous version. Rollback is performed by selecting the previous image and configuration, with database compatibility preserved. A rollback drill will be completed before launch and measured from decision to restored service; the target is ten minutes or less.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Availability and reliability

The service will record:

- successful and failed requests by endpoint and status;
- uptime during configured library opening hours;
- database connection and transaction failures;
- application instance health;
- outbox backlog and worker failure count;
- iCal and inventory synchronisation age;
- kiosk connection status and age of last successful refresh;
- percentage of kiosk updates delivered within ten seconds.

Alerts:

- page the on-call team if rolling monthly availability is projected below 99.5%;
- alert if the service has five minutes of continuous opening-hours unavailability;
- alert if the outbox is older than two minutes or grows continuously for ten minutes;
- alert if more than 5% of kiosks have not refreshed for five minutes;
- alert if kiosk update compliance falls below 95% over 15 minutes.

Diagnostic logs include timestamp, severity, correlation ID, endpoint, campus, room internal ID where necessary, duration and outcome. They exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions, free-text reservation information and access tokens.

#### Performance

Metrics will include request count, error rate and p50/p95/p99 latency for availability search separately from reservation commands. Database query duration, cache hit rate, CPU, memory, connection pool use and slow-query counts will also be measured.

Alerts:

- warn when search p95 exceeds 350 ms for ten minutes;
- page when search p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten minutes under normal load;
- alert when search error rate exceeds 2%;
- alert when database connection pool utilisation exceeds 80% for ten minutes.

Dashboards will show results by campus and time of day so that a global average does not hide a poorly performing library.
