## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the existing study-room reservation tool used across three university libraries. Students and staff will search for rooms and equipment, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks located outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems: the university identity provider through SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release includes room search, reservation management, staff block bookings, kiosk schedules, reminders and utilisation reports.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify implementation-level code. The most important constraints are 99.5% monthly availability during opening hours, search response time below 400 ms at the 95th percentile under 2,000 concurrent users, SAML authentication, staff auditability, configuration-only onboarding of new campuses, database-independent testing of reservation rules, and deployment and rollback by a two-person team within ten minutes.

The design prioritises a small operational footprint and strong isolation of business rules from frameworks and external systems. The proposed solution is a hexagonal modular monolith with a single deployable application and explicit ports and adapters.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C — Hexagonal architecture** as its primary architectural style.

The first release will be deployed as a modular monolith. Its domain and application components will be organised around ports, while adapters will handle HTTP, persistence, SAML, iCal, notifications, kiosk access and reporting. The architecture will use one primary application deployment and one relational database, with background workers running from the same release where practical.

Hexagonal architecture is appropriate because the core reservation rules are the most important source of correctness and must be testable without a database or network. The domain core will contain rules such as:

- a room cannot have overlapping reservations;
- a user cannot reserve more than three hours per day;
- staff block bookings have priority according to the 48-hour notice rule;
- only authorised staff can manage rooms or create blocks;
- reservation changes produce notifications and kiosk schedule updates.

These rules will depend on interfaces, not on PostgreSQL, SAML libraries or HTTP frameworks.

### 2.2 Relationship to quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A modular monolith has fewer independently failing services and fewer network hops than a microservice solution. It can be deployed as two application instances behind a load balancer, with health checks and a highly available database. Kiosk schedules will be cached locally by the kiosk and served from a schedule cache in CLRS. If a kiosk loses connectivity, it displays the last-known schedule and its last successful update time. This satisfies graceful degradation, although it does not make every dependency highly available automatically.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
The application can perform room availability searches using indexed reservation data and a denormalised availability/read table. The search adapter will avoid querying the legacy inventory database synchronously for every request. Inventory and iCal data will be synchronised into a local read model. Horizontal application instances and caching can support the 2,000-user semester-start load. A single process boundary also avoids unnecessary inter-service network latency.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
SAML authentication is implemented as an inbound adapter. The domain receives an authenticated user identity and roles rather than handling SAML details. Staff commands pass through an authorisation service and create an audit record. Structured logs will contain correlation IDs, operation names and non-sensitive identifiers, but no names, email addresses, SAML assertions or other PII.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific information such as campus ID, opening hours, rooms, equipment mappings, time zone and notification settings will be configuration data. The domain uses campus identifiers and policies rather than hard-coded library names. A new campus can therefore be onboarded by adding validated configuration and importing its room data. The design does not claim that all future changes require configuration only; a new business rule may still require code.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation domain will be a framework-independent core. It will accept entities, value objects and in-memory repositories through ports. Rule tests can execute without a database, network, SAML provider or notification service. This makes boundary cases such as time zones, recurring blocks, cancellation and the three-hour limit inexpensive to test thoroughly.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A single deployable is easier for a two-person team to understand, monitor and release than several independently deployed services. Immutable container images, automated database backups, backward-compatible migrations and blue-green or rolling deployment support rollback within ten minutes. The trade-off is that a defective deployment can affect all functions unless the previous application version is retained and quickly reinstated.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

**Method A — Layered monolith.**  
A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and could satisfy QR-1 and QR-6. However, conventional layers often allow the application and domain logic to become coupled to persistence or framework classes. That would make QR-5 weaker. It also provides less explicit control over external integrations. Hexagonal architecture keeps the same operational simplicity while enforcing dependency direction. The cost is additional interfaces, adapters and design discipline.

**Method B — Microservices.**  
Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting, and could isolate some failures. However, the first release does not yet justify the operational cost. Distributed reservation transactions, authentication, service discovery, monitoring, deployment and contract compatibility would increase complexity for a two-person team. Network failures could make QR-1 harder to achieve, and end-to-end testing would be more expensive. Microservices would give stronger independent scaling but sacrifice simplicity and fast rollback under QR-6.

**Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS.**  
CQRS and an event log would fit kiosk updates, audit history and high-volume search projections. It could improve scalability and provide strong traceability. However, it introduces eventual consistency, replay and projection-recovery concerns. A reservation may be accepted before a search or kiosk projection is updated, complicating the ten-second kiosk requirement and reservation conflict handling. Eventual consistency is not required for the first release. The proposed design may use reliable internal domain events and an outbox for notifications, but it is not event-driven CQRS as its primary architectural style.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. The user signs in through the SAML adapter. The adapter validates the assertion and creates an authenticated user context containing a stable university user ID and roles.
2. The HTTP adapter validates campus, capacity, equipment and time-window parameters.
3. The search application service queries the local inventory and availability ports. These ports are implemented by indexed PostgreSQL repositories and a cache adapter.
4. The availability query excludes overlapping student reservations, staff block bookings, unavailable opening hours, iCal conflicts and rooms that do not meet the requested capacity or equipment.
5. Results are returned through the HTTP adapter. The legacy database and iCal feeds are not called synchronously during normal search, preventing slow external dependencies from affecting QR-2.
6. Background synchronisation updates local inventory and calendar data. Failed synchronisation is exposed through metrics and alerts.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk schedule

1. When a reservation, cancellation, modification or block booking changes a room, the domain emits a reservation-changed event.
2. The application service updates the room’s kiosk schedule cache and writes an outbox entry in the same database transaction.
3. Kiosks poll `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` every five seconds, or use a push channel where supported. The response includes a version, update timestamp and current/next reservation.
4. The expected propagation time is under ten seconds: five seconds maximum polling delay plus processing and network time.
5. If the kiosk cannot contact CLRS, it displays its locally stored schedule, marks it as stale and retries with exponential backoff. The kiosk must not present stale data as current.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application services using in-memory ports or fakes. They will test:

- overlapping reservations and conflict responses;
- the three-hour daily limit;
- modifications and cancellations;
- recurring staff blocks;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- opening hours and time-zone boundaries;
- equipment and capacity rules;
- role-based authorisation decisions;
- event generation after successful changes.

Property-based or table-driven tests will cover combinations of reservation intervals, daylight-saving transitions, recurring bookings and multiple campuses. These tests satisfy QR-5 because no database or network is required.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will verify adapters against real or containerised dependencies:

- PostgreSQL schemas, indexes, constraints and transaction behaviour;
- uniqueness or exclusion constraints preventing double booking;
- cache invalidation and kiosk schedule persistence;
- SAML assertion mapping using representative test assertions;
- iCal parsing, time zones and malformed feeds;
- email and push provider clients;
- database migrations and rollback compatibility.

Concurrency tests will submit simultaneous reservations for the same room and verify that exactly one valid reservation succeeds.

#### Contract tests

Consumer/provider contracts will cover:

- HTTP request and response schemas;
- error codes such as `409 Conflict`, `401 Unauthorised` and `403 Forbidden`;
- kiosk schedule fields and version semantics;
- notification adapter payloads;
- SAML attribute and role mappings;
- imported iCal and inventory data formats.

These tests reduce the risk that an external system changes its format without detection.

#### End-to-end tests

A small critical-path suite will run in a staging environment:

1. authenticate through the test SAML provider;
2. search for a room;
3. create a reservation;
4. verify the reservation appears in search and on the kiosk endpoint;
5. modify and cancel the reservation;
6. create a staff block booking and verify the override workflow;
7. verify a reminder is queued.

End-to-end tests will not attempt to cover every rule; that responsibility belongs to unit tests. This keeps the suite reliable and fast.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

Load tests will model 2,000 concurrent users at semester start, with realistic search filters and a smaller proportion of write operations. The release gate is p95 search latency below 400 ms in the agreed test environment, with no unacceptable error-rate increase.

Resilience tests will disconnect the iCal service, notification provider, cache and one application instance. Search must continue using synchronised local data, notifications must retry through the outbox, and kiosks must display last-known schedules.

Security tests will include SAML signature validation, session expiry, privilege escalation attempts, audit completeness, injection tests and log inspection for PII.

### 4.2 Delivery

The team will use trunk-based development with short-lived branches and pull requests. Every pull request requires code review and passes:

- compilation and static analysis;
- unit and integration tests;
- contract tests;
- security and dependency scanning;
- migration validation;
- API compatibility checks.

The main branch automatically builds an immutable versioned container and deploys it to a disposable staging environment. Performance and end-to-end suites run before production approval.

Production deployment will use two application instances behind a load balancer. The database migration process must be backward-compatible: add new columns or tables first, deploy code that supports both versions, and remove obsolete structures only in a later release. This permits the previous application image to run during rollback.

A release is deployed to one instance first. Health checks, error rates, search latency and reservation-conflict behaviour are checked before completing the rollout. If checks fail, traffic is returned to the previous image. The previous image and configuration remain available, and deployment scripts are automated and rehearsed. A rollback drill must demonstrate completion within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests receive a correlation ID. Logs contain timestamp, severity, operation, campus ID, room ID where non-sensitive, response status, duration and correlation ID. User IDs are pseudonymised or omitted. Reservation content, email addresses, SAML assertions and other PII are not logged. Staff actions are written to a protected audit store containing actor identity, action, target, timestamp, result and reason.

Metrics include:

- successful and failed requests by endpoint;
- availability and health-check failures;
- search latency p50, p95 and p99;
- search error rate;
- database query latency and connection pool saturation;
- cache hit ratio;
- reservation conflict rate;
- outbox queue depth and notification delay;
- time from reservation change to kiosk schedule update;
- kiosk polling success rate and stale-schedule age;
- iCal and inventory synchronisation age and failure count.

Alerts include:

- calculated monthly availability trending below 99.5%;
- five-minute error rate above 1%;
- search p95 above 400 ms for ten minutes under normal load;
- database saturation above 80% for ten minutes;
- any kiosk schedule update taking more than ten seconds for more than 1% of changes;
- kiosk schedules stale for more than five minutes;
- outbox messages older than five minutes;
- inventory or iCal data older than the agreed freshness threshold.

A synthetic monitor will search for a configured test room during opening hours every minute. Availability reporting will exclude planned maintenance only if the product owner agrees how it is measured; otherwise all opening-hour downtime counts against QR-1.

# Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS)  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It supports students and staff across three campus libraries. Students can search for rooms and equipment, create or change reservations, and cancel them. Library staff can manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities iCal feeds and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release will expose HTTP APIs and a web interface, together with a kiosk API suitable for polling or push updates.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify the implementation of every feature. It establishes architectural boundaries, quality targets, testing, delivery, operational monitoring and risk mitigations that the Assignment 3 implementation team will follow.

The most important constraints are a 99.5% monthly availability target during opening hours, search latency below 400 ms at the semester-start load, SAML authentication, configurable onboarding of new libraries, database-independent reservation-rule tests, and deployment and rollback by a two-person team within ten minutes.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Selected style: Hexagonal architecture

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith with one deployable application. The reservation domain will be framework-independent and will communicate with the outside world through explicit ports. Infrastructure and user-interface technologies will be implemented as replaceable adapters.

The principal components are:

- **Domain core**: reservation entities, policies and business rules.
- **Application services**: use cases such as searching, creating reservations, cancelling reservations and creating block bookings.
- **Inbound adapters**: REST controllers, SAML authentication middleware and kiosk endpoints.
- **Outbound ports**: reservation repository, room-inventory gateway, facilities-calendar gateway, notification gateway, audit logger and event publisher.
- **Outbound adapters**: PostgreSQL repositories, iCal client, SAML integration, email/push provider and operational logging system.
- **Read/search adapter**: a denormalised availability index or cached query store used by the search use case.
- **Outbox worker**: reliably publishes reservation-change notifications and reminder jobs after a transaction commits.

Hexagonal architecture is selected because the most important business rules must remain independent of databases, networks and frameworks. The architecture also provides a relatively small operational footprint, which is appropriate for a two-person team.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A modular monolith avoids the additional network calls and independent failure modes that would exist between several microservices. It can be deployed as two interchangeable application instances behind a load balancer, allowing maintenance without taking the service offline. External dependencies are isolated behind adapters. For example, temporary unavailability of the iCal feed does not prevent users from viewing existing CLRS reservations. Kiosks retain the last successfully retrieved schedule locally and display its timestamp when disconnected.

The outbox prevents a notification or kiosk-update failure from causing the reservation transaction itself to fail. Health checks, database backups and a tested rollback procedure further support the 99.5% target.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
The search use case reads from a denormalised availability index rather than joining the legacy inventory database and repeatedly calling external systems. Appropriate indexes are created for campus, capacity, equipment and time interval. Search is stateless and can be scaled horizontally if required. The 2,000-user load test will measure p95 latency and identify whether additional replicas or caching are needed.

The domain remains the authority for reservation conflicts. A search result is only an indication of availability; the create-reservation command performs an authoritative transaction and returns `409 Conflict` if another reservation won the race.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is implemented at the inbound boundary using SAML. The application receives a validated identity and role/attribute set, then passes an authenticated actor context into application services. Authorisation is enforced in the application layer rather than only in the user interface. For example, only authorised staff can create block bookings or export reports.

Staff actions produce structured audit records containing actor identifier, action, target resource, result and timestamp. Normal application logs contain correlation IDs and technical data only; names, email addresses, SAML assertions and reservation notes containing PII are excluded or redacted.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Library-specific information is configuration, not code. Configuration contains campus and library identifiers, opening hours, room mappings, equipment metadata, calendar-feed URLs and kiosk settings. The same domain and application services process every campus. A new library can therefore be onboarded by validated configuration and data import. The inventory and iCal adapters translate source-specific formats into stable internal models.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The domain core depends on abstractions rather than PostgreSQL, SAML or HTTP. Reservation policies can be tested with in-memory objects and fake clocks. Tests can cover the three-hour daily limit, overlapping reservations, block-booking precedence and the 48-hour notice rule without a database or network. This is the primary reason for selecting hexagonal architecture.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A single deployable reduces the number of services, pipelines, dashboards and incidents that a two-person team must manage. The application will be packaged as an immutable container. Backward-compatible database migrations, automated smoke tests and a previous-image rollback make rollback within ten minutes realistic.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

**Method A — Layered monolith.**  
A layered monolith would be simpler to understand and deploy, and it could meet the initial scale. However, ordinary layering often allows domain code to become coupled to ORM entities, HTTP objects or framework services. That would make QR-5 weaker and make replacement of the legacy inventory database more difficult. Hexagonal architecture gives up some initial implementation simplicity and requires explicit ports, adapters and dependency-injection wiring.

**Method B — Microservices.**  
Microservices would allow reservation, notification, reporting and inventory workloads to scale independently. They could isolate failures and support separate team ownership. However, CLRS has only a two-person operational team. Multiple services would add service discovery, distributed tracing, deployment coordination, network failures, API-version management and more complex end-to-end testing. Reservation consistency across services would also be harder. Microservices could improve independent scalability, but they risk QR-1 and QR-6 for the first release. The chosen design keeps module boundaries sufficiently clear that a high-load module can be extracted later if evidence justifies it.

**Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS.**  
CQRS and an event log would naturally support kiosk updates, reporting projections and audit history. It could also improve read scalability for QR-2. Its disadvantages are eventual consistency, projection recovery, event-schema evolution and operational complexity. A kiosk could temporarily show an old schedule after a successful reservation, making the 10-second requirement more difficult to guarantee. The selected design uses a transactional outbox and targeted asynchronous updates, gaining much of the decoupling benefit without making every operation event-sourced or eventually consistent. The trade-off is less independent read scaling and less built-in historical reconstruction than full CQRS.

```text
                          |          |          |
                    +-----v--+  +----v-----+ +--v----------+
                    | CLRS DB |  | Read/    | | Outbox      |
                    |         |  | search   | | worker      |
                    |         |  | index    | +--+----------+
                    +---------+  +----------+    |
                                                +v---------+
                                                | Email/push|
                                                | kiosk     |
                                                | updates   |
                                                +----------+

External adapters:
  SAML identity provider
  Facilities iCal feeds
  Legacy PostgreSQL inventory database (read-only)
```

The CLRS database stores reservations, block bookings, configuration, audit references and outbox messages. The search index stores query-oriented room and availability data. It is rebuildable from authoritative data and is not the source of truth for conflict decisions.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: search available rooms

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&from=&to=` over HTTPS.
2. SAML middleware validates the authenticated session and creates an actor context.
3. The REST adapter validates query parameters, including time-zone and maximum search-window rules.
4. The application service queries the availability-query port.
5. The search adapter uses indexed room metadata and availability intervals from the read/search store. It does not call the legacy database synchronously.
6. Results are filtered by campus configuration, capacity, equipment, opening hours, facilities closures and existing reservations.
7. The response contains room identifiers and availability details, but no unnecessary personal data.
8. Search duration, result count, campus and success status are recorded as metrics and structured logs.

When a user subsequently creates a reservation, the command uses the reservation repository and a database transaction with a uniqueness/overlap protection strategy. Search results therefore do not create a race-condition guarantee.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A kiosk calls `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` using a kiosk credential limited to that room.
2. The kiosk API returns the current and next reservation plus a version or last-updated timestamp.
3. A reservation creation, modification, cancellation or block-booking change commits to the CLRS database and writes an outbox record in the same transaction.
4. The outbox worker publishes a room-specific update or invalidates the kiosk schedule cache.
5. Kiosks either receive a push notification or poll using the version/ETag. Polling at a suitable interval provides a fallback.
6. The target is that the changed schedule is available to the kiosk within ten seconds of the committed reservation change.
7. The kiosk stores the last-known schedule and displays it with an “offline/last updated” indicator if the network or CLRS is unavailable.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

**Domain unit tests.**  
These are fast, deterministic tests of the framework-independent core. They cover:

- no overlapping student reservations;
- the three-hour-per-day limit;
- create, modify and cancel rules;
- block bookings overriding student bookings only when the 48-hour notice rule is satisfied;
- opening-hours and closure rules;
- role-based authorisation decisions;
- time-zone and daylight-saving transitions;
- idempotency and duplicate-command handling.

A fake clock and in-memory repositories are injected through ports. These tests directly satisfy QR-5 because they require neither a database nor a network.

**Application-service unit tests.**  
Mocks or fakes verify orchestration: authentication context is required, the correct repository methods are called, transactions are committed, audit records are created for staff actions, and outbox messages are written for reservation changes. Failure paths, including notification failure after a successful reservation, are tested.

**Adapter and integration tests.**  
Containerised PostgreSQL tests verify schema, indexes, transaction isolation, overlap protection, migrations and report queries. Adapter tests verify the iCal parser, inventory mapping and SAML assertion handling against representative fixtures. The kiosk cache/outbox worker is tested with a real or containerised queue where applicable.

**Contract tests.**  
Contracts define REST request and response schemas, error codes, authentication requirements, kiosk schedule versions and report formats. Consumer-driven or schema-based tests verify that the web client and kiosks remain compatible with the API. External-provider contracts cover the expected SAML attributes, iCal format and notification-provider responses. These tests are particularly important because the hexagonal adapters isolate external systems but cannot control their future changes.

**End-to-end tests.**  
A staging environment uses a SAML test identity provider and representative inventory/calendar data. Critical journeys include:

- student signs in, searches, reserves and cancels a room;
- two users attempt the same room simultaneously and only one succeeds;
- staff creates a block booking and affected reservations are handled correctly;
- a reservation change reaches a kiosk within ten seconds;
- a reminder is scheduled and delivered;
- staff exports a monthly utilisation report.

E2E tests remain focused on critical workflows rather than duplicating the large domain-unit suite.

**Performance and resilience tests.**  
A realistic dataset and 2,000 concurrent virtual users will exercise availability search. CI or pre-release testing must demonstrate p95 below 400 ms, with separate measurements for cache hit and miss. Failure tests stop the iCal service, notification provider and search index temporarily to verify graceful degradation, retries and outbox recovery. A kiosk network-disconnection test verifies last-known schedule behaviour.

**Security and privacy tests.**  
Tests verify SAML signature validation, expired-session rejection, role enforcement, CSRF protection where relevant, input validation, rate limiting and absence of PII in application logs. Dependency and container scans run in CI.

### 4.2 Delivery and rollback

Development uses short-lived branches merged into `main` through pull requests. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer where practical and must pass:

- compilation and static analysis;
- formatting and linting;
- domain and application unit tests;
- adapter/integration tests;
- API contract tests;
- dependency, secret and container scans;
- migration validation;
- minimum coverage thresholds for domain rules.

A successful merge builds and tags an immutable container. Deployment proceeds automatically to a development environment, then manually to staging and production after smoke tests and approval. Database changes use expand-and-contract migrations: add compatible structures first, deploy code that supports both versions, migrate data, then remove obsolete structures in a later release.

Production uses two application instances behind a load balancer. A rolling or blue-green deployment keeps the previous version available. Health checks include database connectivity, ability to read configuration and outbox-worker health. A deployment is halted if smoke tests fail, error rate increases, or latency breaches the release threshold.

Rollback consists of selecting the previous container image and reversing traffic. Database migrations are designed to remain compatible with the previous application version; destructive rollback migrations are avoided. A rehearsed runbook, automated image selection and pre-tested database backup support the QR-6 requirement of rollback within ten minutes. Rollbacks are practised in staging at least once per release cycle.

### 4.3 Observability

**Logs**

Structured logs contain timestamp, severity, service version, correlation ID, route, campus identifier, room identifier where operationally necessary, status code, duration and error category. Audit logs contain actor ID, role, staff action, target, outcome and timestamp in a restricted store. User names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens and free-text personal details are never written to normal logs. Identifiers are hashed or tokenised where possible.

**Metrics for QR-1**

- successful request rate and availability by route;
- HTTP 5xx, timeout and dependency-failure rates;
- database connection-pool exhaustion;
- outbox backlog age and failed-delivery count;
- iCal and inventory adapter success rates;
- kiosk heartbeat and percentage of kiosks with schedules updated within ten seconds;
- kiosk offline count and age of last-known schedule;
- deployment and restart events.

Alert thresholds include a projected monthly availability below 99.5%, sustained 5xx rate above 1% for five minutes, any outbox item older than two minutes, or more than 5% of kiosks missing the ten-second update target for ten minutes. Kiosk dashboards explicitly distinguish “current” from “last-known” data.

**Metrics for QR-2**

- request count and latency percentiles, especially p50, p95 and p99;
- availability-search latency by campus, query type and cache status;
- concurrent requests;
- database query duration and slow-query count;
- search-index hit/miss rate;
- CPU, memory and garbage-collection pressure.

An alert fires if availability-search p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal operating load, or if p99 and resource saturation indicate imminent degradation. Synthetic searches from each campus run continuously and are included in the availability dashboard.

Tracing across the REST adapter, application service, search adapter, database and outbox worker allows an incident to be diagnosed without exposing PII.

## Assignment 2 — Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing room-reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three campus libraries. Students will search for rooms, create or modify reservations, cancel reservations and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems: the university identity provider through SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds and the read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release is not required to replace these systems; it must provide reliable adapters around them.

This document selects an architectural style for the first release and defines the structure, testing, delivery, observability and risk-management plans. The design prioritises reliable reservation rules, simple operation by a two-person team and the ability to add libraries through configuration. The design covers FR-1 to FR-6 and QR-1 to QR-6. It does not specify detailed user-interface designs, the final email/push provider or the physical kiosk hardware.

The recommended architecture is a **hexagonal architecture implemented as a modular monolith**. This combines a framework-independent reservation domain with explicit ports and adapters, while keeping the first release as one deployable application.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, with a modular monolith as its initial deployment unit.

The system will contain:

- A framework-independent domain core containing reservation rules.
- Application services that coordinate use cases.
- Inbound adapters for HTTP APIs, kiosk requests and scheduled jobs.
- Outbound ports for persistence, SAML authentication, iCal synchronisation, notifications and reporting.
- Replaceable adapters implementing those ports.
- A relational database for authoritative reservation data.
- A cache/read store for high-volume availability and kiosk queries where necessary.

The use of a modular monolith is intentional. The architecture provides strong internal boundaries without introducing the operational cost of multiple independently deployed services.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A single deployable application is easier for a two-person team to operate than multiple services. It can be deployed with at least two application instances behind a load balancer, while the database is backed up and monitored. The kiosk adapter stores the last successful schedule locally on the kiosk. If the API or network is temporarily unavailable, the kiosk displays the cached schedule with its last-updated time rather than showing an empty or misleading screen.

The hexagonal boundary also prevents failures in external systems from directly contaminating the reservation domain. For example, a temporary iCal failure can be handled by an adapter with retries and a stale-data status, rather than making the entire application unavailable.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability searching is exposed through an application port and can use a specifically indexed availability query or a materialised availability cache. The read path does not need to call SAML, iCal or the legacy inventory database on every request. Room metadata can be synchronised into a local store, and reservation queries can be indexed by room and time interval. This supports a target of p95 below 400 ms under 2,000 concurrent users.

The design separates the read-heavy search path from write operations internally, without adopting full CQRS as the primary architecture. This provides an appropriate performance optimisation while retaining a simpler consistency model for reservations.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
SAML is implemented as an outbound identity-provider adapter. The application core receives an authenticated user identity and roles through an internal authentication port; it does not depend on SAML libraries or HTTP session details. Staff-only use cases enforce authorisation in the application layer, not merely in the user interface.

Audit logging is a separate port so staff actions can be recorded consistently. Log events contain an internal user or actor identifier, action type, target entity identifier and result, but not names, email addresses or other PII. Sensitive values are excluded through structured logging rules and automated log scanning.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Libraries, opening hours, room attributes, equipment and external-system identifiers are represented as configuration and data rather than hard-coded branches. Adding a library should involve creating campus and room records, configuring its calendar feed and setting opening hours. The adapters use stable ports, so a new calendar source or notification provider can be added without changing reservation rules.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation domain is framework-independent and uses injected abstractions such as `ReservationRepository`, `Clock` and `AvailabilityQuery`. It can therefore be tested entirely in memory, without a database, network, SAML provider or notification service. Rules such as the three-hour daily limit, overlapping reservations, cancellation and block-booking precedence can be tested as deterministic unit tests.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
The first release has one application artifact and a small number of managed dependencies. This reduces deployment coordination and makes rollback practical. Immutable container images, automated database migration checks and a previous-image deployment strategy will allow rollback within ten minutes. A two-person team can operate the system using documented runbooks and standard health checks.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and would have low operational overhead. It would also be suitable for QR-6 and could meet QR-2 with suitable database indexes.

It was rejected as the primary style because conventional layered designs often allow the application and domain layers to depend directly on frameworks, database models and external clients. That would weaken QR-5 and make integration replacement more difficult. It could also make QR-4 harder to maintain if campus-specific behaviour became embedded in controllers or persistence code. The selected hexagonal architecture retains the deployment simplicity of a monolith while providing stronger dependency boundaries.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale the reservation, inventory, notification and reporting workloads. This might help search performance and isolate failures. It would also allow separate teams to deploy components independently.

However, the project has only a two-person operations team. Microservices introduce service discovery, API versioning, distributed tracing, multiple deployment pipelines, inter-service authentication and more complicated rollback procedures. Reservation consistency across services would be harder to guarantee, especially for conflict detection and block-booking overrides. These costs threaten QR-6 and may reduce QR-1. The first release does not have enough organisational or operational scale to justify the split. The hexagonal modules leave open the possibility of extracting a service later if measurements show that it is needed.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

Event-driven CQRS would be attractive for kiosk refreshes, notifications, reporting and high-volume search. Reservation changes could publish events to update read models, and kiosks could receive near-real-time updates.

The disadvantages are eventual consistency, event schema/version management, replay and projection recovery, message delivery guarantees and additional infrastructure. A search result or kiosk could temporarily disagree with the authoritative reservation state. This is particularly risky for reservation conflict handling. Event-driven processing would also increase operational burden and threaten QR-6. The selected architecture may publish domain events asynchronously for notifications and cache invalidation, but the reservation write remains transactionally authoritative in the database.

### 3.2 Main structural decisions

The domain core does not import web, database, SAML or notification libraries. Application services use ports to request persistence and external operations. Adapters translate external formats into internal models.

The authoritative reservation database uses transaction isolation and a database-level non-overlap constraint or equivalent transaction-safe conflict check. This prevents two concurrent requests from successfully reserving the same room. Reservation writes also produce an internal `ReservationChanged` event after commit. The event is used for cache invalidation, kiosk refresh and notification scheduling; it is not the source of truth.

Campus and room data include:

- Campus identifier and display name.
- Opening hours and holiday exceptions.
- Room capacity and equipment.
- External inventory and calendar identifiers.
- Kiosk identifier and configuration.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search available rooms

1. The client sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=`.
2. The REST adapter validates the request format and forwards a search command to the application service.
3. The application service queries local room and availability ports.
4. The room adapter uses synchronised inventory data. The availability adapter queries indexed reservations and block bookings.
5. The application service applies opening hours, room attributes, time-window overlap and booking status rules.
6. Results are returned to the client, including room details and any relevant availability information.

The request does not synchronously call the SAML provider, iCal feeds or legacy inventory database. Authentication is validated using the application’s SAML session/token adapter, while synchronisation jobs update local data in advance. This supports QR-2 and avoids external-system latency.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. When a reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden, the transaction commits an internal `ReservationChanged` event containing the room identifier and version.
2. A cache invalidation handler refreshes that room’s schedule.
3. Kiosks use either server-sent events or polling with an `ETag`/schedule version. A changed version causes the kiosk to download the latest schedule.
4. The target is for the event, cache refresh and kiosk response to complete within ten seconds.
5. The kiosk stores the last valid schedule locally. During network failure it displays that schedule with an “updated at” timestamp and an offline indicator.
6. On reconnection, the kiosk requests the current version and replaces its cache.

The API may expose `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` with a schedule version and `lastUpdated` field. A kiosk should never interpret a missing response as an empty schedule.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Domain unit tests

The largest test suite will target the framework-independent domain core. Tests will use fake repositories and a fixed clock. They will cover:

- Reservations cannot overlap for the same room.
- A user cannot exceed three reserved hours per day.
- Create, modify and cancel behaviour.
- Opening-hours and holiday restrictions.
- Recurring block-booking expansion.
- Staff block bookings override student bookings only according to the 48-hour notice rule.
- Authorisation rules for student and staff actions.
- Boundary cases involving midnight, daylight-saving changes and inclusive/exclusive end times.

These tests satisfy QR-5 because they require neither a database nor a network. Property-based or parameterised tests will be used for time-window and overlap combinations.

#### Application-service tests

Application tests will use fake implementations of ports. They will verify orchestration, including:

- Correct repository calls.
- Transaction boundaries.
- Audit events for staff operations.
- Notification scheduling after successful commits.
- Cache invalidation after reservation changes.
- Idempotency for retries.
- Appropriate conflict responses, such as HTTP 409.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Database integration tests will run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance. They will verify:

- Schema constraints and indexes.
- Concurrent reservation conflict handling.
- Transaction rollback.
- Reservation queries and report aggregation.
- Database migration forwards and backwards where supported.
- Correct mapping to the read-only legacy inventory database.

External adapters will be tested against controlled SAML, iCal and notification-provider stubs. Failure, timeout, malformed-feed and retry behaviour will be included.

#### Contract tests

Consumer/provider contracts will cover:

- REST request and response schemas.
- Error formats and status codes.
- Kiosk schedule versions and caching headers.
- SAML claim and role mapping.
- iCal parsing assumptions.
- Notification-provider requests.

Contract tests reduce the risk that the CLRS adapter and an external service change incompatibly.

#### End-to-end tests

A small, stable E2E suite will run in a staging environment. It will cover:

1. Student SAML login.
2. Search for a room.
3. Create a reservation.
4. Verify the reservation appears in the kiosk schedule.
5. Modify and cancel the reservation.
6. Staff create a block booking and verify the required override behaviour.
7. Generate a monthly report.
8. Simulate a kiosk disconnection and verify last-known schedule behaviour.

Performance tests will simulate 2,000 concurrent users, with realistic search distributions and reservation writes. The release gate is search p95 below 400 ms and no unacceptable error increase.

#### Security and resilience tests

Security testing will include dependency scanning, static analysis, authentication/authorisation tests, log-PII scanning, session-expiry tests and API rate-limit tests. Resilience tests will inject failures into iCal, SAML, PostgreSQL, the notification provider and the cache. The expected outcome is graceful degradation rather than cascading failure.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use short-lived feature branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires code review by the other team member unless an emergency procedure is documented.

Continuous integration gates are:

- Formatting and linting.
- Static type/code analysis.
- Domain and application unit tests.
- Database integration tests.
- Adapter and contract tests.
- Dependency and container vulnerability scanning.
- Log-PII scanning.
- Build of an immutable versioned container image.

A staging deployment runs smoke, E2E and representative load tests. Production deployment requires both team members’ approval during the initial release and a verified database backup.

The deployment process is:

1. Build and sign an immutable image.
2. Apply backward-compatible database migrations.
3. Deploy the new image beside the old version.
4. Run health checks and smoke tests.
5. Shift traffic gradually.
6. Monitor error rate, latency, database health and kiosk update delay.
7. Complete the rollout if metrics remain within thresholds.

Rollback uses the previous image and traffic switch. Database changes must be backward compatible so that the old application version can continue to run during rollback. A documented rollback runbook and rehearsal must demonstrate completion within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6.

Feature flags will be used for risky functionality such as kiosk push updates and a new availability cache. This allows functionality to be disabled without redeploying.

### 4.3 Observability

All application logs will be structured and correlated using a request or trace identifier. Logs will contain timestamp, severity, component, operation, result, duration, campus identifier where appropriate and an internal entity identifier. They will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions or other PII.

Metrics include:

**For QR-1:**

- Successful request rate by endpoint and campus.
- HTTP 5xx rate and timeout rate.
- Application instance health.
- Database connection pool saturation.
- Database availability and backup success.
- iCal synchronisation success, age and failure count.
- Kiosk connection status.
- Age of each kiosk’s last successful schedule.
- Percentage of reservation changes reflected on kiosks within ten seconds.
- Number of kiosks displaying stale schedules.

Alerts will fire if monthly availability projection falls below 99.5%, if the rolling five-minute 5xx rate exceeds 2%, if a critical dependency is unavailable for five minutes or if more than 1% of kiosk updates exceed ten seconds. A kiosk alert will distinguish a single offline kiosk from a campus-wide failure.

**For QR-2:**

- Search request count and error rate.
- Search p50, p95 and p99 latency.
- Database query latency by query type.
- Cache hit ratio.
- CPU, memory and connection-pool utilisation.
- Concurrent request count.
- Slow-query count.

The main performance alert is search p95 above 400 ms for five consecutive minutes at representative load. Capacity warnings will occur when CPU or database connections exceed 70% for ten minutes, allowing scaling or query optimisation before failure.

Dashboards will show availability and performance by campus, endpoint and dependency. Synthetic probes will periodically perform a search and kiosk schedule request from outside the production network.

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s existing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosk displays outside rooms will show current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities iCal feeds and the read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release will provide the reservation, availability, kiosk, notification and reporting capabilities described in FR-1 to FR-6.

The design prioritises reliable reservation rules, simple deployment by a two-person team, integration isolation, and a clear path for future campus expansion. The proposed solution is a modular monolith using hexagonal architecture. It will be delivered as one deployable application with replaceable adapters for external systems. Asynchronous processing will be used for notifications, kiosk updates and selected synchronisation tasks, but the primary architectural style remains hexagonal architecture.

The design covers the application structure, quality plan, delivery approach, observability, risks and questions requiring product-owner decisions. It does not cover detailed user-interface design, infrastructure procurement or implementation code.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a **modular monolith**.

The central domain and application services will be independent of web frameworks, databases and external services. Communication with the core will occur through explicit inbound and outbound ports. Adapters will implement those ports for HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email/push providers and kiosk clients.

The application will use one deployable unit and one authoritative reservation database. An outbox table will support reliable asynchronous delivery of domain events such as `ReservationChanged` and `ReminderDue`. This provides some event-driven behaviour without making event-driven CQRS the primary style.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation rules will be implemented in framework-independent domain services. Rules such as:

- no overlapping reservations;
- a maximum of three hours per user per day;
- staff block-booking precedence;
- the 48-hour notice rule; and
- opening-hour restrictions

will receive plain domain objects and return domain results. They will not directly access PostgreSQL, SAML or a network service. Fake repositories and clocks can be supplied through ports. Consequently, the most important business rules can be tested quickly with unit tests and without a database or network.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
SAML authentication will be isolated behind an identity adapter. The HTTP adapter will convert a validated SAML identity into an internal user identity and role. Authorisation remains an application-level concern, so every use case can enforce rules consistently rather than relying only on controller checks. Staff operations will call an audit port. Audit records will contain user ID, role, action, target and timestamp, but not unnecessary personal information. Logging interfaces will use structured redaction to prevent PII from entering application logs.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific information will be represented as configuration: campus identifier, opening hours, room mappings, equipment, time zone, iCal source and kiosk associations. A new campus should therefore require configuration and data migration only. The domain will use campus and room identifiers rather than hard-coded library names. External systems are accessed through ports, so a future inventory API could replace the PostgreSQL adapter without changing reservation rules.

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A single deployable modular monolith is operationally simpler than multiple independently deployed services. It can be run with two application instances behind a load balancer, allowing rolling deployments and continued service if one instance fails. The reservation database will be backed up and monitored. Kiosks will cache the most recent valid schedule locally and display its timestamp and an “offline” status when the server cannot be reached. This satisfies graceful degradation rather than making kiosk availability depend entirely on a live network connection.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability search is separated from the write path through a search application service and suitable database indexes on campus, capacity, equipment and reservation time ranges. Frequently requested room and configuration data can be cached. Because the system is initially one deployable unit, there is no mandatory API-gateway or inter-service network overhead for a search request. Load testing will validate the p95 target of under 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A modular monolith requires fewer deployment pipelines, dashboards and failure modes than a collection of services. Container images will be versioned and deployed using a rolling or blue-green process. The previous image can be restored quickly, with backward-compatible database migrations, to meet the ten-minute rollback requirement. This is appropriate for a two-person operational team.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would also be simple to deploy and could meet QR-1, QR-2 and QR-6. However, conventional layers often allow application code to depend directly on frameworks or persistence classes. That makes external integration and isolated domain testing less reliable. It also increases the risk that campus-specific logic becomes scattered through controllers and database code, weakening QR-4.

Hexagonal architecture gives up some initial simplicity: developers must define ports, adapters and domain boundaries. The benefit is stronger testability, clearer integration isolation and easier replacement of external systems.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. A separate notification service could also isolate failures. However, for a two-person team, several services would increase deployment, monitoring, security and debugging costs. Distributed reservation transactions could make conflict prevention and consistency more difficult. Network calls between services would also add latency to availability search and introduce more failure modes, threatening QR-1 and QR-2.

Microservices would provide stronger independent scaling and team autonomy, but those benefits are not justified by the first-release scope. The modular monolith gives up independent service deployment and per-service scaling. If a future workload justifies decomposition, the hexagonal ports provide seams for extracting modules later.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and event projections would be attractive for FR-4 because reservation changes could update kiosk and search read models asynchronously. It could also scale read-heavy searches. However, eventual consistency creates a difficult question for reservation availability: a stale projection must never allow two users to reserve the same room. The system would still require an authoritative transactional command store. Event replay, projection repair, schema evolution and event-log operations would increase complexity and operational burden.

The proposed design gives up the potentially high read scalability and replay capabilities of CQRS. Instead, it uses indexed transactional queries, caching and an outbox for targeted asynchronous updates. This is simpler while still allowing kiosk updates within ten seconds.

### 3.2 Walkthrough: FR-1 availability search

1. The client sends `GET /rooms?campus=...&capacity=...&equipment=...&from=...&to=...`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates the query, obtains the authenticated user context and invokes the `SearchAvailability` use case.
3. The use case obtains room and equipment data through the `RoomCatalog` port and reservation data through the `ReservationRepository` port.
4. The domain’s availability policy excludes rooms that:
   - do not match the campus, capacity or equipment;
   - are outside opening hours;
   - overlap an existing student or staff booking; or
   - are unavailable according to the facilities calendar.
5. The repository uses indexed queries and bounded time windows. Room metadata and campus configuration may be served from a short-lived cache.
6. The adapter maps the result to a response containing room ID, campus, capacity, equipment and available intervals.

Search is read-only and does not hold a reservation lock. The create-reservation use case performs an authoritative transactional conflict check again, preventing a race between search and booking.

### 3.3 Walkthrough: FR-4 kiosk refresh

1. A successful reservation creation, modification, cancellation or block-booking operation commits its transaction.
2. The transaction writes a `ReservationChanged` record to the outbox in the same database transaction as the reservation change.
3. An outbox worker publishes the room ID and a monotonically increasing schedule version to the kiosk update channel.
4. Connected kiosks receive the update through server-sent events, or poll `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` using the version/ETag.
5. The kiosk retrieves the current and next reservation and stores it locally as the last-known schedule.
6. The target kiosk refreshes within ten seconds. If the network or server is unavailable, it continues displaying the cached schedule, its retrieval timestamp and an offline indicator.

The outbox prevents a committed reservation change from being lost merely because the notification channel was temporarily unavailable. Updates are idempotent using room ID and schedule version.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application services using fake ports. Important cases include:

- overlapping and adjacent reservations;
- the three-hour daily user limit;
- create, modify and cancel permissions;
- recurring block bookings;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- opening hours and time zones;
- facilities-calendar conflicts;
- invalid campus or room configuration; and
- idempotent processing of repeated commands.

These tests directly satisfy QR-5 because they run without a database or network. Property-based tests will generate random booking intervals to test invariants such as “two confirmed bookings cannot overlap the same room.”

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests will run against containerised PostgreSQL and test:

- transaction boundaries and unique/exclusion constraints;
- reservation conflict handling under concurrent requests;
- indexes and query plans for availability search;
- outbox insertion and retry behaviour;
- database migrations and rollback compatibility;
- iCal parsing and time-zone conversion; and
- SAML metadata and assertion mapping using a test identity provider.

The legacy inventory database will be accessed through a read-only test account. Failures and malformed feeds will be tested explicitly.

#### Contract tests

Consumer/provider contracts will cover:

- HTTP request and response schemas;
- error responses, including `409 Conflict`;
- kiosk polling or SSE payloads;
- notification provider requests; and
- identity adapter assumptions.

The API contract will be versioned. Contract tests ensure that an adapter change does not silently break kiosk clients or external providers.

#### End-to-end tests

A small set of automated end-to-end tests will run in a staging environment:

1. authenticate through the test SAML provider;
2. search for a room;
3. create a reservation;
4. verify the kiosk schedule changes;
5. modify and cancel the reservation; and
6. create a staff block booking and verify its precedence and audit record.

A reminder test will use a controllable clock or test scheduler rather than waiting fifteen minutes.

#### Performance and resilience tests

A representative dataset will be used for load testing at 2,000 concurrent users. The release gate is availability-search p95 below 400 ms, with error rate below 1% during the test. Tests will include cache-disabled and realistic cache-enabled conditions.

Failure injection will test database unavailability, delayed iCal feeds, notification-provider failure, lost kiosk connections and worker restarts. The expected result is that committed reservations remain correct, notifications retry, and kiosks show their last-known schedule.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development will use short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer, except for an explicitly documented emergency fix.

Continuous integration gates will include:

- compilation and static analysis;
- unit and domain invariant tests;
- integration tests with PostgreSQL;
- contract tests;
- migration validation;
- dependency and container vulnerability scanning;
- API specification validation; and
- test coverage for changed domain code.

A merge is blocked if any gate fails. Main-branch builds produce an immutable container image and deploy automatically to a non-production environment.

Production deployment will use a rolling or blue-green strategy:

1. run database migrations that are backward-compatible with both old and new application versions;
2. deploy the new image to a small percentage of instances;
3. run smoke tests and compare error, latency and reservation-conflict metrics;
4. complete the rollout if the health checks pass; and
5. retain the previous image and configuration for immediate rollback.

Rollback is performed by redeploying the previous image. Destructive schema changes are deferred until a later release after the old code is no longer needed. A documented runbook and one-command deployment script allow a two-person team to roll back within ten minutes. Database backups and restore drills are performed before major releases.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests receive a correlation ID. Logs are structured and include timestamp, component, operation, status, duration, campus ID, room ID where appropriate and correlation ID. Logs must not include names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens or reservation descriptions. User identifiers in operational logs are replaced by non-reversible or approved pseudonymous IDs. Staff audit records are stored separately with controlled access.

Metrics include:

- application availability during configured opening hours;
- HTTP error rate by endpoint;
- search latency p50, p95 and p99;
- concurrent request count;
- database connection-pool utilisation;
- slow-query count;
- reservation conflict rate;
- outbox age and retry count;
- kiosk update propagation latency;
- number of kiosks offline and age of their last successful refresh;
- SAML authentication failures;
- notification delivery and failure rates; and
- CPU, memory and container restarts.

Alerts include:

- monthly projected availability below 99.5%;
- search p95 above 400 ms for five consecutive minutes under normal load;
- HTTP 5xx rate above 2% for five minutes;
- outbox oldest message older than 30 seconds;
- more than 1% of kiosks not refreshed for two minutes;
- any kiosk update exceeding ten seconds at the 95th percentile; and
- failed backups or database replication health checks.

A dashboard will show QR-1 and QR-2 directly, rather than relying only on infrastructure health. Synthetic probes will periodically authenticate in a test account, search availability and check a test kiosk endpoint.

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, cancel reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems: the university identity provider through SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release covers the functional requirements FR-1 to FR-6 and the quality requirements QR-1 to QR-6.

The proposed system prioritises correctness of reservation rules, dependable operation during semester-start demand, simple deployment by a two-person team, and isolation from unreliable external systems. The design must also allow a new library to be added through configuration rather than code changes.

The selected architecture is **Method C: Hexagonal Architecture**, implemented as a modular monolith. The domain and application logic will be independent of web frameworks, databases, authentication providers and notification services. External systems will be accessed through explicit ports and adapters. This provides strong unit testability while retaining the operational simplicity of one deployable application.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use a **hexagonal architecture with a framework-independent domain core**. The first release will be deployed as one application with separate internal modules for reservations, room availability, staff administration, kiosks, notifications and reporting.

The architecture has three conceptual areas:

1. **Domain core**  
   Contains reservation entities, room rules, booking conflicts, daily limits, recurring block-booking rules and domain events. It has no dependency on HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL or a particular notification provider.

2. **Application services**  
   Coordinate use cases such as searching rooms, creating reservations, modifying reservations, cancelling reservations, creating block bookings and generating reports. They depend on interfaces, or ports, rather than concrete infrastructure.

3. **Adapters**  
   Translate external protocols into application calls and application results into external protocols. Examples include the HTTP API, SAML adapter, PostgreSQL adapter, iCal importer, email/push adapter and kiosk adapter.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A single deployable application is easier for a two-person team to operate than several independently deployed services. It can use multiple application instances behind a load balancer and a highly available database. External integrations are isolated behind adapters, so a failure in iCal synchronisation or notifications does not prevent reservations. Kiosks cache their last successful schedule locally and display it with an “offline/last updated” indicator when the CLRS API cannot be reached.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability searches will use a local, indexed availability representation rather than querying the legacy inventory system on every request. Room metadata imported from PostgreSQL and calendar data from iCal will be cached in the CLRS database. Indexes will cover campus, capacity, equipment and time ranges. The application can scale horizontally because requests are stateless apart from the database and cache. A performance test will verify p95 search latency below 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is represented by an inbound `IdentityProvider` port. The SAML adapter validates assertions and maps them to an internal user identity and role. The domain never handles SAML details. Staff operations pass through an audit port, which writes an immutable audit record containing the actor, action, target, timestamp and outcome. Application logging uses user and reservation surrogate IDs rather than names, email addresses or SAML assertions, ensuring that PII is not written to logs.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific information will be represented as configuration: campus identifier, opening hours, timezone, room source, feature mappings and kiosk settings. Room and equipment metadata are data, not conditional code. The application services operate against generic campus and room ports. Therefore, onboarding a fourth library should involve configuration and data loading only.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation rules are implemented in the domain core using in-memory values and interfaces. For example, the three-hour daily limit and overlap rules can be tested by passing a user, requested time interval and existing reservations to a domain service. No database, SAML provider or network connection is required. Hexagonal boundaries also permit fake clock, fake reservation repository and fake notification ports in tests.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
The system will initially have one deployable artifact and one primary database, reducing operational overhead. Container images will be immutable and deployments will be automated. A previous image remains available for rapid rollback. Backward-compatible database migrations and blue/green or rolling deployment support rollback within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would also be simple to deploy and could satisfy QR-1, QR-2 and QR-6. However, conventional layered systems often allow application code to depend directly on framework and persistence classes. Over time, this makes reservation rules difficult to test without a database, weakening QR-5. It can also make external-system failures leak into core logic. Hexagonal architecture adds interfaces and adapter discipline to avoid this coupling.

The cost of the selected approach is additional design overhead: ports, adapters and dependency-injection configuration require more code than a straightforward layered implementation.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They would provide stronger fault and deployment isolation if CLRS became very large. However, they would introduce multiple repositories, services, deployment pipelines, network calls, monitoring systems and possibly distributed transactions. This conflicts with QR-6 because a two-person team would need to operate more infrastructure. Reservation consistency would also be harder to guarantee across service boundaries. The first release does not justify that complexity.

The selected design gives up independent service scaling and independent release schedules. Internal module boundaries preserve a future extraction path if later demand requires it.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and event sourcing could provide excellent kiosk and search read performance, replayable history and natural asynchronous notifications. It would also support high write/read separation. However, it introduces eventual consistency: a search result or kiosk could temporarily lag behind a reservation command. That complicates FR-2 conflict handling and the ten-second kiosk requirement. Event schemas, projections, replay operations and an event-log platform would add significant operational and testing complexity.

The selected architecture may use small internal domain events, such as `ReservationChanged`, for notification and kiosk invalidation, but it will not make the whole system event-sourced or CQRS-based. This retains synchronous reservation correctness while allowing asynchronous side effects.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: search available rooms

1. A user sends `GET /rooms?campus=L1&capacity=4&equipment=display&from=...&to=...`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates syntax, obtains the authenticated internal user identity and invokes `SearchAvailableRooms`.
3. The use case asks the room catalogue and availability ports for matching rooms.
4. The PostgreSQL and iCal adapters have already imported room metadata, opening hours and external calendar exclusions into the local database.
5. The search repository uses indexed campus, capacity, equipment and time-range data. It excludes student reservations, staff block bookings, closures and external calendar conflicts.
6. Results are returned without exposing internal database details.

Search is read-only and can use a short-lived cache. Cache invalidation occurs when a reservation changes or synchronisation imports new calendar data. The reservation creation operation still performs an authoritative conflict check in a database transaction, preventing two users from successfully reserving the same interval.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk schedule refresh

1. A kiosk authenticates using a kiosk-specific credential and requests `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule`.
2. The kiosk stores the complete response and its timestamp locally.
3. When a reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden by a block booking, the domain emits `ReservationChanged`.
4. An application event handler invalidates the room schedule cache and sends a lightweight update notification to the affected kiosk, using server-sent events or polling as a fallback.
5. The kiosk retrieves the new schedule. The service records the change time and the kiosk acknowledgement time.
6. The target is that the updated schedule is visible within ten seconds. If the network or server is unavailable, the kiosk continues displaying its last-known schedule and clearly shows its last refresh time. It does not claim that the cached schedule is current.
